e: From wipe + -ette.

s: To revoke (a former command); to cancel or rescind by giving an order contrary to one previously given.
To recall a person or unit with such an order.
To cancel an order for (some specified goods).
To counteract, to act against, to frustrate.
To prohibit (a course of action or behavior).
To oppose or revoke the command of (someone).
To maintain control of, to keep under command.
An order to the contrary of a previous one.
e: From Old French contremander, from Medieval Latin contramandō, from contra + mandō (“to order; to command”).

s: Gerund of splutter: the act of one who splutters.
e: From splutter + -ing.
From Middle English supernaturaly; equivalent to supernatural + -ly.

s: One who complains, or is known for their complaints.
A complainant (an alleged victim in a criminal trial).
e: From complain + -er.

s: A jangle, the sounds of a jangle.
Of French fries or potato crisps: given a crinkled or ridged texture.

e: From ludicrous + -ly.

s: The sound produced by anything that creaks; a creaking.
To make a prolonged sharp grating or squeaking sound, as by the friction of hard substances.
To produce a creaking sound with.
To suffer from strain or old age.
e: From Middle English creken, criken, metathesis of Old English cearcian (“to chatter, creak, crash, gnash”), from Proto-West Germanic *krakōn (“to crash, crack, creak”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to make a sound, cry hoarsely”), ultimately of Onomatopoeic origin. Compare also Old English crǣccettan, crācettan (“to croak”), Albanian grykë (“throat”).

s: A minced oath of "fucking" as an intensifier.
To attract and delight, to charm.
To cast a spell upon (often one that attracts or charms).
To magically enhance or degrade an item.
e: From Middle English enchaunten, from Old French enchanter, from Latin incantāre. Doublet of incant.

s: Small forms of finger food or snacks such as nuts or potato chips (crisps), often eaten as an accompaniment to drinks.
e: From nibble + -s.

s: Having down, covered with a soft fuzzy coating as of small feathers or hair.
A blanket filled with down; a duvet.
e: From down + -y.

s: Agitation; the state of being perturbed.
A small change in a physical system, or more broadly any definable system (such as a biological or economic system).
Variation in an orbit due to the influence of external bodies.
e: Borrowed from Middle French perturbation, from Old French perturbacion, from Latin perturbatio.

s: Of, relating to, or characteristic of putrefaction; especially, having a bad smell, like that of rotting flesh.
e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French putride or directly from Latin putridus (“rotten, decayed”), from putreō (“to be rotten or putrid”), from puter (“rotten, decaying, putrid”).
From Middle English loveles; equivalent to love + -less.

s: An organism showing abnormal development or deformity.
A monstrous person, thing, or act.
e: From Middle English monstruosite, from Middle French monstruosité and its etymon Late Latin mōnstruōsitās, mōnstrōsitās (“monstrousness”), from Latin mōnstruōsus, mōnstrōsus; monstrous + -ity.

s: The process by which something is expelled.
Of the chest, rising and falling noticeably from exertion, emotion, or laboured breathing.
Of the bosom, full, ample, or voluptuous in form, irrespective of movement.
An occasion on which something heaves or is heaved.
e: From Middle English hevynge, from Old English hebbende, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjandī, from Proto-Germanic *habjandz, from *habjaną, from heave, -ing.
Inherited from Middle English hevynge.

s: An absorbent garment worn by a baby or toddler who does not yet have voluntary control of their bladder and bowels or by someone who is incontinent; a diaper.
Having a nap (of cloth etc.); downy; shaggy.
Of hair: tightly curled or twisted; frizzy (often specifically in reference to Afro textured hair)
A shallow, flat-bottomed earthenware or glass bowl with sloping sides.
A kind of strong ale; nappy ale.
e: A diminutive in -y. The base is probably napkin but possibly French nappe directly (note that napkin is already a diminutive).
From nap + -y.
From Middle English nap, from Old English hnæp, hnæpp, hnæpf (“cup, bowl”), from Proto-West Germanic *hnapp, from Proto-Germanic *hnappaz (“bowl, goblet, cup”). See hanaper.
Related to knap.

s: A shelf or shelves for storing books for easy visual reference.
e: From book + shelf.

s: A tank, especially a German one of World War II.
The armoured units employed by the German forces in World War II.
e: . Borrowed from German Panzer, from Middle High German Panzer (“armour”), from Old French panciere (“coat of mail”), from Latin pantex (“paunch”).
See plum.
From feather + head.

s: In a slighting manner; belittlingly, contemptuously.
e: From slighting (“in the manner of a slight, belittling, deprecative”) + -ly.
From un- + sewn.
From Middle English cursedly, cursidli, curstely, corsedlich, equivalent to cursed + -ly.

s: In a speechless manner; without speaking.
e: From speechless + -ly.
From searching + -ly.

s: To make bad or worse; to vitiate; to corrupt
To speak ill of; to depreciate; to malign; to revile
e: From Middle English depraven, from Old French depraver, from Latin dēprāvāre (“pervert, distort, corrupt”), from de- + pravus (“crooked, distorted, perverse, wicked”).
From inexpressible + -ly.
From un- + graceful.

s: Undecided or unsure how to act.
e: . Borrowed from French irrésolu or composed from in- + resolute.
From meditative + -ly.

s: To deviate, transgress; to go astray (from).
To speak or act in a manner that is intentionally ambiguous or evasive; equivocate.
To collude, as where an informer colludes with the defendant, and makes a sham prosecution.
To undertake something falsely and deceitfully, with the purpose of defeating or destroying it.
e: Borrowed from Latin praevāricātus, of praevāricor (“to walk crookedly; to play a false or double part”), from prae- + vāricō (“to stand with feet apart, straddle”), from vāricus (“with feet spread apart”); see -ate.

s: Not utterable; incapable of being physically spoken or voiced; unpronounceable.
Incapable of being articulated or expressed; indescribable, inexpressible.
Not allowed to be spoken; taboo, unspeakable.
Something which is unutterable (incapable of being physically spoken, incapable of being articulated or expressed, etc.).
e: From un- + utterable.

s: The act of one who wheedles.
e: From wheedle + -ing.
From questioning + -ly.

s: In an impetuous manner; with sudden force.
e: From impetuous + -ly.
From distracted + -ly.

s: The framework that supports a bed; the rigid structural components of a bed, excluding the mattress, box spring, etc.
e: From Middle English bedsted, bedstede, bedestede, from Old English bedstede (“bedstead”), equivalent to bed + stead. Cognate with Dutch bedstede, bedstee (“closet-bed”).

s: The act of concealing the truth; hypocrisy or deception.
e: Inherited from Middle English dissimulacioun, from Old French dissimulation, from Latin dissimulātiō; equivalent to dissimule + -ation.

s: In a doubtful manner, in context of doubt or ambiguity, questionably.
e: From Middle English dowtfully, doutefulli, equivalent to doubtful + -ly.
From shabby + -ly.

s: The quality or state of being imprudent; lack of prudence, caution, discretion or circumspection.
e: From in- + prudence. From Middle French imprudence, from Latin imprudentia.

s: In an absent-minded or abstracted manner.
e: From absent + -ly.
From devoted + -ly.

s: A small bow, generally performed by a woman or a girl, where she crosses the shin of one leg behind the calf of her other leg and briefly bends her knees to lower her body in deference.
e: Variant of courtesy (1525) (from court + -esy), from Middle English curteisie, curtesie, from Anglo-Norman curtesie, from Old French curteisie, cortoisie.

s: Unable to relax: fidgety; restless; worried; anxious.
e: From fret + -ful.

s: The act by which a candle, etc. is snuffed out.
The act of one who, or that which, snuffs or makes a low sniffing sound.
The lowest servant in a household charged with pots, pans, and other kitchen equipment.
An unprincipled, contemptible person; an untrustworthy person.
A man who uses foul language in front of a woman (typically a woman of high standing).
To revile or abuse in scurrilous language.
To act like a blackguard; to be a scoundrel.
e: From black + guard, thought to have referred originally to the scullions and lower menials of a court, or of a nobleman's household, who wore black liveries or blacked shoes and boots, or were often stained with soot.

s: A soft biscuit or cookie prepared with almond or coconut dough.
e: Borrowed from French macaron. Doublet of macaron, macaroni.
Borrowed from Italian maccarone.

s: Someone or something that cannot be conquered.
e: From un- + conquerable.

s: Alternative form of hello (expressing puzzlement or discovery)
The act or practice of making and throwing snowballs.
A situation which rapidly gets out of control.
Of or relating to a spasm; resembling a sudden contraction of the muscles.
or fitful; occurring in abrupt bursts.
Of or relating to the spasmodic poets, a group of British Victorian poets who wrote introspective drama in verse.
e: From New Latin spasmōdicus, from Ancient Greek σπασμώδης (“spasmodic”), from σπασμός (“spasm”).

s: A manufacturer of or dealer in confections (sweets, candies, sweet pastries, and other sweet food items).
e: From confection#Verb + -er.
From heed + -less.

s: In a disrespectful or discourteous manner; condescendingly.
e: From contemptuous + -ly.

s: The craft of making custom clothing for women, such as dresses, blouses, and evening gowns.
e: From dress + making.

s: Without great care; without sufficient attention or thought.

e: From Middle English pratily, prately, pratyly, pratylych; equivalent to pretty + -ly.
From un- + recognisable.

s: The period of one's life when one attends school, particularly, primary school (as opposed to college days); one's youth.
To invent by an exercise of ingeniosity; to devise
To invent, to make devices; to form designs especially by improvisation.
To project, cast, or set forth, as in a projection of light.
e: From Middle English contrive (15th c.), an alteration of contreve(n), controve(n) (“to invent”, 14th c.), from Old French controver, derived from trover (“to find”). Cognate with Modern French controuver. The Middle English form with -e- reflects the Old French tonic stem (il contrueve), but the shift to -i- seems to be unclear.

s: To stitch a decorative design on fabric with needle and thread of various colours.
To add imaginary detail to a narrative to make it more interesting or acceptable.
e: From Middle English embrouderen, frequentative of embrouden (“to decorate, embroider”), equivalent to embroid + -er. Middle English embrouden itself comes from Anglo-Norman embrouder, from Old French embrosder (“to embroider”), ultimately of origin, though the exact pathway is Uncertain.

s: In a punctual manner; on time.
e: From punctual + -ly.
From indescribable + -ly.

s: Rightly, correctly; in the right way or form.
To or on the right-hand side.
To make right; put right; arrange or treat properly.
e: From Middle English ariȝt, ariht, from Old English āriht (“aright, properly”), from earlier *an riht, on riht (“rightly”), corresponding to a- + right.

From Middle English arighten, arihten (“to raise up”); and Middle English iriȝten, irihten, ȝerihten (“to make right, correct, erect”), from Old English ġerihtan (“to set right”), equivalent to a- + right.

s: In an incredulous manner; tending to disbelieve; skeptically.
e: From incredulous + -ly.

s: Someone who spends money improvidently or wastefully.
Anything that distributes its attributes profusely, without restraint.
e: From spend + thrift (“(archaic) savings; profits; wealth”).

s: The state, or an act, of stubbornness or doggedness.
A group or herd of bison or buffalo.
e: From Middle English obstinacie,obstinacy,obstynacy,obstynacye, from Latin obstinācia.

s: Of a person, with the hair uncombed.
e: From earlier dishevely, from Old French deschevelé (modern French déchevelé and échevelé), from des- (“dis-”), + chevel (“hair”) (modern French cheveu). See there for more details.

s: having no tact; unaware or intentionally inconsiderate of someone else's feelings
e: From tact + -less.

s: Of a person, given to vulgar verbal abuse; foul-mouthed.
e: From Latin scurrīlis (“buffoon-like”) + -ous, from scurra (“a buffoon”).
From un- + savoury.
From expression + -less.
From unspeakable + -ly.

s: The act of producing chirping sounds, or twitters.

e: From uneasy + -ly.
From prudent + -ly.

s: Not prudent; lacking prudence or discretion; indiscreet; injudicious; not paying attention to the consequences of one's actions.
e: From Middle French imprudent, from Latin imprūdens (“not foreseeing, ignorant”), prefix im- (“not”) + prūdens (“foreseeing, skilled, judicious”).
From frightful + -ly.

s: Like, or in the manner of, a zealot; with great zeal or zealotry.
e: From zealous + -ly.

s: In a breathless manner, usually due to excitement, exertion, etc.
e: From breathless + -ly.
From sun + lit.

s: With lavish expenditure or behaviour; in an extravagant manner.
e: From extravagant + -ly.

s: A person who makes tailor-made women's clothes.
e: From dress + maker.

s: A small brown passerine bird, Alauda arvensis, that sings as it flies high into the air.
To jump about joyfully, frolic; to play around, play tricks.
e: From sky + lark. Verb sense 1809, originally nautical, possibly influenced by northern English dialectal term lake/laik (“to play”) (from Old Norse leika (“to play (as opposed to work)”)); see lark for details.

s: Chiefly in the form I daresay: to say something boldly; to affirm or assert.
Chiefly in the form I daresay: to venture to say (as the speaker believes something is likely to be the case); to think something probable; to presume.
e: From dare say: dare (“to have enough courage (to do something)”) + say.

s: Unwanted depressions or other marks on the surface of an object caused when a tool is pressed too hard or vibrates against the surface.
e: From utter + -s. The noun is imitative of the sound of a tool repeatedly striking the surface of an object.
From helm + -er.

s: To slowly become limp; to bend gradually.
To lose all energy, enthusiasm or happiness; to flag.
To allow to droop or sink.
To proceed downward, or toward a close; to decline.
Something which is limp or sagging.
A condition or posture of drooping.
A hinged portion of the leading edge of an aeroplane's wing, which swivels downward to increase lift during takeoff and landing.
e: Inherited from Middle English droupen, from Old Norse drúpa (“to droop”), from Proto-Germanic *drūpaną, *drupōną (“to hang down, drip, drop”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewb- (“to drip, drop”). Doublet of drip, drop.

s: Considered typical of, stereotypical of, or appropriate to women; feminine.
In the manner of a woman.
e: From Middle English womanly,wommanlich,wommanly,wommanlych,wummonlich, equivalent to woman + -ly.
From Middle English wommanliche,wommanly, equivalent to woman + -ly.

s: An evil spirit supposed to oppress people while asleep, especially to have sex with women as they sleep.
A feeling of oppression during sleep, sleep paralysis; night terrors, a nightmare.
Any oppressive thing or person; a burden.
One of various of parasitic insects, especially subfamily Aphidiinae.
e: From Late Latin incubus, from Latin incubō (“nightmare, one who lies down on the sleeper”), from incubō (“to lie upon, to hatch”).

s: A box into which mail is put.
A collection point for mail intended for onward delivery, a secure box or receptacle for this purpose.
A delivery point for mail, a box, compartment or slot for this purpose.
A hidden container that holds a logbook and rubber stamp, found by following clues as a form of recreation.
Transferred to home video formats while preserving the original aspect ratio, having black bars above and below the picture area.
To transfer a widescreen motion picture to home video formats while preserving the original aspect ratio, with the placing of black bars above and below the picture area.
To hunt for letterboxes (containers with logbook and rubber stamp) by following clues.
e: From letter + box. thumb|Letterboxes next to a stop sign in California.

s: Something, such as a belief, that cannot be assailed.
e: From un- + assailable.

s: A room, allocated as a children's play area, in which noisy or boisterous activities are tolerated.
A room dedicated to sadomasochistic sexual activity.
e: From play + room.
From tasteful + -ly.

s: The art or process of working with a needle especially in embroidery or needlepoint.
The product of such art or process.
The occupation or employment of a person skilled in embroidery, needlepoint, etc.
e: From needle + -work.

s: Impossible to prevent or stop; inevitable.
Unable to be persuaded; relentless; unrelenting.
The quality or state of being indiscreet; lack of discretion
An indiscreet or imprudent act; indiscreet behavior.
e: From Old French, from Late Latin indiscrētiō.

s: Having or showing pluck, courage or spirit in trying circumstances.
e: From pluck (“nerve, persistence”) + -y.

s: A series of chisel points mounted on one piece of steel. For example, the toothed stone chisel shown here.
An awl; a bodkin; also, a wooden rod or pin, sharpened at each end, used by thatchers.
A spire rising from a tower.
A spit-like start on the head of a young stag.
The stick from which candle wicks are suspended for dipping.
The pin in a lock which enters the barrel of the key.
To make a hole in, especially a cask of liquor, and put in a tap in order to draw the liquid.
To open, to make an opening into; to pierce.
To be turned sideways to oncoming waves, especially large or breaking waves.
To cause to turn sideways to oncoming waves, especially large or breaking waves (usually followed by to; also figurative).
of a submerged submarine, torpedo, or similar
To break the surface of the water.
e: From Middle English broche, from Old French broche, from Vulgar Latin *brocca, originally a feminine form of Latin broccus, perhaps ultimately of origin (see Scottish Gaelic bròg). Doublet of brochure.

s: To make (someone or something) work too hard.
To fill too full of work; to crowd with labour.
e: From Middle English overwerken, possibly from Old English oferwyrċan (“to overwork, overlay”), equivalent to over- + work. Cognate with Dutch overwerken (“to overwork”).
From Middle English overwerc, from Old English oferweorc, oferġeweorc (“an overwork, superstructure, tomb”), equivalent to over- + work.

s: Streaked, spotted, or otherwise marked with a variety of color.
e: From variegate + -ed.

s: The act of one who shrugs.
Confined to bed because of infirmity or illness.
e: From Middle English bedreden (also as bedrede), from Old English bedreda (“bedridden”), from bedreda, bedrida, bæddryda (“one who is bedridden”), from bed, bedd (“bed”) + rida (“rider”), with -en by analogy with past participle adjectives.

s: A percussion instrument consisting of a small, usually wooden, hoop closed on one side with a drum frame and featuring jingling metal disks on the tread; it is most often held in the hand and shaken rhythmically; by extension, any frame drum.
To make a sound like a tambourine.
e: From French tambourin (“little drum”), from French tambour (“drum”). Ultimately from Arabic طُنْبُور; see it and Persian تنبور for more.

s: The sensation resulting from exposure to low temperatures.
e: From Middle English coldnesse, from Old English cealdness, cealdnys (“coldness”), from Proto-West Germanic *kaldanassī (“coldness”), equivalent to cold + -ness. Cognate with West Frisian kâldens (“coldness”), Middle Low German koldenisse, kōldenisse (“coldness”), Middle High German kaltnisse, keltnisse (“coldness”).

s: The act or sound of one who nibbles.
e: From nibble + -ing.

s: of a room in a building
The value of six old pence; half of a shilling; or one-fortieth of a pound sterling.
A former British or Irish coin worth six pennies, first minted in 1551.
e: From six + pence.

s: A bird having a melodious song or call.
Any bird in the passerine suborder Passeri, which are distinguished by a more sophisticated vocal apparatus.
A person, especially a woman, with a melodious voice.
Someone who confesses, informs, or divulges secrets to the authorities.
e: From song + bird.

s: The act or process in which things are tidied.
In a cold or uncaring manner; indifferently.
e: From Middle English coldliche, caldeliche, perhaps borrowed from Old Norse kaldliga (“coldly”); equivalent to cold + -ly. Displaced Middle English colde (“coldly”), from Old English cealde (“coldly”).
Inherited from Middle English dredfully, dradefullich, dredefullich; equivalent to dreadful + -ly.

s: The act by which something is wrung.
e: From Middle English wryngynge; equivalent to wring + -ing.

From Middle English lothsum, from Old English *lāþsum, from Proto-West Germanic *laiþasam, equivalent to loath + -some. Cognate with Middle Low German lêtsam (“arduous”), German leidsam (“sad, sorry”).

s: To undo the process of reading.
To flag (a previously read e-mail or similar message) as not having been read.
An unread email or instant message.
e: From un- + read.
From re- + arrangement or rearrange + -ment.

s: Characterized by an absence of antagonism, especially in commonly difficult situations.
e: From Middle English amcabily, equivalent to amicable + -ly..

s: Causing repugnance; unpleasant to the feelings or senses; displeasing.
Not suitable; that does not conform or fit.
Something or someone displeasing; anything that is disagreeable.
e: Inherited from Middle English disagreable, from Middle French desagreable, from Old French desagraable (compare French désagréable). dis- + agreeable.

s: Stubbornly adhering to an opinion, purpose, or course, usually with implied unreasonableness; persistent.
Of an inanimate object, not easily subdued or removed.
Of a facial feature or expression, fixed and unmoving.
e: Inherited from Middle English obstinat (“obstinate, stubborn”), from Latin obstinātus, perfect passive participle of obstinō (“set one's mind firmly upon, resolve”) (see -ate), from ob (“before”) + *stinare, from stare (“to stand”). Doublet of ostinato.

s: Stranded as a result of a shipwreck.
In a manner that demonstrates excellence; very well.
e: From excellent + -ly.
From deject + -ed.

s: Random; chaotic; incomplete; not thorough, constant, or consistent.
Simple chance, a random accident, luck.
e: From archaic hap (“chance, luck”) + hazard.

s: A pin or fastener for the hair.
A kind of ribozyme; hairpin ribozyme.
A very tight bend in a road; a hairpin bend.
An elongated horizontal v-shaped sign placed underneath a staff to indicate a crescendo or decrescendo.
e: From hair + pin, 1788 (as hair pin). Adjective sense 1906 in hairpin turn etc.

s: A short, sharp or high note or noise, as of a bird or insect.
A pulse of signal whose frequency sweeps through a band of frequencies for the duration of the pulse; the quality of having a such a variation in frequency.
To make a short, sharp, cheerful note, as of small birds or crickets; to chitter; to twitter.
To speak in a high-pitched staccato.
To modify (a pulse of signal) so that it sweeps through a band of frequencies throughout its duration.
To cheer up; to make (someone) happier.
To speak rapid insulting comical banter back and forth; to bicker or argue.
e: From Middle English *chirpen (attested only in the derivative Middle English chirpinge, cyrpynge, chyrypynge (“chirping”). Compare Middle English chirken and chirmen. More at chirk, chirm. Compare also Middle English chirten (“to smack, chirrup”). Compare German zirpen and Dutch tjirpen.
From hurried + -ly.

s: Impulsive and unpredictable; determined by chance, impulse, or whim.
e: Borrowed from Middle French capricieux, from Italian capriccioso, from capriccio. caprice + -ious.

s: Amazement or horror that confounds the faculties, and incapacitates for reflection; terror, combined with amazement; dismay.
e: From French consternation, from Latin consternātiō. consternate + -ion.

s: That which makes sure; that which confirms; ground of confidence or security.
A promise to pay a sum of money in the event that another person fails to fulfill an obligation.
One who undertakes to pay money or perform other acts in the event that his principal fails therein.
e: From Middle English surete, attested since the early 1300s in the sense "guarantee, promise, pledge, assurance", from Anglo-Norman seurté/Old French seurté with the same meaning (whence modern French sûreté), from Latin sēcūritās. Equivalent to sure + -ty.

s: Full of something causing fright, whether
Unpleasant, dreadful, awful (also used as an intensifier).
e: From Middle English frightful (“afraid”), from Old English forhtfull (“fainthearted, timorous”). Equivalent to fright + -ful.

s: Output fluctuation before reaching a stable condition.
Suitable to effect some desired end or the purpose intended.
Affording short-term benefit, often at the expense of the long-term.
Governed by self-interest, often short-term self-interest.
A method or means for achieving a particular result, especially when direct or efficient; a resource.
e: From Middle English expedient, from Old French expedient, from Latin expediens (stem expedient-), present participle of expedire (“to bring forward, to dispatch, to expedite; impers. to be profitable, serviceable, advantageous, expedient”), from ex (“out”) + pēs (“foot, hoof”).

s: The water held back by a dam or other obstruction.
A remote place: somewhere that remains unaffected by new events, progresses, ideas, etc; any field of endeavor that figuratively resembles such a place.
A rowing stroke in which the oar is pushed forward to stop the boat; see back water
Water used in the papermaking process. Recycled to reduce usage of fresh water, and usually containing residual amounts of chemicals and fibres.
To row or paddle a backwater stroke.
To vacillate on a long-held position.
e: From back + water.

s: One in a race who is catching up to others and shows promise of winning.
An ambitious person; one who is catching up in some contest and has a likelihood of victory
e: From Middle English comere, equivalent to come + -er.

s: An act of becoming visible; appearance; visibility.
The thing appearing; a visible object; a form.
An unexpected, wonderful, or preternatural appearance; especially, one by a ghost, phantom or suchlike; the entity itself.
The first appearance of a star or other luminary after having been invisible or obscured; opposed to occultation.
A period of consecutive days or nights when a particular celestial body may be observed, beginning with the heliacal rising of the body and ending with its heliacal setting.
e: From Middle French apparition, from Latin apparitio, from appareo.
From Middle English wedlok, wedlocke (“wedlock, marriage, matrimony”), from Old English wedlāc (“marriage vow, pledge, plighted troth, wedlock”); compare wed.

s: The motion of something that is wagged.
In an earnest manner; being very sincere; putting forth genuine effort.
e: From Middle English ernestly, from Old English eornostlīċe (“earnestly, strictly”), equivalent to earnest + -ly.

s: Able to be borne; tolerable; endurable.
Able to be borne or carried; portable.
e: From Middle English berable, equivalent to bear + -able.

s: Marked by or showing lack of due thought or care.
Especially of depth: physically incapable of being measured; immeasurable.
Impossible to grasp the extent of, or to fully know or understand.
e: From un- + fathom (“to measure the depth of (water); (figurative) to deeply understand (someone or something)”) + -able.

s: A feeling of inadequacy or impotence.
e: From helpless + -ness.

s: To abandon, to give up, to leave (permanently), to renounce (someone or something).
To avoid or shun (someone or something).
To cause disappointment to; to be insufficient for (someone or something).
e: From Middle English forsaken (“to abandon, desert, repudiate, withdraw allegiance from”), from Old English forsacan (“to oppose; to give up, renounce; to decline, refuse”), from Proto-West Germanic *frasakan (“to forsake, renounce”). for- + sake.

s: The act of procuring, or amount procured.
That has been interrupted, suppressed etc
The act by which something is mended or repaired.
A patch of land adjoining a church, often used as a graveyard.
e: Inherited from Middle English chircheyerd (also kirkeyerd > English kirkyard), equivalent to church + yard. Compare also Middle English kurk-garth, kyrkgarth, kirrkegærd, from Old Norse kirkjugarðr (“churchyard; graveyard”). Replaced Middle English chirchetoun from Old English ċirictūn (churchtown).

s: The condition of being hidden or concealed.
e: From Old French concelement (“concealment, secrecy”). conceal + -ment.

s: A false statement, especially an intentional one; a lie.
e: From Middle English falshede, from false + -hede, equivalent to false + -hood.

s: Wrong; faulty; out of order; improper or otherwise incorrect.
Fault; wrong; an evil act, a bad deed.
e: From a- + miss.

s: An English dessert made from a mixture of thick custard, fruit, sponge cake, jelly and whipped cream.
Anything that is of little importance or worth.
Utensils made from this particular kind of pewter.
To deal with something as if it were of little importance or worth.
To act, speak, or otherwise behave with jest.
To make of little importance or worth, to make trivial.
e: From Middle English trefle,trifel,trifle,triful,trufful,truyfle (“false or idle tale; nonsense; playful activity; something unimportant”), from Old French trufle (“mockery”), a byform of trufe, truffe (“deception”), of uncertain origin.
From Middle English treoflen,trifelen,trifulen,troflen,truflen,trufyllen,tryflen,tryfullen, from Old French truffler,truiffler or directly from the noun.

s: Very quiet; expressed using soft tones.
The action of the verb to spring.
A set of springs in a vehicle, etc.
The spring of an arch: the lowest part of an arch on both sides.
That takes effect only after the incapacity of the grantor or some other definite future act or circumstance.

e: From absurd + -ly.

s: Being in the state of delirium.
e: From delirium ous; see also Latin delirus (“silly, doting, crazy”).
From playful + -ly.
From deceit + -ful.

s: In an intent or focused manner.
e: From intent + -ly.

s: At rest, stationary, immobile, not moving.
e: From motion + -less.
From ugly + -ness.

s: In a rash or reckless manner, without regard for cost or consequence.
With contempt for the rights, feelings, or well-being of others.
e: From Middle English reklesly, from Old English rēcelēaslīce; equivalent to reckless + -ly.
From un- + disturbed.

s: To restore (someone) to their former state, reputation, possessions, status etc.
To vindicate; to restore the reputation or image of (a person, concept etc.).
To return (something) to its original condition.
To restore or repair (a vehicle, building); to make habitable or usable again.
To restore to (a criminal etc.) the necessary training and education to allow for a successful reintegration into society; to retrain.
To return (someone) to good health after illness, addiction, etc.
To go through such a process; to recover.
e: Medieval Latin rehabilitātus, perfect passive participle of Latin rehabilitō. See habilitate.

s: A time when children can play outside during the school day.
A duration of time when one is not as serious or committed as one could be, especially in a conflict of sorts.
e: From play + time.
From certifiable + -ly.
From loud + -en.
From dishonorable + -ly.
From criminology + -ist.

s: Completed or done with efficiency and speed; facilitating speed.
e: From Middle English expedycius (“useful, fitting”), from Latin expedītus (“disengaged, ready, convenient, prompt; unfettered, unencumbered”), past participle of expediō.

s: A person of weak or even sickly physical constitution.
A person of weak character, lacking in courage and/or moral strength.
weak, either physically, morally or mentally
e: From weak + -ling.

s: Resembling or characteristic of mucus, especially in texture.
Ill-tempered or impertinent in an arrogant, conceited manner.
The lion's mane jellyfish, which secretes a mucus that can foul fishing nets.
e: From snot + -y.
From counter- + intelligence.
From strenuous + -ly.

s: The period during which something continues or goes on; duration.
An order issued by a court granting a postponement of a legal proceeding for a set period.
e: From Middle English continuance, contynuaunce, from Old French continuance, from continuer.

s: The act of giving a salute.
A holder with a socket or spike for a candle.
A gymnastics move in which the legs are pointed vertically upward.
A color-coded bar showing the open and closing prices of a stock on a candlestick chart.
The central ignition tube connecting the fuse and charge of a WWI shrapnel shell, shaped like a candle stick.
To catch on fire, so that the chute resembles a tapered candle with a flame on top.
To analyze stock behavior using Japanese candlestick charts.
To form a tall, thin, tapering shape similar to a candle.
e: From Middle English candelstik, candelstikke, from Old English candelsticca (“candlestick”), equivalent to candle + stick. Cognate with Scots candilsteke, candilstik (“candlestick”). Compare Old Norse kertastika, kertistika (“candlestick”).

s: A platform or stand used to lift or elevate something.
A vertical part of a step on a staircase.
The main body of a bow.
A vertical utility conduit, pipe or path between floors of a building for placement of cables (e.g. telephone, networking), or to convey fluids (e.g. gas, water).
A pipe connecting an individual exhaust port of an internal combustion engine to the muffler, particularly on aircraft.
A Manx cat with a showable short tail.
A strip of webbing joining a parachute's harness to the rigging lines.
A reservoir built into a metal casting mold to prevent the formation of cavities in the casting as the metal shrinks on cooling.
An audio effect that gradually increases in frequency, pitch or volume.
e: From Middle English ryser, risere, equivalent to rise + -er.

s: The act of one who treads.
e: From Middle English tredynge, tredyng; equivalent to tread + -ing.

s: Not meeting the minimum quality requirements.
Not conforming to the standard variety; nonstandard.
e: From sub- + standard.

s: The act of commending; praise; favorable representation in words; recommendation.
That which is the ground of approbation or praise.
A message of affection or respect; compliments; greeting.
An award or recognition for performance; a medal.
e: From Middle English commendacioun, from Old French commendacion (“approval, praise”), from Latin commendatio (“recommendation, commendation”), from commendare.

s: Silly talk or writing; nonsense, silliness, or fake assertion(s).
A hog-tie performed in a rodeo show.
e: Compare hooie and German hui.

s: Not chartered; not supplied with a charter.
e: From un- + chartered.

s: A maid who handles the chores in a hotel room or a bedroom in a wealthy household.
e: From chamber + maid.

s: A fish of the genus Istiophorus, having a characteristic sail-like fin on its back.
e: From sail + fish.

s: Of or relating to vibrations of a spiritual, etheric, or astral nature.
e: From vibrate + -ory.

s: To tilt back and forth on an edge.
To be close to becoming a typically negative situation.
e: Alteration of titter#Etymology_1.
From crazy + -ly.

s: The act of divining; a foreseeing or foretelling of future events.
The apparent art of discovering secrets or the future by preternatural means.
An indication of what is to come in the future or what is secret; a prediction.
e: From Old French divination, from Latin divinatio.

s: Having taken physical form; having become real.

e: From fun + -less.

s: To move something, especially one's arms or legs, from a crossed position.
To undo the crossing or traversal of (something).
e: From un- + cross.
From drink + -y.

Victorian Era euphemism, specifically the category of euphemism known as indirection (compare privates, behind, sleep together). First intended meaning was "trousers", attested from 1823. Meaning "underwear" is recorded from 1910.
From homeo + path, related to German Homöopath.
From moustache + -ed.

s: The act or process of extricating or disentangling; a freeing from perplexities; disentanglement.
Rescue of a trapped person in a vehicle or machinery.
The act of sending out or evolving.
e: From extricate + -ion.

s: A practitioner of naturopathy, a nature healer
e: From naturopathy.

s: A job, task, or other activity that is easy to complete or simple.
A hornless animal; a pollard or doddy.
e: Uncertain. Possibly from dialectal English doddle (“to toddle, to sway, to nod drowsily”).

s: A cesspool; a pit or covered cistern used to collect sewage and waste water.
A place or situation characterised by corruption, filth or immoral activities.
e: Uncertain. The first part, cess-, is undoubtedly the same as for cesspool, whose origin is likewise uncertain. The second part is pit, a hole in the ground.

s: A non-physician healthcare practitioner who practices osteopathy by manipulating the skeleton and muscles. Not to be confused with Doctors of Osteopathic Medicine (D.O.) (also known as osteopathic physicians) who are full physicians like Doctors of Medicine (M.D.).
e: From osteo + path.

s: The study and interpretation of behavior in terms of simple and complex reflexes.

A form of complementary medicine involving the stimulation of points on the feet, hands, or ears, in the belief that it will have a beneficial effect on some other parts of the body or to improve general health.
e: From reflex + -ology, derived from Russian.

s: A form of massage, using the thumbs and palms, employed as therapy.
e: Borrowed from Japanese, from +.

s: The region between the external genitalia and anus.
That which retains or confines; a restraint.
e: Borrowed from Middle French rétentif, from Old French retentif, from Medieval Latin retentivus, from Latin retentus.

s: Used to protect against infection by disease-causing microbes.
e: From a- + septic.

s: Equipped with a sucker or suckers.

e: From gynaecology + -ist.

s: Someone (or something) doomed; a hopeless case, especially someone who is bound to die soon.
A ball hit out of the playing area for a home run.
e: From gone + -er. First attestations around 1850.

s: Of a door or a window: bevelled so as to be larger on one side of the wall than on the other.
e: From splay + -ed.
From Latin ante (“before”) + nātālis (“natal”), from nāscor (“to be born”), equivalent to ante- + natal.

s: The motion of something that skids.
The logging operation for pulling cut trees out of a forest.
A dry-cured ham from Italy, thinly sliced.
e: Borrowed from Italian prosciutto (meaning 'ham', in general), from asciutto, with a change of prefix, or from a Vulgar Latin *perexsūctus, from per + Latin exsūctus.

s: The use of selected fragrances in lotions and inhalants in an effort to affect mood and promote health.
e: From aroma + therapy.

s: The motion of something that wobbles.

e: Learned borrowing from Latin āsthmaticus, from asthma, -ic.

s: Blood that is needed for continued life; blood regarded as the seat of life.
That which is required for continued existence or function.
e: From life + blood. Compare English heart-blood (“lifeblood”).

s: A dead body; especially the corpse of a human to be dissected.
e: From Middle English cadaver, from Latin cadāver.

s: A mild expression of surprise or enthusiasm.
A type of black rag doll.
To spit out phlegm that has been forced up into the mouth from one's throat.
A collection of saliva and phlegm collected in the mouth and spat out.
e: Euphemism for God, dating from the 18th century. Possibly a compaction of “God′s body”.
From golliwog.
Nonstandard diminutive of galosh.
Compare east Anglia dialect golls (mucus; pendent matter hanging from children's noses).

s: The act or result of something that trickles.
Skin dimpling caused by the herniation (protrusion) of subcutaneous adipose tissue (fat within connective tissue), especially on the pelvic area of women.
e: Borrowed from French cellulite. cellule + -ite. Doublet of cellulitis..

s: Having an ancestry characterized by inbreeding.
Describing a strain produced through successive generations of inbreeding resulting in a population of genetically identical individuals which are homozygous at all genetic loci.
Insular or self-contained, primarily interacting with and drawing upon one another.
A plant or animal produced by inbreeding.
e: From the past participle of inbreed, equivalent to in- + bred.

s: Underwear covering the genitalia and often buttocks as well as adjacent areas, usually going no higher than the navel.
e: From under- + pants.

s: Plastic surgery to the face to remove wrinkles, fat or various signs of aging.
Any activity undertaken to renew, revamp, update, or improve the appearance of something.
e: From face + lift.

s: Something that provides support or nourishment.
e: From Middle English sustenaunce, from Old French sustenance, from sustenir with the suffix -ance, from Vulgar Latin *sustenire, from Latin sustinere. Compare also Late Latin sustinentia. Equivalent to sustain + -ance.

s: The posture of one who squats.
The act or general practice of occupying a building or land without the permission of the owner.
The cavity beneath the junction of the arm and shoulder.
Somewhere or something unpleasant or undesirable.
e: From Middle English armpitt, arme-pitt, armput, equivalent to arm + pit. (something unpleasant) Presumably a reference to underarm body odor.

s: A piece of broken glass or pottery, especially one found in an archaeological dig.
A piece of material, especially rock and similar materials, reminding of a broken piece of glass or pottery.
A food preparation similar in shape to a shard of, e.g., glass, generally made from a sheet of a hard product that is then shattered to produce smaller pieces.
A tough scale, sheath, or shell; especially an elytron of a beetle.
An instance of an MMORPG that is one of several independent and structurally identical virtual worlds, none of which has so many players as to exhaust a system's resources.
A component of a sharded distributed database.
To fall apart into shards, usually as the result of impact or explosion.
To divide (an MMORPG) into several shards, or to establish a shard of one.
e: From Middle English shard, scherd, scheard, schord, from Old English sċeard (“a broken piece; shard”), from Proto-West Germanic *skard, from Proto-Germanic *skardą (“notch; nick”), from *skardaz (“damaged; nicked; scarred”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).

s: A textile or garment made of wool from a lamb.
A festive drink of ale mixed with the pulp of roasted apples.
e: From lamb + -s- + wool.

Probably identical to Etymology 1, referring to the layer of froth that is produced in making the drink, though starting with Charles Vallancey in 1786, historically supposed to be a corruption of an earlier lamasool or La Maes Abhal "Day of the Apple Fruit" (corresponding to Irish lá measa abhla).

s: The act of cleaning something with shampoo.
A small (typically pork) sausage, usually served fried.
e: Borrowed from German Bratwurst. The word is partly from braten (“to fry”) + Wurst (“sausage”), and partly from an older Middle High German brātwurst, in which brāt is an unrelated word meaning “ground meat” (compare German Brät). In modern German, the term Bratwurst is used almost exclusively for sausages fried or to be fried.

s: A small spot or streak; a speckle.
e: From Middle English *flekk, *flekke (attested in Middle English flekked (“spotted, flecked”)), from Old Norse flekkr (“spot”), from Proto-Germanic *flekka-. Cognate with Dutch vlek, German Fleck, Swedish fläck.

s: A high, close-fitting collar, turned back on itself and covering all or most of the neck, on a sweater or similar garment.
e: From turtle + neck.

s: The arrangement of pages in a book or other publication.
A transfer of pages between main memory and an auxiliary store, such as hard disk drive.
Easy work, especially a subject at school that requires little effort.
To live off the earnings of a prostitute.
To not earn one's keep, to live off someone else or off welfare when one could be working.
To avoid one's responsibilities; to leave it to others to perform duties that one is expected to perform.
To do nothing, to be idle, especially when there is work to be done.
To take some benefit and give nothing in return.
e: Back-formation from English bludger.
See -illion.

s: Extreme need or want; destitution, poverty; an instance of this.
Often followed by of: a lack of something; a dearth, a scarcity.
The quality of being miserly; miserliness, parsimoniousness, stinginess.
e: From Late Middle English penuri, penurie (“destitution, need, poverty; dearth, lack, scarcity”), borrowed from Latin pēnūria (“need, scarcity, want”) + Middle English -i, -ie; further etymology uncertain, possibly related to paene (“almost, nearly; barely, hardly, scarcely”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate; to hurt”).
From Greek ταβέρνα, from Latin taberna. Doublet of taberna, tavern.

s: Not decipherable; impossible to decode, read, understand or comprehend.
e: From in- + decipherable.
From Middle English wantounly, wantounliche, equivalent to wanton + -ly.
From un- + hygienic.

s: To remove the nap of (cloth), by passing it rapidly over a red-hot bar, or over a flame, preliminary to dyeing it.
To remove the hair or down from (a plucked chicken, etc.) by passing it over a flame.
A burning of the surface; a slight burn.
e: From Middle English sengen, from Old English senġan, sænċġan (“to singe, burn slightly, scorch, afflict”), from Proto-West Germanic *sangijan (“to burn, torch”), from Proto-Indo-European *senk- (“to burn”).

s: The horizontal member protruding from the base of a window frame.
e: From window + sill.
From Middle English somery; equivalent to summer + -y. Compare Swedish somrig (“summery”).

s: Matter flowing from a wound or sore; pus.
One who succeeds in desisting from a vice, especially smoking, drinking, or drugging.
e: From Middle English quitter, from Anglo-Norman quiture, quyture et al., specialised use of quiture (“burn mark, burning”), from the participle stem of cuire (“to cook”), or from Latin coctura (“cooking”).
From quit + -er.

s: Exceptionally large; whopping (often followed by an adjective such as great or big).
The act of making an unreasonable profit not justified by the corresponding assumption of risk, or by doing so unethically or opportunistically.
Tending to make one (actually or metaphorically) dizzy or confused, as of great speed or height.
An indirect or deceptive device or stratagem; a blind. Refers especially to war and diplomatics.
Deception; misrepresentation of the true nature of an activity.
e: Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg- Borrowed from Middle French subterfuge, from Medieval Latin subterfugium, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugiō (“to flee”).

s: Of, characterized by, or preferring privacy and isolation; secluded.
e: From recluse + -ive.

s: A normally deep-red-colored root vegetable usually cooked or pickled before eating.
The edible part of the root of a beet plant, raw or prepared.
To turn a bright red or purple color.
e: From beet + root.
From Middle English writhyng; equivalent to writhe + -ing.

s: To remove or force out from a position or dwelling previously occupied.
To move or go from a dwelling or former position.
To force out of a secure or settled position.
e: From Middle English disloggen, from Old French deslogier. Compare French déloger. Equivalent to dis- + lodge.

s: A piece of hard candy on a stick; a lollipop.
Any confection made from sugar, or high in sugar content; a sweet, a piece of candy.
The head (or, by extension, the tongue).
A child. Alternative form of lully.
Something simple to do or understand.
Snow or fine ice floating on water.
Eliciting a response of LOL; funny.
e: A clipping of lollypop.
From loll + -y.
Shortened from loblolly (“gruel”).
From lol + -y.

s: A flavored alcoholic beverage that is usually very sweet and contains a high percentage of alcohol.
to flavor or treat (wine) with a liqueur
to top up bottles of sparkling wine with a sugar solution
e: French liqueur. Doublet of liquor.

s: The experience of auditory sensations, such as a ringing or pulsating sound, occurring in the absence of any external stimulus.
e: Latin tinnītus (“a jingling, ringing”).

s: Any of numerous species of songbirds of the cosmopolitan family Turdidae, such as the song thrush, mistle thrush, bluebird, and American robin.
A fungal infection caused by species of genus Candida, affecting the mouth or vagina; candidiasis.
e: From Middle English thrusche, þrusch, þresche, from a combination of Old English þrysċe (from Proto-Germanic *þruskijǭ, a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *þruskō) and Old English þræsċe (from Proto-Germanic *þrauskǭ and/or *þrastuz); all from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos (“thrush”).

Uncertain, though likely not related to the "bird" sense of Etymology 1; perhaps compare Icelandic þröstur, Danish torsk, Norwegian trauske or also frosk. Perhaps also related to Old French fourchette (“frog of a horse's hoof”).

s: An instance in which someone chuckles
Of a turn, achieved by the buttering action.
Filled with unexpressed anger; in a state of being livid.
In a state of extreme volatility; about to boil over; boiling, bubbling.
In a state of unceasing and furious activity.
The action of the verb to seethe.
e: From Middle English sethyng; equivalent to seethe + -ing.

s: A type of chewy confectionery made by boiling sugar (or treacle, etc) with butter or milk, then cooling the mixture so that it becomes hard.
A small, individual piece of toffee.
e: An alteration of taffy.

s: A blind alley or dead end street.
A circular area at the end of a dead end street to allow cars to turn around, designed so children can play on the street, with little or no through-traffic.
A sacklike cavity, a tube open at one end only.
e: Borrowed from French cul-de-sac, from cul (“bottom”) + de (“of”) + sac (“bag, sack”).

s: A Marian shrine, usually built in a cavern-like structure.
A local organization of cavers that typically organizes trips to caves and provides information and training for caving; a caving club.
A secretive name for a local group of underground Satanists.
A garden or roadside shrine with a small cave containing a statue of the Blessed Virgin Mary (usually Our Lady of Lourdes and sometimes paired with a water feature)
e: From Italian grotta, from Vulgar Latin grupta, from Classical Latin crypta. Doublet of crypt. The Philippine sense is from the holy cave in Lourdes, France.

s: A love song that is sung directly to one's love interest, especially one performed below the window of a loved one in the evening.
An instrumental composition in several movements.
To sing or play a serenade for (someone).
e: Borrowed from French sérénade, from Italian serenata, from the past participle of serenare, from Latin serenare, from serenus (“calm”), of uncertain origin (see there).
From ambient + -ence.
By genericization from the trademark Frisbee.

s: A flexible branch or twig of a plant such as willow, used in weaving baskets and furniture.
e: From Middle English wiker, cognate with Old Swedish vikker (“willow”), Old Norse veikr (“weak”), English weak.

s: In a spanking manner; vigorously; freshly.
e: From spanking + -ly.
From turn up.
plot + -est.
From dung + ball.

s: Suitable for plopping into; soft and comfortable.
Tending to plop; limp and heavy.
e: From plop + -y.

s: To disconnect (an IRC server) from a network.
A light squishing or splattering sound.
e: Possibly related to squirt (“small child”); from 19th c.
Short for server quit.
Onomatopoeic.
Compare French globuleux.
From cow + pat.

s: Someone who is not a Romani, Sinti, Gypsy, or Traveller.
A well-dressed man; a swell; sometimes an employer, or principal, as the manager of a theatre.
e: From gorge + -er.
Possibly from gorgeous, or of Romani origin like the previous word.

s: An act of sexual intercourse, especially one that is rough.
e: From roger + -ing.
From yob + -o.

s: One of a group of young men who would carouse in taverns, then pick brawls on the street for entertainment.
e: From roar + -er.
From thick + -o.

s: To engage in noisy, drunken, or riotous behaviour.
To walk with a swaying motion.
A session of noisy, drunken, or riotous behaviour.
e: From Old French rustre, from Latin rusticus. Doublet of rustic.
From whiff + -y.

s: Urination, or a piece of excrement.
A homosexual man, especially one with camp mannerisms.
e: From whoops + -y.
From whoops + -y.
From whoops + -y.

s: A person who caricatures the manner of speech of a disc jockey or announcer, using affected, back-of-the-throat speech that is likened to puking.
e: From puke + -er.

s: A political philosophy opposed to the separation of a religious group (church) and a government (state), especially the belief held by those in 19th-century England opposed to separating the Anglican church from the civil government, or the separation of church and state.

e: A variant of tadger, perhaps related to dialectal todge (“anything of a thick consistency”), todgey (“short and fat”).

s: Nifty; impressive, often in a superficial or showy way.
e: From whizz + -y.

s: A person who does menial work, a servant.
Alternative form of of dog's body
To act as a dogsbody, to do menial work
e: From dog + -s- + body. 1818, British navy slang (dog's body), originally derogatory reference to unappetizing pease pudding (compare dog's breakfast), as if it were made of mashed dog meat. In 20th century applied to low-ranked sailors, thence menial servants in wider usage.

s: A former British silver coin, worth nine old pennies.
A Spanish real, valued at twelve and a half cents.
e: From nine + pence.

s: Plural of gooly: pebbles, small rocks.
e: From gooly.

s: Constituting bait (something intended to allure), especially Oscar bait or clickbait.
e: From bait (“fit of anger”) + -y.
From bait (“something alluring”) + -y.

s: A salted, and lightly smoked herring or mackerel.
A freshwater fish native to the Great Lakes (Coregonus hoyi).
e: From bloat + -er, because they swell during preparation.
From bloat + -er, in the sense of the person having a "bloated" appearance.
From inane + -ly.

s: mainly as a term of address
e: From nurse + -ie.

s: Having a specified kind of breasts.
The down of the eider duck, used for stuffing pillows and quilts.
A quilt stuffed with this down.
e: From eider + down.
From wrong + -er.
From wrong + -er.

s: Senseless talk or writing; nonsense; rubbish.
Used to express disbelief: nonsense!; rubbish!
e: Unknown. Attested from a 1959 episode of the UK TV series Hancock's Half Hour. The writers (Galton and Simpson) state that the phrase was in general use when the show was broadcast. A national TV appeal in the UK in 2006 failed to find earlier references, though a humorous newspaper column from 1947 does use the fictional name "Sir Aubrey Codswallop".

s: Alternative form of diddly (a trill sound)
A joint of the horse's leg below the knee or hock and above the hoof.
The tuft of hair that grows at this joint.
e: From Middle English fitlokes, feetlakkes, taken to be foot + lock (“tuft of hair”) but actually a misdivision of Old English -oc. Cognate with Middle Low German fitlok, fitlock (“fetlock”), Dutch vitlok, vittelokke, vitslok, German Fissloch, Fisloch, Fislach (“fetlock; pastern”).

s: A horse that jibs, i.e. refuses, stops short.
e: From jib + -er.
gaol + -er.

s: A person who is habitually gloomy, sullen or miserable; a grouch; a scowling person.
To make a gloomy, sullen or miserable facial expression; to scowl.
e: From sour (“bad-tempered”) + puss (“slang for mouth”).

s: A cloth which usually covers the head and is worn around the neck and chin. It was worn by women in medieval Europe and is still worn by nuns in certain orders.
A fold or pleat in cloth.
A ripple, as on the surface of water.
To draw down; to lower, like a veil.
To cause to appear as if laid in folds or plaits; to cause to ripple or undulate.
e: From Middle English wympel, wimpel, from Old English wimpel (“veil, an article of women's dress; a covering for the neck, a cloak, a hood”), from Proto-Germanic *wimpilaz (“wimple, scarf, veil”).
From Middle English wimplen (“to cover, conceal; to fold, drape”).

s: Used to emphasize the size or extent.
A series of wallops or blows; a beating.
to act in a sluggish or slovenly manner
Of a horse: to move with a gait between a trot and a gallop; to canter.
e: Origin Uncertain; apparently connected with the Middle English trollen (“to go about, stroll, roll from side to side”). Ostensibly influenced, if not derived, in some way by a word from Old Norse trǫll (“troll, witch, mage, monster, etc.”).

s: A disreputable fellow, a good-for-nothing, a scapegrace, a blackguard
A badly behaved person, especially a child; a mischief-maker; a rascal
e: Unknown.

s: A stupid or annoying person; a simpleton; a fool.
A part of male dress in the 15th and 16th centuries, worn in front of the breeches to cover the male genitals.
A conspicuous protection for the male genitals in a suit of plate armor.
e: From cod (“bag, pouch, scrotum”) + piece.
From floss + -y.

s: High in starch; tending to break down easily when cooked.
e: From Middle English floury, equivalent to flour + -y..

s: A specialist in marketing (promoting and selling products and services).
One who promotes and sells products or services; called a marketer in US English.
Someone who works in or supports a certain kind of system of selling and buying, for example free marketeer, black marketeer.
e: From market + -eer.

s: One who regularly goes to church; a practicing Christian.
e: From church + goer.

s: A facial expression in which the lips are pushed outwards in a pout.
e: From duck + face, suggesting a duck's bill.
From mustachio + -ed.

s: The state of being deviant, abnormal or anomalous.

e: From scrounge + -er.

s: The characteristic or quality of being gorgeous
e: From gorgeous + -ness.

s: Decline in judgment and other cognitive functions, associated with aging; senility.
Fondness or attentiveness, especially to an excessive degree.
e: From Middle English dotage, from doten (“to dote”) + -age; equivalent to dote + -age.
From Middle English dullard, dollard, equivalent to dull + -ard. Compare Faroese døll (“dullard, good-for-nothing, blockhead”), Norwegian døl (“idiot, simpleton”).

s: Shaped like an arch or vault; resembling a fornix.
e: Borrowed from Latin fornicātus, perfect active participle of fornicor (see -ate), from fornix (“arch, vault; brothel”). It was customary for courtesans of the era to wait for their customers out of the rain in arched passageways.
From fornix + -ate.

s: An expression of disgust or distaste.
e: Similar to the sound of someone vomiting.

s: sexually attractive women considered collectively; usually connoting a connection with the upper class.
e: Compare totter.
From tot (“small child”).
Borrowed from French brassière. Doublet of brachiaria.

s: A girl or young woman who milks the cows on a farm.
e: From milk + maid.
From dangle + -y.
From Middle English graceles; equivalent to grace + -less.

s: Used as a cadence-count used for synchronized walking, marching, pulling, lifting, etc.
An English nobleman, especially one traveling Europe in grand style; a wealthy British gentleman.
e: From French milord, from English my Lord. Compare milady.
A variant spelling of m'lord, elided from my + lord.

s: Resembling, or flavoured with, oranges (the fruit).
e: From orange + -y.

s: An article of clothing covering each leg separately, that covers the area from the waist to the ankle.
Of, similar to, or related to paper.
e: From paper + -y.

s: Any of various insects of the order Dermaptera that have elongated bodies, large membranous wings folded underneath short leathery forewings and a pair of large pincers protruding from the rear of the abdomen.
One who whispers insinuations; a secret counsellor.
To fill the mind of with prejudice by insinuations.
To attempt to influence by persistent confidential argument or talk.
e: From Middle English erwigge, from Old English ēarwicga, from ēare (“ear”) + wicga (“insect”), so named from the appearance of the hindwings, which are unique in their resemblance to human ears when unfolded.

s: Possessing physical strength and weight; rugged and powerful.
e: Inherited from Middle English synwy, synewy, synowy (“tendonous”); equivalent to sinew + -y.
From Middle English varty, equivalent to wart + -y.

s: Making an unfriendly, sullen, or scowling face.
Having thick, large, or projecting eyebrows.
A type of savoury cake, typically flat and round, made from batter and yeast, containing many small holes and served toasted, usually with butter.
A sexually attractive person or, collectively, people; usually referring to women.
e: First appears c. the 17th century, either from crompid cake (“wafer, literally, curled-up cake”), from crompid, form of crumpen (“to curl up”); cognate to crumpled. An alternate etymology is from; compare Breton krampouezh (“crepe, pancake”) and Welsh crempog (“pancake”).

s: Any of various old coins of England and Scotland.
Any unit of currency worth four pence.
A historical English coin representing such a unit: a silver coin worth four English pennies, still minted as one of the set of Maundy coins.
A proverbial small sum; a whit or jot.
e: From Middle English grot, from Old English grot, from Proto-West Germanic *grot, from Proto-Germanic *grutą, related to *greutą. More at grit, grout.
Possibly from Middle Dutch groot, the Old French gros Tournois (“a coin of Tours”), gros being from Medieval Latin denarius grossus (“large coin”). Related to German Groschen.

s: A small or puny person; one regarded as insignificant, contemptible.
A person who can be bullied playfully, or easily teased. Sometimes used as a pet-name (often for a younger sibling).
e: Of Uncertain origin; originally British slang of the 1910s. In a letter, dated 6 October 1944, J. R. R. Tolkien mentions a contemporary of his at Oxford University T.W. Earp, calling him "the original twerp"; but no corroborating evidence for this etymology has come to light.

s: An incompetent, indolent, or clumsy person.
A player having little skill, especially a golfer who duffs.
A pedlar or hawker, especially one selling cheap or substandard goods.
Cheap or substandard goods sold by a duffer.
Anything substandard, such as a counterfeit or a defective instance.
A cow that does not produce milk or produces substantially less than her peers do.
A cattle thief or thief of other livestock; one who alters the brands of cattle.
A racing pigeon that does not perform well.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the genus Discophora.
e: Cognate with duff#English:_particles or detritus, which see (origin is uncertain).

s: A clumsy, unsophisticated person; a yokel.
A short boom or spar used to extend a sail or secure a stay.
Dance, a series of reels, Scottish.
e: From Dutch boomken (“shrub, little tree”), equivalent to boom + -kin. Note that the English word boom is etymologically related to the aforementioned in the sense of "large stem", or "big tree". Compare German Baumke, Bäumchen.

s: Any of the long boards laid over joists to make a floor.
To sink the gas pedal into the floorboard of the car, in order to bring the car to the highest possible speed.
e: From floor + board.

s: A pain in the middle or inner ear.
Annoyance or aggravation caused by noise, especially the sound of someone nagging, complaining, issuing orders, etc.
e: From ear + ache.
From fats + -o.

s: The action of the verb to cavort
Pairing; the period of time when certain ungulates mate.

e: From me + -self.

s: Abandoned or forsaken by one's lover; having constant bad luck in romance; desperate for love.
e: From love + lorn.

s: Any member of the species Scophthalmus maximus (syn. Psetta maxima) of flatfish native to Europe.
Any of various other flatfishes of family Scophthalmidae that are found in marine or brackish waters.
e: From Middle English turbot, turbut, from Anglo-Norman turbut, Old French turbot, torbot, from Old Swedish tornbut, from törn (“thorn”) + but (“butt, flatfish”).

s: A shrub, Ribes nigrum, that produces small, very dark purple, edible berries.
The berry borne by this shrub.
e: From black + currant.
Borrowed from Swedish krona (“crown”). Doublet of corona, crown, korona, koruna, króna, krone.
From perverse + -ity, from Middle French perversité, from Latin perversitās.
From Middle English man servant, man servaunt; equivalent to man + servant.

s: To make (someone) a victim or sacrifice.
e: From victim + -ize.

s: The act of one who gorges, or eats to satiety.
A classroom, a room in a school used for instruction.
e: From school + room.

s: The art of speaking, especially public speaking, with expert control of gesture and voice, diction (articulation and word choice) and usage.
e: From Middle English elocucioun, ellocucioun, from Late Latin ēlocutiōnem. Doublet of elocutio.

s: A darkening of the skin resulting from exposure to sunlight or similar light sources.
To obtain a suntan by exposure to ultraviolet light.
To attempt to obtain a suntan.
e: From sun + tan.
Borrowed from French ignominie, from Latin ignōminia, from ig- (“not”) + nomen (“name”) (prefix assimilated form of in-).

s: A low chest of drawers on short legs.
A stand for a washbowl and jug.
A chair containing a chamber pot.
A kind of woman's headdress, raising the hair and fore part of the cap to a great height.
e: Thumb|Rococo commode, from circa 1760 thumb|Neoclassical commode, from circa 1780 Borrowed from French commode. Doublet of comodo.
From un- + principled.

s: Characteristic of a spindle; slender and of weak appearance.
e: From spindle + -y.
From Middle English legles, equivalent to leg + -less.

s: frailty or ailment, especially due to old age.
e: From infirm + -ity.

s: A mixture of solid and liquid food scraps fed to pigs etc; especially kitchen waste for this purpose.
A large quantity of liquid drunk at one swallow.
To drink (or, rarely, eat) greedily or to excess.
To wash (something) by flooding with water.
To move (a liquid or liquid-filled vessel) in a circular motion.
To move around or over a surface.
To inebriate; to fill with drink.
e: From Middle English swilen (“to wash; swirl; wash away”), from Old English swillan, swilian (“to wash; wash down; swill; gargle”), from Proto-West Germanic *swilljan, from Proto-Germanic *swiljaną (“to gulp, swallow”), from Proto-Indo-European *swel- (“to drink, gulp, swallow”). Related to swallow.

s: A split, salted and smoked herring or salmon.
raf world war ii code name
A patrol to protect fishing boats in the Irish and North Seas against attack from the air.
An Englishman who has moved to Australia.
A young Aboriginal man who has been initiated into to the rights of manhood.
To prepare (a herring or similar fish) by splitting, salting, and smoking.
To damage or treat with smoke.
To dry out with heat or harsh chemicals; to desiccate.
To drink or give a drink of alcohol, especially to intoxication.
To punish by spanking or caning.
To lead astray or frame; to cause to get into trouble.
e: From Old English cypera (“male salmon”), perhaps related to Old English coper (“reddish-brown metal”) (see copper), on resemblance of color. Another theory connects it to kip (“sharp, hooked lower jaw of the male salmon in breeding season”), from Middle English kippen (“to seize, snatch”), but OED doubts this.
Short form of UKIP er, influenced by kipper, the type of fish.

Perhaps akin to Old Norse kjapt (“briskly; impetuously”), kippa ("to snatch; pull; jerk" > Middle English kippen (“to seize”)), kipra (“to wrinkle; draw tightly”), Norwegian kjapp (“fast; brisk”), Dutch kippen (“to seize; catch; grip”). More at kip.
Short for "kids in parents' pockets eroding retirement savings".

s: A person, usually mounted on horseback, who robbed travelers on public roads.
e: From highway + man.
From lad + -ie.
From cunning + -ly.
A phonetic respelling of breeches (“trousers, pantaloons”), in use since at least the 18th century in Britain and British colonies.

s: The act by which somebody is maimed.
The time when dinner takes place, as
The midday mealtime as the main one: lunchtime.
The evening mealtime as the main one: suppertime.
e: From dinner + time.

s: The art of producing a belch.
Any of several forms of women’s divided garment for the lower body.
Women’s underpants with short legs; knickers or drawers.
e: Thumb Named after Amelia Bloomer.

s: A mixture of solid and liquid food scraps fed to pigs; swill.
e: From Middle English *hoggewasch (found only as Middle English hoggyswasch (“refuse of the kitchen for feeding pigs”)), equivalent to hog + wash.

s: An area near the entrance of mines which is used to load and unload coal.
An apparatus for unloading railroad freight cars by tipping them; the place where this is done.
To sell alcoholic liquor by retail.
To drink alcohol regularly or habitually, but not to excess.
To put up (hay, etc.) in bundles in order to dry it.
e: Unknown but possibly from a Scandinavian source (see Norwegian tipla), or from tip + -le.

s: The nocturnal, insectivorous, burrowing mammal Orycteropus afer, of the order Tubulidentata and somewhat resembling a pig. Common in some parts of sub-Saharan Africa.
e: Borrowed from Afrikaans aardvark (now rare), erdvark, from aarde (“earth”) + vark (“pig”). Early European colonists in South Africa noticed that the animal was similar to a pig, while aarde hints at the animal's habit of burrowing.

s: A platform where candidates in an election give speeches; a husting.
A debate during an election campaign where the public can question some or all of the candidates.
e: Originally the plural of husting, later construed as a singular.
See the etymology of the main entry.

s: A pale yellow raisin made from a seedless grape.
A wife or mistress of a sultan.
A female ruler of a sultanate.
A type of viol, a cither viol.
e: 1580s, Italian sultana. Displaced existing sultaness. Doublet of sultan, soldan.

s: The cry of a hen or goose, especially when laying an egg.
A laugh resembling the cry of a hen or goose.
To make a sharp, broken noise or cry, as a hen or goose does.
To laugh with a broken sound similar to a hen's cry.
To talk in a silly manner; to prattle.
To pretend to rattle (dice) in one's hand while gripping them so that they maintain their orientation.
e: From Middle English caclen, cakelen, perhaps from Old English *caclian, *cacolian, from Proto-West Germanic *kakulōn, *kakilōn (“to cackle, gaggle, yelp, snarl”), perhaps of Onomatopoeic origin. cack + -le.

s: The area of a farm, excluding the fields, usually surrounded by or adjacent to farm buildings.
e: From farm + yard.

s: To withdraw or repudiate a statement or opinion formerly expressed, especially formally and publicly.
To give a new cant (slant, angle) to something, in particular railway track on a curve.
e: First attested in 1535, from Latin recantare (“to sing back, reecho, sing again, repeat in singing, recant, recall, revoke, charm back or away”), from re- (“back”) + canto (“to chant, to sing”), frequentative of cano.
From re- + cant.

s: Having insufficient or no money; broke, penniless.
Infl of skin (Alternative form of skinned).
e: A variant of Doublet of skinned. Any similarity to skin a flint (“to go to great lengths to gain or save something, particularly money”) (referring to the brittleness and hardness of flint which makes it almost impossible to remove just its outer layer without shattering it) and its derivative skinflint (“one who is excessively cautious or stingy with money”) is coincidental.

s: A large two-handed sword historically used by the Scottish Highlanders.
e: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic claidheamh-mòr.

s: A worm that lives in the ground.
A worm of the family Lumbricidae, or, more generally, of the suborder Lumbricina.
e: From Middle English erthe-worm, erþe-worm, erþe worm (also as worm of þe erthe, worm of þe erþe), equivalent to earth + worm. Compare Äidwurm (“earthworm”), West Frisian ierdwjirm (“earthworm”), Dutch aardworm (“earthworm”), less common German Erdwurm (“earthworm”).

s: whether from age or hair powder.
e: From mould + -y.

s: One who minds, tends, or watches something such as a child, a machine, or cattle; a keeper.

A monitor assigned by the authorities to someone, such as a foreign visitor (to exercise control over their contacts with the populace) or a journalist or someone who is speaking to journalists (to monitor and control what they say).
One who is taken care of, such as a pauper child in the care of private person; a ward.
e: From Middle English mynder, mendowre (“one who has a good memory; bears in mind; watches over; a keeper”); equivalent to mind + -er.

s: Having the knees abnormally close together, and the ankles spread apart.
Of a person or animal, suffering from genu valgum (or tibia valga).
A half-god or hero; the offspring of a deity and a mortal.
Someone held up for reverence as a supreme example.
e: From demi- + god, from Latin semideus (“half-god”), which is probably a coining by the Roman poet Ovid for less important gods such as dryads.

s: A person who fails to develop mentally and physically due to a congenital hypothyroidism.
e: From French crétin (“cretin, idiot”), likely from crestin, an Alpine dialectal form of chrétien, from Latin christiānus in the lost sense of “anyone in Christendom”, often with a sense of “poor fellow”. Doublet of Christian.

s: Expressing a desire or a command for someone or something to go away.
e: . Compare English beware.
Inflected forms.

s: Executed in the manner of a master; showing competence and skill; masterful.
Like a master; arbitrary; domineering, imperious.
In a masterful manner; competently, masterfully.
e: From Middle English maisterli, from maister (“leader, ruler; high official; official in charge of a place; person in control; employer; owner; schoolmaster, teacher; scholar, sage; holder of a master's degree; religious teacher; master craftsman; expert; magician; social superior; husband; lover; Jesus Christ; a god; male stud animal”) + -li.
From Middle English maisterli (“artistically; skilfully; in the manner of a conqueror or master; overconfidently”), from maister (see etymology 1) + -li; analysable as master + -ly.

s: The handle of a broom (sweeping tool); (sometimes) the entire broom.
A broom imbued with magic, enabling one to fly astride the handle.
A control stick of an airplane or other vehicle.
To fly on a broomstick, as witches are said to.
e: From broom + stick.
Borrowed from French paralytique, from Latin paralyticus, from Ancient Greek παραλυτικός (“paralyzed”).

s: Dishonest and sneaky; done in a secret or sly manner.
in various ball games, of a ball
Thrown (etc.) with the hand brought forward and up from below.
In a sly, sneaky or secret manner.
To toss or lob with an underhand movement.
To excavate downward in successive steps or horizontal slices while positioned above on unbroken ore.
The lower of two hands, the hand under the work.
e: From under + hand.

s: The process by which something is mashed or beaten to pulp.
The action of soaking malted barley etc., in order to convert starch into sugars as part of the brewing process.
The process of preparing tea in a teapot.

e: From fond (“love, admire”) + -le.

s: Any of various flowering shrubs in the genus Rhododendron.
Especially, the common rhododendron or (Rhododendron ponticum).
e: The obsolete sense derives from Latin rhododendron (“oleander”), from Ancient Greek ῥοδόδενδρον (“oleander”), from ῥόδον (“rose”) + δένδρον (“tree”). The modern sense comes through the intermediary of the genus name Rhododendron, not closely related taxonomically, but with similar flowers to those of oleander.

From Middle English uncouth, from Old English uncūþ (“unknown; unfamiliar; strange”), from Proto-West Germanic *unkunþ, from Proto-Germanic *unkunþaz (“unknown”), equivalent to un- + couth. The modern pronunciation does not show /aʊ/, the usual development of the Middle English vowel from the Great Vowel Shift.

s: A short polite conversation before a serious conversation.
To move about smoothly and from side to side.
e: From Middle English slitheren, alteration of slideren (“to slither, creep”), from Old English slidrian (“to slip, slide, slither”), from Proto-West Germanic *slidrōn (“to slide, slither”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃sleydʰ- (“to slip”), equivalent to slide + -er.
From Middle English contemptible, from Latin contemptibilis. contempt + -ible.

s: The act of debriefing, or the state of being debriefed.
The report of a mission or project, or the information so obtained.
Having a pleasing shape, pleasant to look at.
e: From Middle English schaply, schappely (“well-shaped, beautiful, attractive”), perhaps from Old English *ġesċeaplīċ (“according to design, proper, fit”) (suggested by Old English ġesċeaplīċe (“properly, fitting, well”)), equivalent to shape + -ly.
From cease + -less.

s: The act of one who rummages.
Somewhat indignant, irritated, angry, in a snit, put out or annoyed.
e: From miff + -ed.

s: One of the four humors making up the body in ancient and mediaeval medicine; said to be cold and moist, and often identified with mucus.
Viscid mucus produced by the body, later especially mucus expelled from the bronchial passages by coughing.
A watery distillation, especially one obtained from plant matter; an aqueous solution.
Calmness of temperament, composure; also seen negatively, sluggishness, indifference.
e: From Middle English flewme, fleume, fleme, from Old French fleume, Middle French flemme (French flegme), and their source, Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (“flame; inflammation; clammy humor in the body”), from φλέγειν (“to burn”). Possible burning sensation when coughing up phlegm.

s: To run with quick light steps, to scamper.
e: Perhaps from hurry-skurry, a reduplication of hurry.

s: A herbaceous plant, Rubia tinctorum, native to Asia, cultivated for a red-purple dye (alizarin) obtained from the root.
The root of the plant, used as a medicine or a dye.
A dye made from the plant.
A deep reddish colour, like that of the dye.
Of a deep reddish purple colour, like that of the dye.
e: From Middle English mader, madere, mædere, from Old English mædere, mæddre, mædre, from Proto-Germanic *madarǭ (compare Swedish måra, Old Norse / Icelandic maðra), from Proto-Indo-European *modʰro-, cognate with *modrъ (“blue”), and compare Irish madar (“madder”), Latvian madara (“madder”).
Inflected forms.
Borrowed from Irish meadar.
From code + name.

s: The archetypal figure of a wise woman.
An ugly, evil-looking, or frightening old woman; a hag.
An old man, especially one who talks and acts like an old woman.
e: From Middle English crone, from Anglo-Norman carogne (compare central Old French charogne, whence modern French charogne). Doublet of carrion.

s: The motion of something that swoops.
A high-speed landing technique in skydiving.

e: From mis- + calculation.

s: In a manner that is extraordinary or amazing.
The plebeian class of Ancient Rome or its equivalent in other ancient societies.
The common people, especially the mob.
e: From Latin plēbs (“the plebeian class”), variant of earlier plēbēs. Later also understood as the plural of pleb.
