e: Borrowed from French purée.

s: summing up; adding (adding up) of a series of items.
e: From sum + -ation.

s: An aura of heightened interest, meaning or mystery surrounding a person or thing.
e: Borrowed from French mystique (“a mystic”), from Latin mysticus. See also the doublet Doublet of mystic.

s: To have an affinity for clumping into a glob.
e: See glum.
glom or glob + clump.
From un- + climb + -able.
From un- + trainable.

s: In the fifth place; fifth in a row.
e: From fifth + -ly.

s: To sniff; also, to snivel or snuffle.
Followed by out: to speak (words) in a nasal, snuffling manner.
A small, wide, pear-shaped glass used for drinking aromatic liquors such as bourbon and brandy.
Synonym of nip (“a small amount of an alcoholic beverage, especially one equivalent to what a snifter might hold”)
Synonym of cocaine addict; a sniffer.
A small amount of cocaine taken by inhaling through the nose.
A handheld device used to detect signals from radio transmitters; a sniffer.
e: [[File:Cognac served in a brandy snifter - Evan Swigart (cropped).jpg|thumb|Cognac in a snifter.]] The verb is derived from Middle English snifteren, snifter, snyfter (“to sniffle”), possibly from *snift (possibly derived from an Old Norse word—compare Old Danish snifte and Swedish snyfta (“to sniffle; to sob”); probably ultimately imitative) + -er- + -en.

s: Tending to impoverish (To weaken in quality; to deprive of some strength or richness); limiting.
To weaken in quality; to deprive of some strength or richness.
e: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).

s: A woman who is insane or mentally disturbed.
e: From mad + -woman.

s: The adult female members of a community.
e: women + folk.
From brick + -er.

s: The art or practice of transferring a design by means of pounce.
A sudden leap, as of an animal when it pounces.
That cannot be overcome or defeated.
A ship that was designed to be unsinkable.
e: From un- + sink + -able.

s: A person who is anti-fun, or prevents others from having fun.
e: From kill + joy, first attested in 1776.

s: An English noblewoman or gentlewoman; the form of address to such a person; a lady.
e: Partly representing a colloquial pronunciation of my + lady, partly from French milady, from English my Lady. Compare milord.

s: One who plots or schemes, who formulates devious plans.
e: From scheme + -er.

s: The act of giving a scowl.
The route taken by a party of Native Americans going on a warlike expedition.
A course of action that leads to battle or hostility.
e: From war + path.

s: To pull, to pull out or away, to pull sharply.
To drag or haul, especially with a rope; specifically to haul or hoist and tie up by means of a rope.
Now only in the phrase in a trice: a very short time; the blink of an eye, an instant, a moment.
e: From Middle English trīcen, trice, trise (“to pull or push; to snatch away; to steal”), from Middle Dutch trīsen (“to hoist”) (modern Dutch trijsen) or Middle Low German trissen (“to trice the spritsail”); further etymology uncertain.

From Middle English trīce, trise, in the phrase at a trīce (“with a single, quick motion; at once”), later also in the phrases in a trice, on a trice, and with a trice. The word is ultimately from Middle English trīcen: see etymology 1 above.

From Middle English trīce, tryys, tryyst, from Middle Dutch trīse, trijs (modern Dutch trijs (“hoisting-block, pulley, windlass”)) or Middle Low German trīsse, trītse (“hoisting-rope, tackle”); probably related to the verb trice (see etymology 1 above), and perhaps to Old English tryndel (“roller, wheel”) (see further at trend, trindle).
From Middle English corrector, correctour, equivalent to correct + -or.

s: A complication of pregnancy characterized by seizures and coma due to hypertension.
e: Borrowed from New Latin eclampsia, from French éclampsie, from Ancient Greek ἔκλᾰμψῐς (“sudden development, violent onset”), from ἐκλᾰ́μπω (“to shine or beam forth; to burst forth violently”) + -σῐς.

s: Of or related to the appearance or behaviour of a well-mannered woman.
In the manner of a lady.
e: From lady + -like.
Euphemistic substitute for Christ, perhaps a corruption of Christ King. Compare criminy, cripes, crivvens. Attested from the 19th century.

s: A soldier who marches and fights on foot; a foot soldier.
A man in waiting; a male servant whose duties are to attend the door, the carriage, the table, etc.
A servant who runs in front of his master's carriage.
A metallic stand with four feet, for keeping anything warm before a fire.
A moth of the family Arctiidae (or subfamily Arctiinae); so called from its livery-like colors.
A bar that connects the treadle of a spinning wheel to the wheel.
e: From Middle English fotman, footman, foteman (“foot soldier, running footman”), from Old English *fōtman, *fōtmann (attested only as Old English fēþman, fēþemann (“footman”), equivalent to foot + man.

s: A skin disease of nonhuman mammals caused by parasitic mites (Sarcoptes spp., Demodecidae spp.).
e: From Middle English manjewe, manjeue, from Old French manjue, derived from mangier (“to eat”) (modern French manger (“to eat”)), from Latin manducare.

s: The wrinkling of the brows or face in frowning; the expression of displeasure, sullenness, or discontent in the countenance; an angry frown.
To wrinkle the brows, as in frowning or displeasure; to put on a frowning look; to look sour, sullen, severe, or angry.
To look gloomy, dark, or threatening; to lower.
To look at or repel with a scowl or a frown.
e: From Middle English scowlen, scoulen, skoulen (also as Middle English schoulen), probably of origin. Compare Danish skule (“to scowl”), Norwegian skule (“to scowl”).

s: Term of respect for a woman of the peerage without using her title.
Formal form of address for a lady judge (as opposed to the informal "judge").
e: From Middle English ladyschipe, ladyshipe; equivalent to lady + -ship.

s: Marked by unthinking recklessness with disregard for danger; boldly rash; hotheaded.
Indecency; corruption; unkindness, meanness, spite, harshness, cruelty.
A nasty action, object, quality, etc. (all senses of nasty).
e: From nasty + -ness.

s: To debase; to lower; to degrade.
To manage; to conduct; to treat.
To conduct; to behave; to comport; followed by the reflexive pronoun.
To subtract the mean from (a value, or every observation in a data set).
e: (1595) From de- + mean (“lowly, base, common”), from Middle English mene, aphetic variation of imene (“mean, base, common”), from Old English ġemǣne (“mean, common”). Compare English bemean.
From Middle English demenen, demeinen, from Anglo-Norman demener, from Old French demener, from de- + mener (“to conduct, lead”), from Latin mināre, from minārī (“to threaten”).
Variant of demesne.
de- + mean.

s: An offensive or obscene act or expression.
e: From vulgar + -ity, from Latin vulgaritas.

s: Used to express discontent with a situation or occurrence.
Senses relating to colour, and to dipping something into a liquid.
A pigment or other substance that colours or dyes; specifically, a pigment used as a cosmetic.
A medicine consisting of one or more substances dissolved in ethanol or some other solvent.
To colour or stain (something) with, or as if with, a dye or pigment.
Followed by with: to add to or impregnate (something) with (a slight amount of) an abstract or physical quality; to imbue, to taint, to tinge.
To dissolve (a substance) in ethanol or some other solvent to produce a medicinal tincture.
To have a taint or tinge of some quality.

e: From splendid + -ly.

s: A swift or rapid turning or rotation; a circling movement.
An organized attack where a group of people, usually teenagers, surround and attack women, with sudden physical assaults or harassment.
Subject to sudden or frequent changes.
Capable of camouflaging itself by changing colour.
e: From Middle English chaungeable, from chaungeable, from Late Latin cambiāre (“to change”), equivalent to change + -able.

s: Any of the Old World plants, of the genus Calendula, with orange, yellow or reddish flowers.
Any of the New World plants, of the genus Tagetes, with orange, yellow or reddish flowers.
Alternative form of Marigold (rubber glove for cleaning).
Having the color of marigolds, a bright yellowish-orange hue.
e: From Middle English marigolde, marygoldye, from Mary + enm:golde (“marigold”).

s: The act of one who pines.
To eat hastily or greedily; to scoff or scarf (often used with up)
An act of eating hastily or greedily.
A rapid straight putt so strongly played that, if the ball had not gone into the hole, it would have gone a long way past.
Of a turkey, to make its characteristic vocalisation; also, used of certain other birds.
To make the sound of a turkey.
The sound of a turkey; or, a similar vocalisation of another bird.
e: From Middle English gobben (“to drink or swallow greedily”), of Uncertain origin le. Middle English gobben is perhaps an alteration of Middle English globben (“to gulp down”), related to English gulpen (“to gulp”). However, compare also French gober.
Onomatopoetic of the sound of a turkey.

s: A two-player cue sport played with two cue balls and one red ball, on a snooker sized table.
Any of various games played on a tabletop, usually with several balls, one or more of which is hit by a cue.
e: From French billard, originally referring to the wooden cue stick, diminutive of Old French bille (“log, tree trunk”), from Vulgar Latin *bilia, probably of origin (compare Old Irish bile (“large tree, tree trunk”)), from Proto-Celtic *belyos (“tree”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yos (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”).
From un- + invited.

s: The son of one's spouse from a previous relationship.
e: From Middle English stepsone, stepsune, from Old English stēopsunu (“stepson”), from Proto-Germanic *steupasunuz (“stepson”), equivalent to step- + son.

s: The act of one who pries.
The act of one who canvasses or solicits.
The Christian sacrament at which someone, usually a child, is baptized and given a Christian name.
Any instance of someone's or something's being christened.
e: From Middle English cristenynge, from Old English cristnung; compare christen + -ing.

s: A severe, formal or official reproof; reprehension, rebuke, private or public.
To reprove in a formal or official way.
e: From French réprimande, from réprimer (“to repress”).

s: Offensive or repulsive; arousing disgust or aversion.
e: From Middle English repugnaunt, from Old French repugnant, borrowed from Latin repugnans, present participle of repugnare (“to oppose, to fight against”), from re- (“back, against”) + pugnare (“to fight”); see pugnacious. re- + la:pugnare + -ant.

s: of being repaired, amended, cured or rectified; unrepairable.
e: From Middle French irréparable, from Old French, from Latin irreparabilis, equivalent to ir- + reparable.

s: of a person or group of people
The state of being mad, insanity
A cyclical mental disease, apparently linked to the lunar phases.
e: From lunatic + -acy.

s: A mineral of pegmatite deposits, often used as a gemstone (molecular formula Be3Al2Si6O18).
An example (a stone) of the mineral beryl.
Of a dull bluish green colour.
e: Prakrit pi Inherited from Middle English beryl, from Old French beril, from Latin bērillus, bēryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (“beryl”), in turn borrowed from Middle Indic forms like Pali veḷuriya or Prakrit 𑀯𑁂𑀭𑀼𑀮𑀺𑀅, from, probably named after Velur (modern day Belur) in southern India.

s: A woman present at the christening of a baby who promises to help raise the child in a Christian manner; a female godparent who sponsors the baptism of a child.
e: From Middle English godmoder, from Old English godmōdor (“godmother”), equivalent to god- + mother. Cognate with Old High German gotmuoter (“godmother”), Old Norse guðmóðir (“godmother”), Icelandic guðmóður (“godmother”), Swedish gudmoder (“godmother”), Danish gudmor (“godmother”).

s: Lacking fulfillment; marked by a feeling of failure to achieve goals or desires.
Not yet provided as promised, particularly with respect to a contract or an order for a supply of something.
e: From un- + fulfilled.

s: To persist steadfastly in pursuit of an undertaking, task, journey, or goal, even if hindered by distraction, difficulty, obstacles, or discouragement.
To stay constant; to continue in a certain state; to remain.
e: From Middle English perseveren, from Old French perseverer, from Latin persevērāre (“to continue steadfastly, persist, persevere”), from perseverus (“very strict or earnest”), from per (“through, by the means of”) + severus (“strict, earnest”). Doublet of perseverate.

s: Miscellaneous items, especially the set of equipment required for a particular activity.
Objects that a married woman owns, such as clothing and jewellery, apart from her dowry.

s: Not amused; thus often offended or put off.
e: From un- + amused.

s: To sow (to disperse or plant seeds).
To impregnate (to cause to become pregnant).
e: Borrowed from Latin inseminātus, the perfect passive participle of insemināre (“to sow”). in- + seminate.

s: To revolve round a central point; to move spirally about an axis, as a tornado.
To revolve and behave unsteadily around a central axis.
e: From gyrus (“fold, convolution”) + -ate.

s: Syn of hairball; a ball of fur, especially one coughed up by a cat.
A particularly furry person or animal.
A large, disorganized battle involving many different aircraft (especially fighters) or warships.
e: From fur + ball.

s: Any small passerine bird mostly of the genus Baeolophus, which are found in the woods of the Northern Hemisphere and of Africa.
e: From Middle English titmose, compound of tit#Etymology 3 (“small bird”) and mose, from Old English māse (“titmouse”), from Proto-West Germanic *maisā, from Proto-Germanic *maisǭ (compare Dutch mees, German Meise, Old Norse meisingr, French mésange), from *maisaz (“tiny, puny”) (compare Norwegian meis (“skinny weakling”)).

s: Constantly complaining, especially in a childish way due to insignificant matters; fretful, whiny.
Quick to become bad-tempered or cross, especially due to insignificant matters; irritable, pettish, petulant.
Of weather: blustery, windy; also, of wind: cold and strong; bitter, sharp.
Harmful, injurious; also, mischievous; or malicious, spiteful.
Obstinately in the wrong; perverse, stubborn.
Of a thing: evoking a feeling of distaste, horror, etc.
e: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English pievish, peuysche, pevish, pevysh (“capricious, wilful; perverse, wayward”); further etymology Uncertain, possibly from one of the following: The adverb is derived from the adjective.

s: A person who is skilled at, professes, or practices seismology.
e: From seismology + -ist.

s: In a scornful manner; contemptuously, derisively.
e: Inherited from Middle English scornfully; equivalent to scornful + -ly.

s: The act by which something is blighted.
To approach and speak to boldly or aggressively, as with a demand or request.
To join side to side; to border.
To sail along the coast or side of.
To approach; to come up to.
To speak to first; to address; to greet.
e: From Middle French accoster, acoster, from Old French acoster (“to stand beside”) (whence Medieval Latin accostare), from Old French a- + coste (“side, flank”).
From insufferable + -ly.

s: Gerund of dawdle: the act of one who dawdles.
e: From dawdle + -ing.

s: A musical instrument consisting of a flat sounding box with numerous strings placed on a horizontal surface, played with a plectrum or fingertips.
Related or similar instruments in other cultures, such as the Chinese guqin or Norwegian harpeleik; especially any chordophone without a neck, and with strings that pass over the body.
To make a sound similar to that made by a zither; to move while making such a sound.
e: Borrowed from German Zither, from Old High German zithara, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (“a kind of harp”). Doublet of cithara, cither, guitar.

s: The state of being grandiose (pompous or pretentious).
e: From grandiose + -ity.
Childish mispronunciation of little.

s: A pair of knee-breeches made of leather, typical of Bavaria and Austria.
e: Borrowed from German Lederhose. The final -n probably from the German plural; alternatively influenced by Lederhosn. 180px|right.

s: The ability to be, or the characteristic of being, at all places at the same time (usually only attributed to God).
e: From omni- + presence.

s: The act of making something quiet.
In an indignant manner; with indignation.
e: From indignant + -ly.

s: An approach focusing on observable behavior which, generally assuming that behavior is determined by the environment and denying any independent significance for mind, largely ignores any pathophysiological processes which may, or may not, underlie subjective, behavioral phenomena.

The theory that a mental state is identical to the disposition or tendency to behave in accordance with the physical causes; statements about the mind are reducible to statements of physical behavior.
e: From behavior + -ism.
From infinitesimal + -ly.

s: The side of a right triangle opposite the right angle.
e: From Latin hypotenusa, from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνουσα πλευρά (“side subtending [the right angle]”), from ὑποτείνουσα (“stretching, extending, subtending”), active participle of ὑποτείνω (“subtend, stretch under”).

s: Of or relating to the glottis.
A sound made with the glottis
e: From glottis + -al.

s: The muscular substance of the heart; the middle of the three layers forming the outer wall of the human heart.
e: From New Latin myocardium, from Ancient Greek μῦς (“muscle”) + καρδίᾱ (“heart”).

s: A whirling or turning on the toes in dancing, primarily in ballet.
The whirling about of a horse.
A wooden mouthpiece assembly or lip rest used in some European double-reed instruments.
To perform a pirouette; to whirl on the toes, like a dancer.
e: Borrowed from French pirouette, see there for more; attested since 1706.

s: Irritable; impatient; short-tempered; often, in a condescending way.
e: From snip + -y. Compare snippig, snippich (“short, brief, blunt”), Dutch snippig (“snippy, shrill”), Low German snippig (“snippy, snappy”), German schnippisch (“snippy, snappy”).

s: An undertaker or funeral director; especially, one who is also the embalmer or cremator.
A room, rooftop, balcony, or terrace, used for its abundant sunlight, especially when used as a medical treatment.
Synonym of tanning salon, a room or business used for its sunlamps or tanning beds.
An earthen structure constructed by certain ants for the purpose of brood incubation.
e: Borrowed from Latin sōlārium (“sundial, place for enjoying sunlight”), from sōl (“sun”) + -ārium (“-arium: indicating related places or devices”).

s: An acrobat who is capable of twisting their body into unusual positions.
One who twists words and phrases.
e: From contortion + -ist.

s: In mort, bridge, and similar games, the partner of dummy.
e: Borrowed from French vivant (“living”).

s: A crustless quiche: a molded omelette in which vegetables, cheese, etc., are mixed into the eggs and cooked together.
e: Borrowed from Italian frittata, from fritto (“fried”).
From Middle English reverently, equivalent to reverent + -ly.

None of the various attested forms appear in the OED, in Victor & Dalzell’s Concise New Partridge Dictionary of Slang and Unconventional English, nor in Webster’s New Universal Unabridged Dictionary. According to the RHD, 'looky' (also 'lookee') is an interjection attested from 1875–80 which is an alternative form of the imperative look ye! Similarly, the linguist Andrew L.

s: In an authoritative manner; with authority.
e: From Middle English auctoritatively, auctoritativeli; compare Medieval Latin auctoritātīve; equivalent to authoritative + -ly.

s: The sound of fabric or fur moving in the air.
The movement that produces such a sound.
A switching; a beating with twigs or a cane.
The mutual exchange of pre-owned clothes, especially at an organised party.
Having a round, spherical or curved shape; circular; orbicular.
Having a round body shape; portly or pudgy; obese.
Full and rich; orotund; sonorous; full-toned.
e: Latin rotundus (“round”), from Latin rota (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreth₂- (“to run, to roll”). Doublet of round.

s: To cause (a sound) to be (repeatedly) bounced against one or more surfaces; to re-echo.
Followed by on (to): to deflect or divert (flames, heat, etc.) on to something.
To heat (something) by deflecting flames on to, or passing flames over, it.
To repeatedly reflect (heat, light, or other radiation).
Of sound: to (repeatedly) bounce against one or more surfaces; to echo or re-echo, to resound.
Chiefly followed by to or with: of a place or thing: to ring or vibrate with many echoing sounds; to re-echo, to resound.
Often followed by from: of heat or light: to be (repeatedly) reflected.
Of a thing: to be heated by having flames, hot gases, etc., deflected or passed over it.
Ringing or vibrating with many echoing sounds; re-echoing, resounding, reverberating.
e: Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, perfect passive participle of reverberō (“to rebound; to reflect; to repel”) (see -ate), whence Middle French reverberer (French réverbérer) and Middle English reverberen (“to send back”)), from re- and verberō (“to beat; to lash, whip”) (from verber (“rod; lash, whip”) + -ō).

Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate for more. (“ringing or vibrating with many echoing sounds”) was popularized by its use in Twelfth Night (written; published 1623) by the English playwright William Shakespeare (1564–1616): see the quotation.

s: In a rueful manner; causing, feeling or expressing regret or sorrow.
Characterized by brawn; muscular, thewy; strong.
e: From Middle English brawny; equivalent to brawn + -y.

s: Prim and fussy; too precise; overparticular.
e: 1895, either an alteration of precise, prim + sissy, or a prim + fussy; first attested in a work of American writer Joel Chandler Harris.

s: An American feline carnivore (Leopardus pardalis, syn. Felis pardalis) covered with blackish ocellated spots and blotches which are variously arranged.
e: From French ocelot, a word formed by Buffon from Classical Nahuatl ōcēlōtl (“jaguar”).

s: A Mexican dish made by wrapping a filling in a tortilla, then baking in a sauce.
e: From Spanish enchilada, a use of the of enchilar (“to add chili pepper to”).

s: Soft serve; a cone of soft serve
e: From soft + -ie.

s: The act of one who tills.
e: From Middle English tillynge, tiliyng, tilyenge, tylynge, from Old English tiliende, tilġende, equivalent to till + -ing.
From Middle English tyllynge, tiling, tilinge, telynge, from Old English tilung, teolung, equivalent to till + -ing.

s: Of a person: attractive or pleasing to look at; beautiful, handsome; also, attractive but not particularly beautiful or handsome.
Of a person, an action, behaviour, etc.: meeting accepted moral or social norms; appropriate, becoming, proper.
Of a thing: beautiful, elegant, well-composed; also, delicate, fine.
Pleasing to the feelings or senses; agreeable, nice, pleasant.
e: The verb is derived from the adjective.
From Middle English comli, cumly, cumeliche (“beautifully, handsomely; gracefully; splendidly; fittingly, properly; well”), from Old English cȳme (see etymology 1) + Middle English -li.

s: A game in which each player acts out a word or phrase, usually based on puns of each syllable and without speaking, for the others to guess.
e: See charade. As a game, originally a clipped form of acting charades or, without talking, dumb charades but now usually understood as a plurale tantum.
From Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from Latin omni- (“all”), and scient from the Latin scientia (“knowledge”).

s: The mechanical widening of a narrowed or totally obstructed blood vessel generally caused by atheroma.
e: From angio + plasty.
From Middle English fomy, from Old English fāmiġ, fǣmiġ (“frothy, foamy”), from Proto-West Germanic *faimag, *faimīg, equivalent to foam + -y.

s: A fly ball that is weakly hit just over the infielders.
A filmed or videotaped outtake that has recorded an amusing accident or mistake.
A gaff-rigged fore-and-aft sail set from and aft of the aftmost mast of a square-rigged ship; a spanker.
A radio which interferes with other radios, causing them to bloop (squeal loudly).
The Vietnam-era M79 grenade launcher (due to its distinctive report).
e: From bloop + -er, of US origin.

s: Containing or using more words than necessary; long-winded, wordy.
Producing detailed output for diagnostic purposes.
e: From Latin verbōsus (“prolix, wordy, verbose”). Verbōsus is derived from verbum (“word”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“to say, speak”)) + -ōsus. Equivalent to verb + -ose.

s: A sylvan deity or demigod, male companion of Pan or Dionysus, represented as part man and part goat, and characterized by riotous merriment and lasciviousness, sometimes pictured with a perpetual erection.
Any of various butterflies of the nymphalid subfamily Satyrinae, having brown wings marked with eyelike spots; a meadow brown.
e: From French satyre, from Latin satyrus, from Ancient Greek σάτυρος.

s: To grant a sublease out of property held under a lease.
e: From sub- + let.

s: A French parfait (parfait glacé), an iced dessert made with egg yolks, sugar, cream, and flavouring (usually fruit), sometimes with the addition of a liqueur.
An American parfait, a layered dessert often consisting of fruit, ice cream, pastries, whipped topping, etc. and served in a glass, often a parfait glass.
A smooth pâté, usually made from liver and flavoured with liqueurs.
e: French parfait (“perfect”). Doublet of parfit, perfect, perfecto, perfectus.

s: Someone skilled in the writing of shorthand or the use of a stenotype machine, especially for the purpose of rapid transcription of speech. One employed in such a role: a professional transcriptionist who employs shorthand.
One who invents or studies systems of shorthand.
e: From stenography + -er.
From Middle English stifnen, equivalent to stiff + -en.

s: An electronic device that produces special effects on the sound produced by an electric guitar etc.
Fictional energy weapon, with multiple settings for degree of intensity, from the television series Star Trek (1966–69).
To shoot with a phaser weapon.
One who studies or practices zoology.
e: From zoology + -ist.
Thumb|Pre-sliced American baloney Phonetic spelling of bologna.
Origin unclear. Perhaps from the slang word balonie.

s: Characterized by giving love and affection.
Showing a decline of mental faculties, especially when it occurs in old age.
e: From Middle English dotynge; equivalent to dote + -ing.
From snob + -y.

s: The sound produced when someone or something bellows
The act by which somebody is bewitched; a curse or enchantment.
e: From bewitch + -ing.

[[File:024 WanAlbum (2) (7975894513).jpg|thumb|A couple in Malaysia at their nuptials]] From nuptial, borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”) (also plural only), from nūpta, from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”), from Proto-Indo-European *sneubho-, *snewbʰ- (“to marry, wed”).

s: An eccentric, crazy or foolish person.
Someone addicted to crack cocaine (i.e. a drug addict).
e: Mostly likely a back-etymology of pot, to form crack + pot. Originally, from crack + pate. Compare typologically Russian чо́кнутый (чо́каться, onomatopoeic), see crack for the further typology.
From un- + inspiring.

s: Form of The ordinal numeral form; last in order of a series of a thousand; next after the nine hundred and ninety-ninth.
The person or thing in the thousandth position.
One of a thousand equal parts of a whole.
e: From thousand + -th.

s: A semi-aquatic, herbivorous, African hoofed mammal of the family Hippopotamidae.
e: From Latin and New Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος, from ἵππος (“horse”) (English hippo-) + ποταμός (“river”).. (from native Old English nicor) and river horse.

s: Something or someone that is physically attractive.
Something that is a remarkable example of its type.
e: Either a back-formation from beauty or a clipping thereof.

s: Of or pertaining to the Puritans, or to their doctrines and practice.
Precise in observance of legal or religious requirements; strict; overscrupulous; rigid (often used by way of reproach or contempt).
e: From puritanic + -al.
From stealthy + -ly.

s: The act of something being hurtled or thrown.
To open or undo, as what is wrapped or folded.
To flatten (a three-dimensional model) into a two-dimensional plane.
e: From Middle English unwrappen, equivalent to un- + wrap.

s: To work against; to oppose (especially to incite a reaction).
e: From Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνίζομαι, from ἀντι- + ἀγωνίζομαι. ant- + agon + -ize.

s: The act or process by which a document is proofread.
Causing physical harm or injury; harmful, hurtful.
Causing harm to one's reputation; invidious, defamatory, libelous, slanderous.
e: From Middle English injurious, from Anglo-Norman enjurius, from Latin iniūriōsus; analysable as injury + -ous.

s: of an alcoholic beverage, especially wine
e: From Middle English drinkable, drynkeable, equivalent to drink + -able.

s: Disparaging or derisive in an insinuative way.
An underhanded, tricky person given to sharp practice; a sharper; a cheat.
e: Probably from a dialectal variant of Doublet of snithe. See snithe. Alternatively, possibly a metathetic corruption of Middle English snythand (“piercing (the heart), cold, biting”). More at snithe. Compare typologically cutting, Russian ко́лкий (akin to коло́ть).

s: Specifically, a person whose job it is to kill insects and other pests in a building.
e: Borrowed from Latin exterminātor..

s: To drive back or beat back; to repulse.
To deny the truth of something, especially by presenting arguments that disprove it.
e: Inherited from Middle English rebutten, rebouten, from Old French reboter, rebuter, rebouter, etc., from re- + boter, buter, bouter (“to butt”). Entered English around 1302-1307.

s: an affront to one's dignity or pride
e: Borrowed from Latin indignitās, indignitātem. Equivalent to indign + -ity.

s: Of or relating to the brain.
e: From Middle English brayny; equivalent to brain + -y.
From un- + convinced.

s: Any of a class of non-inflecting words and multiword terms typically employed to connect a following noun or a pronoun, in an adjectival or adverbial sense, with some other word: a particle used with a noun or pronoun (in English always in the objective case) to make a phrase limiting some other wor
A proposition; an exposition; a discourse.
e: From Middle English preposicioun, from Old French preposicion, from Latin praepositio, praepositionem, from praepono (“to place before”), equivalent to pre- + position. Compare French préposition.
From pre- + position.

s: The act of removing somebody's clothes.
Reducing grief, sorrow, or disappointment; comforting.
The act by which somebody is consoled.
A person who sometimes wears clothes traditionally worn by and associated with the opposite sex; typically a male who cross-dresses occasionally by habit or personal choice.

A person, typically a heterosexual male, who compulsively seeks and derives paraphilic sexual arousal from cross-dressing, especially if the urges and behavior cause the patient distress or social impairment.
An animal that engages in sexual mimicry.
e: Borrowed from Latin trāns + vestītus, form of vestiō (“to clothe, to dress”) (as in English vestment, vest). Literally, a "cross-dresser". From transvestitism, from German Transvestitismus, coined in 1910 by Magnus Hirschfeld (the practice itself is much older).

s: A mountebank, someone who addresses crowds in the street; (especially), an itinerant seller of medicines or drugs.
A malicious trickster; a fake person, especially one who deceives for personal profit.
e: From Middle French charlatan, from ciarlatano (“quack”), a blend of ciarlatore (“chatterer”) + cerretano (“hawker, quack”) (Cerreto di Spoleto being a village in Umbria, known for its quacks).

s: To act as a detective; to try to discover who committed a crime, or, more generally, to solve a mystery.
e: Clipping of sleuthhound.
From Old English slǣwþ, corresponding to slow + -th.

s: A wireless telecommunications device that receives text or voice messages.
A computer program running in a text terminal, used to view (but not modify) the contents of a text file moving down the file one line or one screen at a time.
Something (a document, book etc.) that has a specified number of pages.
One who makes up type into pages of a book; one who binds or sorts pages into a book.
e: From page + -er or er (sense 3).

s: To tear up (a plant, etc.) by the roots, or as if by the roots; to extirpate, to root up.
To destroy (something) utterly; to eradicate, exterminate.
To remove (someone or something) from a familiar circumstance, especially suddenly and unwillingly.
Of oneself or someone: to move away from a familiar environment (for example, to live elsewhere).
Of a pig or other animal: to dig up (something in the ground) using the snout; to rummage for (something) in the ground; to grub up, to root, to rout.
e: From up- + root (“to tear up by the roots; (figuratively) to remove forcibly from a place; to eradicate, exterminate”). Root is derived from root (“underground part of a plant”), from Middle English rote, from Old English rōt, rōte, from Old Norse rót, from Proto-Germanic *wrōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).

s: Scented, having been given a pleasant smell.
e: From perfume + -ed.

s: Matter that is composed of the antiparticles of those that constitute normal matter.
A form of matter that has a key property, such as charge, opposite to that of ordinary matter.
e: From anti- + matter. Coined by Arthur Schuster to describe matter that resists gravity in a jocular article in Nature titled "Potential Matter.—A Holiday Dream", but not used in a modern sense until the 1940s.

s: The act of one who gloats.
A short flash of light, usually when reflected off a shiny surface.
To glance; to peep forth, as a flower from the bud; to glitter.
To cause to flash or gleam; to reflect.
e: 15th century. Borrowed from Scots glint, from Middle English glenten (“to shine, gleam; flash”), probably from Old Norse *glenta, from Proto-Germanic *glantijaną, causitive of Proto-Germanic *glintaną (“to gleam, shine”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to shine”).

s: To arrange or score music for performance by an orchestra.
To compose or arrange orchestral music for a dramatic performance.
To arrange or direct diverse elements to achieve a desired effect
e: From orchestra + -ate. Compare French orchestrer.

s: The state or quality of being strange, odd or weird.
The product or result of being strange.
One of the quantum numbers of subatomic particles, depending upon the relative number of strange quarks and anti-strange quarks.
e: From Middle English straungenesse; equivalent to strange + -ness.

s: A release of emotional tension after an overwhelming vicarious experience, resulting in the purging or purification of the emotions, as through watching a dramatic production (especially a tragedy).
Any release of emotional tension to the same effect, more widely.
A purification or cleansing, especially emotional.

A therapeutic technique to relieve tension by reestablishing the association of an emotion with the memory or idea of the event that first caused it, and then eliminating it by complete expression (called the abreaction).
A purging of the digestive system.
e: From Ancient Greek κάθαρσις (“cleansing, purging”), from καθαίρω (“I cleanse”). Coined in the dramatic-emotional sense by Aristotle.
From triumphant + -ly.

s: Any of the about 250 species of flowering plant of the genus Nepeta, family Lamiaceae, certain of which are said to have medicinal qualities.
Nepeta cataria and Nepeta grandiflora (and perhaps other species), which are well-known for causing an apparently harmless pheromone-based intoxication among certain cats.
Something that causes excitement or interest.
e: Compound of cat + nep, nip (“catnip”), from Middle English nep, from Old English nepte, from Proto-West Germanic *nepetā, from Latin nepeta (“catnip”). Compare earlier catmint (“catnip”), from Middle English catt mynte, which very likely existed in Old English (as *cattes minte) as well.

s: A robe usually made of terrycloth intended to be worn when one is still damp from bathing or when there is no immediate need to dress fully.
e: From bath + robe.

s: A motion or gesture that darts.
The use of darts (folds stitched on a garment).
A young person who causes trouble or violence, typically as a member of a gang or other group.
A member of the United States Coast Guard.
A type of fish, an anadromous smelt, Thaleichthys pacificus, found in the North Pacific.
e: Probably a variant of the Irish surname Houlihan, 1890s.
Borrowed from ulakan, from Clatsop, with spelling and pronunciation influenced by the preceding.

s: To trace (a line, etc. in drawing) again.
To go back over something, usually in an attempt at rediscovery.
The period when the beam of the cathode-ray tube returns to its initial horizontal position in order to start the next line of the display.
e: From French retracer, from Middle French retracier.

s: In a surreptitious manner; stealthily, furtively, secretly.
e: From surreptitious + -ly.

s: Consisting of two terms, or parts.
Of or relating to the binomial distribution.
A quantity expressed as the sum or difference of two terms.
A scientific name at the rank of species, with two terms: a generic name and a specific name.
e: Formed from Late Latin binōmium + -al. The derivation of binōmium is unclear. It was used by Gerard of Cremona in the 12th century. Suggested sources are the Latin nōmen (“name”), the Ancient Greek νομός (“distribution, pasture”), or the Old French nom (“name”).

s: A catecholamine hormone and neurotransmitter; as a hormone, secreted by the adrenal gland in response to stress (when it stimulates the autonomic nervous system); as a neurotransmitter, synthesized from norepinephrine. It is also used as a medication.
e: From Ancient Greek ἐπι- (“upon”) + νεφρός (“kidney”) + -ine.

s: Sexual intercourse by people who are not married to each other, or which is considered illicit in another way.
e: From Middle English fornicacioun, from Old French fornicacion, from Latin fornicātiō, from fornix (“brothel”).

s: A receptacle for ash and butts from cigarettes and cigars.
e: From ash + tray. Compare German Aschenbecher.

s: To live longer than; continue to live after the death of; overlive; survive.
To live through or past (a given time).
To live longer; continue to live.
e: From Middle English outliven, equivalent to out- + live.
From un- + tied.
From untie + -ed.

s: A woman's private sitting room, dressing room, or bedroom.
e: Borrowed from French boudoir, from bouder (“to sulk”), of origin.

From Middle English hondywerk, handiwerc, from Old English handġeweorc (“work done by hand, creation”), from hand (“hand”) + ġeweorc (“work”). Equivalent to hand + work, though it may now be reinterpreted as handy (“skilful”) + work. Compare Hondwierk, Dutch handwerk, German Handwerk.

s: Like a living being; resembling life; being an accurate representation.
e: From life + -like.

s: Wild, uncontrolled, especially of animals not domesticated or trained to human contact.
e: From Middle English untamed, untemed, equivalent to un- + tamed and/or untame + -ed. Compare Dutch ongetemd (“untamed”), German ungezähmt (“untamed”), Danish utæmmet (“untamed”), Swedish otämd (“untamed”), Icelandic ótamin (“untamed”).

s: Strong muscles or lean flesh, especially of the arm, leg or thumb.
Head cheese; a terrine made from the head of a pig or calf; originally boar's meat.
Make fat, especially of a boar.
Become fat, especially of a boar.
e: From Middle English brawne, from Old French braon (“slice of meat, fleshy part, buttock”), from Frankish *brādon, *brādan, oblique forms of *brādō (“roasted meat, ham”), from Proto-Germanic *brēdô (“meat, roast”), of uncertain further origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₁- (“to burn, heat”).

s: The branch of mathematics that deals with the relationships between the sides and angles of (in particular) right-angled triangles, as represented by the trigonometric functions, and with calculations based on said relationships.
e: From 1610s, from New Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (“triangle”) + μέτρον (“measure”), equivalent to trigon + -metry.

s: to feel empathy for another person
Not conscionable; unscrupulous and lacking principles or conscience.
e: From un- + conscionable.

s: Inclined or having a propensity to love, or to sexual enjoyment.
Of or relating to, or produced by, love.
Affected with love; in love; enamored.
e: From Middle English amorous, amerous (14th century), from Old French amoros, amoreus, from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, from Latin amor (“love”), related to amāre (“to love”). Compare French amoureux (“in love”). Doublet of amoroso, amoureux.

s: The act of one who parades.
An excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures or scandalous and immoral activities, involving sex, alcohol, or drugs without inhibition.
e: From debauch + -ery. First use appears c. 1642.

s: A portable, usually hand-held, funnel-shaped device that is used to amplify a person’s natural voice toward a targeted direction.
Mouthpiece or promoter; one who speaks for or publicizes on behalf of another.
To use a megaphone; to speak through a megaphone.
A cytotoxic neolignan obtained from the laurel Aniba megaphylla.
e: From mega + phone.
+ (molecule) Named for the root Aniba megaphylla one + -ketone.

s: Not sufferable; very difficult or impossible to endure; intolerable, unbearable.
Preoccupied with something to the exclusion of everything else.
Finalized, written in large letters. (of a document)
To discover again; especially something previously lost or forgotten.
e: From re- + discover.

s: flowers in the family Caryophyllaceae, sometimes called carnations.
The traditional scarlet jacket(s) worn by fox-hunters in the United Kingdom.
Of or pertaining to an acrobat.
e: From acrobat + -ic.

s: A shining with fast intermittent light.
A very short period, notionally the time it takes to blink the eyes.
e: From Middle English twynkelynge, equivalent to twinkle + -ing.
From Middle English twynkelyng, twynkelynge, equivalent to twinkle + -ing.

s: Any of numerous hemiparasitic evergreen plants of the order Santalales with white berries that grow in the crowns of apple trees, oaks, and other trees, such as the European mistletoe (Viscum album) and American mistletoe or eastern mistletoe (Phoradendron leucarpum).
A sprig of one such plant used as a Christmas decoration, associated with the custom that a man may kiss any woman standing beneath it.
e: From Middle English mistelto, mistilto (“European mistletoe”), from Old English misteltān (“mistletoe”), from mistel (“mistletoe; basil; birdlime”) + tān (“sprig, shoot, twig”), possibly as a Calque of Old Norse mistilteinn; equivalent to mistle + tan (“twig”). This was mistaken for the plural of tā (“toe”).

s: The act of placing a telephone call.
Inclined to drowse; heavy with sleepiness
Causing someone to fall sleep or feel sleepy; lulling; soporific.
e: From drowse + -y, despite the fact that drowsy (1520) is recorded before drowse (1570). Compare Old English drūsian (“to droop, drowse, become languid”).

s: Said to wish a final farewell; goodbye.
A farewell, a goodbye; especially a fond farewell, or a lasting or permanent farewell.
e: From Middle English adieu also adew, adewe, adue, from Old French adieu (“to God”), a shortening of a Dieu vous comant (“I commend you to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Doublet of adios.

s: Of an inappropriately or unusually low weight.
Not too heavy for an intended purpose.
Being less invested in a particular area than market wisdom suggests.
The state or quality of being underweight.
To give insufficient weight to (a consideration); to underestimate the importance of.
To invest in less than conventional wisdom would dictate.
e: From under- + weight.
From re- + affirm.

s: Thin nylon tights worn over the legs, usually tan in color.
e: From panty + hose.

s: A martial art from Korea, known for its elaborate kicking techniques. The sparring aspect is a recognised Olympic sport.
e: Borrowed from Korean 태권도(跆拳道).

s: Having been fully removed, including the roots.
Having been removed from a familiar circumstance, especially suddenly and unwillingly.
A small carved or molded figure; a statuette.
e: Borrowed from French figurine, equivalent to figure + -ine.

s: To make reparation, compensation, amends or satisfaction for an offence, crime, mistake or deficiency.
To bring at one or at concordance; to reconcile; to suffer appeasement.
To agree or accord; to be in accordance or harmony.
To absolve (someone else) of wrongdoing, especially by standing as an equivalent.
e: From atone (“reconciled”), from Middle English atone, attone, atoon (“agreed”), equivalent to at + one. Compare Latin adūnō (“to unite, make one”) for the similar formation. Regarding the different phonological development of atone and one, see the note in one.

s: Very good, excellent, typically used sarcastically to indicate a state of misery, resentment or great frustration.
A footman, a liveried male servant.
To attend, wait upon, serve obsequiously.
e: Borrowed from Middle French laquais, which is probably (via Old Occitan lacai?) from Spanish lacayo, itself perhaps from Italian lacchè and Greek λακές, from Turkish ulak. Another possibility is through French, from Arabic الْقَائِد. See French laquais.

or spreading at right angles to the axis.
e: From patent + -ly.
From eerie + -ly. Compare Old English earglīċe, earhlīċe (“in a cowardly manner, timidly, fearfully”).

Side air bags, including the back seat passengers, also prevent inju
A similar inflated bag used in performing stunts, or for lifting objects in firefighting, etc.
A person who talks too much; a windbag or gossip.
e: From air + bag.

s: The act of one who basks.
Whining; tending to whine or complain.
Having a nasally or high-pitched voice.
e: From whine + -y.

The act of burrowing a tunnel.
The quantum mechanical passing of a particle through an energy barrier.
A type of fraud where assets and profits are transferred out of firms for the benefit of those who control them.
A feature of the file system that allows files to preserve certain properties, such as creation date, even after being deleted and recreated.
One blade of a pair of scissors.
To cut using, or as if using, scissors.
To excise or expunge something from a text.
To reproduce (text) as an excerpt, copy.
To move something like a pair of scissors, especially the legs.
To engage in scissoring (tribadism), a sexual act in which two women intertwine their legs and rub their vulvas against each other.
To skate with one foot significantly in front of the other.
e: From Middle English cysour, cysoure, cysowre, altered from sisours (“scissors”), from Old French cisoires, cisours, cisur, from Latin caedere (“to cut”); current spelling influenced by Latin scindere, scissus (“to split”).
From delightful + -ly.

s: The use of a word or phrase to replace another one that is more offensive, blunt or vulgar.
A word or phrase that replaces another in this way.
e: Recorded since 1656; from Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός, from εὐφημίζω, from εὔφημος (“uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (“well”) + φήμη (“a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”), from φημί (“to speak, say”).

s: An instance or example of such overstatement.
e: From Middle English iperbole, yperbole, from Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (“excess, exaggeration”), from ὑπέρ (“above”) + βάλλω (“to throw”). Doublet of hyperbola.

s: Resembling or having the consistency of mush; semiliquid, pasty, or granular.
Overly sappy, corny, or cheesy; sentimental, especially in a romantic way; maudlin.
e: From mush + -y.

An element of an advertisement, etc. serving as a subliminal message.
A digital object embedded within another, which is often a document.
A piece of computer hardware embedded within another physical object, which is often a larger IT device.

s: To place within a fluid (generally a liquid, but also a gas).
e: Borrowed from Latin immersus, from immergō, from in + mergō.

An implement of a broad fabric worn around and connecting both bicipites brachii to support benching the most heavy weights.
The act of passing cars queuing in the left-hand lane and using the right-hand lane to go around a roundabout, exiting at the desired junction having avoided the queue.
To move or cause to move in a manner resembling a projectile shot from a slingshot.

To perform the slingshot manoeuvre (see Noun).

Borrowed from (Hindi पैजामा / Urdu پائِجامَہ), from پایجامه, archaic form of پاجامه.

s: A car with a sloping, hinged rear door that opens upwards.
e: From hatch + back.

s: To attach or connect in a secure manner.
To cause to take close effect; to make to tell; to land.
e: From Middle English fastenen, from Old English fæstnian, from Proto-West Germanic *fastinōn (“to secure, fasten”). Equivalent to fast + -en.

s: Something that causes moisture or a condition of wetness; something that makes things moist.

From gloss + -less.

From chocolate + -ly.

e: From the spoken equivalents of either of the following: of capire (“to understand”), from Latin capere, the of capiō (“to capture, catch, seize; to comprehend, understand; etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grab, seize; to hold”).

s: A frozen dessert consisting of crushed ice and colored fruit flavoring, usually served in a cone or a cup.

s: One with a morbid paroxysmal craving for alcohol; an alcoholic.
A persistently drunken person; a drunkard.
e: From dipso + maniac.

s: The act by which something is garbled or confused.

From unemotional + -ly.

The state of being old; age.

s: Jokey; inclined to or characterised by quipping.
e: From quip + -y.

s: The act or characteristic of being aggressive or combative.
e: From Latin pugnacitas (whence -acity).

s: Agent noun of skulk; one who skulks.

From ass + -less.
From un- + latch.
From pit (“pit bull terrier”) + -ie.

To work as a redcoat (Butlin's entertainer).
e: Bahuvrihi compound of red + coat.

s: The swede, or Swedish turnip; the European plant Brassica napus var. napobrassica
The edible root of this plant
e: Borrowed from Swedish rotabagge, a dialectal word from Västergötland, from rot (“root”) + bagge (“lump, bunch”).

s: Of, relating to, or resembling a word; verbal.

e: Named after Caspar Milquetoast, a character from the comic strip The Timid Soul, created by American cartoonist Harold Tucker Webster (1885–1952) and first published in 1924; the character was named after the American dish milk toast (“a food consisting of toasted bread in warm milk”), from en:milk> + toast.

s: An iron collar formerly used in Spain to execute people by strangulation.
Something, especially a cord or wire, used for strangulation.

To suddenly render insensible by semi-strangulation, and then to rob.
e: From Spanish garrote. Doublet of garrot.

s: Never tiring or lacking energy; without rest; without slowing.
e: From un- + flagging.

A formerly defined psychological disorder characterized by excessive preoccupation or worry about having a serious illness. No longer a current medical diagnosis; see hypochondriasis for more.
e: From New Latin hypochondria (the morbid condition so called, supposed to have its seat in the upper part of the abdomen), from hypochondrium (see English hypochondrium for more).

From un- + escorted.

e: From porter + house.

e: First use appears c. 1750, in the sense of the dance, from French cotillon (“petticoat”), extended to the dance because of the distinctive lift of dress revealing the petticoat, from cotte (“dress”) + -illon. Said to derive from the then-popular song Ma commère, quand je danse, mon cotillion va-t-il bien.
From fruitless + -ly.

An old variety of woollen material.
e: From Doiley, the name of a 17th-century London draper. The surname is Anglo-Norman, from d'Œuilly, name of several places in Calvados, from Old French oeil (“eye”).

A hole in sea ice where cetaceans and pinnipeds come to breathe.
A top-facing opening to a cavity in the ground very near an ocean's shore, leading to a marine cave from which wave water or bursts of air are expelled.
A vent for the escape of steam or other gas.
An unintended cavity filled with air in a casting product.
A vertical opening in the top of a computer case that lets hot air (primarily from the CPU heat sink) escape quickly.
To fill or be filled with air in an unintended cavity.
e: From blow + hole.

s: A joyful, somewhat muffled laugh, rather like a snorting chuckle.
A similar sounding vocalisation of various birds.
To laugh with a chortle or chortles.
e: Perhaps a chuckle + snort. Coined by Lewis Carroll in his poem Jabberwocky, completed in 1855 but only introduced to the public in his 1871 novel Through the Looking-Glass.

s: A person who recycles, or a machine used to recycle.
e: From recycle + -er.

Lacking in conscience or moral principles; unscrupulous.
One who has behaved badly, or illegally.
One not restrained by moral principles; an unscrupulous villain.
One who holds a false religious belief; a misbeliever.
e: From Middle English myscreaunt, miscreaunt, from Old French mescreant (1080) "mis-believer", present participle of mescreire "to misbelieve" (modern mécroire). Cognate with French mécréant.

s: Susceptible to being opposed or resisted.
Capable of being placed opposite something else.
e: From oppose + -able.

A panel or molding between the floor and the interior wall of a structure.
A similar panel at the base of a piece of furniture or equipment.
e: From base + board.

s: A tag with one's name inscribed on it.
e: From name + tag.

s: Used in speech to indicate the end of a quotation.
To convert (a quoted expression) back to its original form.
e: From un- + quote; possibly an eggcorn of end quote.

To act in a way perceived as insecure about one's masculinity or a supposedly small penis (especially, by buying or using a large object).
e: From over- + compensate.

From hose + -ing.
From Middle English hosinge, hosiinge, hosiynge, equivalent to hose + -ing.

A sickness or condition caused by overindulgence.
To feed (someone) to excess (on, upon or with something).
To make (someone) sick as a result of overconsumption.
To supply (someone) with something to excess; to disgust (someone) through overabundance.
To overeat or feed to excess (on or upon something).
e: From Middle English surfeite, surfet, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman surfet, surfeit and Old French sorfet, sorfait, past participle of surfaire (“to augment, exaggerate, exceed”), from sur- (“over”) + faire (“to do”). The adjective is derived from the noun.

s: A behavior among male giraffes where they hold combat for social dominance using their necks as weapons.
Making out; kissing profusely, especially on the neck.
A Philadelphia snack food consisting of chopped steak and melted cheese in a bread roll.
e: From cheese + steak.

s: To cause to be or become black.
To cook (meat or fish) by coating with pepper, etc., and quickly searing in a hot pan.
e: From Middle English blaknen, blakkenen, equivalent to black + -en.

Having been the subject of a scandal; disgraced.

A structure, usually at a circus or amusement park, enclosing several interactive attractions such as distorting mirrors, ramps, slides, stairs, rotating barrel slides, etc., that usually do not involve performers.

s: The section of a passenger ship that provided inexpensive accommodation with no individual cabins.
The effect of the helm on a ship.
e: From steer + -age.

s: Any plant of the genus Nigella of about twelve species of annual flowering plants, the blooms of which are generally blue in colour but also found in shades of pink, white and pale purple.
The seeds of the plant Nigella sativa, used as a culinary spice.
e: Borrowed from Nigella, from Late Latin nigella. Doublet of nielle.

s: A multiservice tactical brevity code for communicating the altitude of friendly aircraft.{{ref|group=n|{{cite-book
e: Hebrew כרוב (“cherub”) + English -s plural suffix.

s: Affectionate in a rather mushy or oversentimental fashion.
e: From love + -y + dove + -y.

The membrane of a fish ovary.

A thin strip of an osier used in basketmaking.
A metallic strengthening band or thimble on the wooden arm of an axle of a wagon.

From Dutch scheen (“strip of metal or wood; (anatomy) shin”), from Middle Dutch schene, from Old Dutch *skina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu (“bar; track; (anatomy) shin; spine”), from Proto-Germanic *skinō (“piece; plate; rim; (anatomy) shinbone”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to dissect; to split”). s: One who, or that which, slams.

In the game of Pogs, the heavier piece used to strike the stack of counters.

A one-piece skintight garment with or without sleeves and without legs (often worn by gymnasts, acrobats, wrestlers, female swimmers, etc.)
e: Named after Jules Léotard.

s: An itinerant composer and performer of songs in medieval Europe; a jongleur or travelling minstrel.
e: From Old Occitan trobar (“to find”) via Old French troubadour..

s: A long loose robe worn mainly by women for sleeping in.
e: From Middle English nyght gowne. en + night + gown.

s: A marine crustacean of the subclass Cirripedia that attaches itself to submerged surfaces such as tidal rocks or the bottoms of ships.
In electrical engineering, a change made to a product on the manufacturing floor that was not part of the original product design.
On printed circuit boards, a change such as soldering a wire in order to connect two points, or addition such as an added resistor or capacitor, subassembly or daughterboard.
A deprecated or obsolete file, image or other artifact that remains with a project even though it is no longer needed.
An instrument like a pair of pincers, to fix on the nose of a vicious horse while shoeing so as to make it more tractable.
A good job, or snack easily obtained.
Infl of hafta: Contraction of has to.
A hand gesture used to depict the meaning of a song
A spear carried by early Roman legionaries.
e: Written form of a reduction of has to.
From Spanish hasta (“until”), especially hasta luego (“until later”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit हस्त.
Thumb|A hasta (sense 2) Latin hasta.
From charming + -ly.

s: A part of poultry when prepared as food
A short item of news, gossip, or information.
e: From tid (“fond, tender, nice”) + bit (“morsel”)

s: An act of bolting or running away.
A sifting, as of flour or meal.
A private arguing of cases for practice by students, as in the Inns of Court.
A soldier trained in special infiltration tactics.
A member of the Sturmabteilung, a Nazi street militia.
(slang) Someone who is bad at aiming.
e: A calque of German Sturmtruppen, from Sturm (“storm”) + Truppen (“troops”), equivalent to storm + trooper. Sense 3 is based on the Stormtroopers from Star Wars.

s: An illegal saloon or tavern, especially one operated during the American Prohibition period in the 1920s.
In modern times, a legal bar in the style of a speakeasy, i.e. one that is hidden away and has a quiet atmosphere.
e: Deverbal from speak#Verb easy#Adverb (= speak quietly [interj.]); for the history, see Wikipedia at speakeasy § Etymology.

s: Plural of taper; thin candles used for lighting other candles.
A dish made of melted cheese, or chocolate etc., or of a boiling liquid into which food can be dipped.
To prepare or serve as a fondue.
e: French fondue (“melted”), from fondre (“to melt”).

s: That appeals to, or stimulates the appetite.
any food traditionally eaten with a bagel, as an accompaniment, topping or filling; including dairy products and pareve but not meat
e: Calque of French appétissant, French -ant being equivalent to -ing. See also appetite.

s: Any person involved in the production of video material, but especially a person who uses a video camera.
e: From video + grapher.

s: Having a specified kind of staple.
Agent noun of bite: someone or something who bites or tends to bite.
A fish that tends to take bait.
A person who takes up an offer or request.
A stone that barely touches the outside of the house.
One who copies someone else's work, style or techniques, especially in hip-hop.
Something (a data unit, machine etc.) with a width of a specified amount of bits.
e: From Middle English biter, bitere, equivalent to bite + -er. Cognate with West Frisian biter (“biter”), Dutch bijter (“biter”), Low German Bieter (“biter”), German Beißer (“biter”).
From bit + -er.
Representing an aphetic pronunciation of potato. Compare patater (“potato”), 'mater (“tomato”), and 'naner (“banana”).

s: To make an incorrect interpretation; to misunderstand.
e: From mis- + interpret.
Likely borrowed from French amniotique, from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (“vessel for collecting the blood from sacrifices”). Equivalent to amnion + -otic.

s: A sweater that must be put on by pulling it over the head; a sweater without buttons or a zipper in front.
An exercise performed lying on the back in which the arms are extended behind the head and exertion lifts the weight above the head.
An exercise in which the gymnast pulls up from a hang lifting the legs up and over the bar thus rolling into a support position.
An instance of a vehicle being pulled over.
e: From pull over.

s: Being the opposite or logical inverse of a familiar person, place, or situation.
e: Variant of bizarre, equivalent to bizarre + -o; see that entry for more information. In the sense of “logical inverse”, derived via the comic book character Bizarro, an inverted version of Superman from a planet where “good” means “bad” and so on, and further popularized by "The Bizarro Jerry", a 1996 episode of the sitcom Seinfeld.

s: A stag that has failed to grow antlers; a cow that has not developed horns.
Especially in hummel corn: grain that lacks awns (beards or bristles), or has had its awns removed (barley, oats, etc.).
Of an animal: to remove the horns; to poll.
To separate (barley, oats, etc.) from the awns.

In an unapologetic manner; in a manner that withholds or refuses to offer an accompanying apology for having said or done something that causes actual or potential harm, especially when being apologetic would be appropriate.
e: From unapologetic + -ally.
From sweet + -y.

s: Especially of a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.: intended to help in remembering.
Something (especially a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.) used to help in remembering a thing; a memory aid.
The human-readable, textual form of an assembly language instruction, not including operands.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin mnemonicus or its etymon Ancient Greek μνημονῐκός (“pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + English -ic. Mνημονῐκός is derived from μνήμων (“mindful, remembering”) + -ῐκός; while μνήμων is from μνάομαι (“to be mindful, remember”) (from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to mind; to think”)) + -μων.

Noun sense 1 (“something used to help in remembering a thing”) is borrowed from Latin mnēmonicum (“something used to help in remembering a thing”), from Ancient Greek μνημονικόν (“something used to help in remembering a thing”), a noun use of the neuter form of μνημονῐκός: see etymology 1.
Probably from skite (“to move lightly and hurriedly; to move suddenly, particularly in an oblique direction (Scotland, Northern England)”) + -ish; compare skitter.

s: The act of sending a ping, as by a submarine or over a computer network.
Any microorganism; especially, a harmful bacterium.
e: Borrowed from French microbe, from Ancient Greek μικρός (“small”) and βίος (“life”). micro- + -obe.

s: A lamp which operates by burning piped illuminating gas (or town gas).
The light produced by the burning gas in such a lamp.
To manipulate someone such that they doubt their own memory, perceptions of reality, or sanity, typically for malevolent#Adjective reasons.
To deceive, trick, or lie to.
e: From gas (“flammable gaseous hydrocarbon or hydrocarbon mixture used as a fuel”) + light.

From the 1938 stage play Gas Light by the English playwright and novelist Patrick Hamilton (1904–1962), and its 1940 and 1944 film adaptations, in which a husband attempts to convince his wife and others that she is insane by manipulating small elements of their environment. For more details, see also Gaslighting § Etymology on Wikipedia.

s: An object given by a person and retained in memory of something or someone; something kept for sentimental or nostalgic reasons.
Specifically, a type of literary album popular in the nineteenth-century, containing scraps of poetry and prose, and engravings.
e: From keep + sake.

s: Appealing or stylish in appearance or manner; classy, flashy.
Of a person: elegant in dressing; of clothes: elegant, fashionable.
Adept or ingenious in behaviour or operation; excellent, nifty.
e: Unknown; the following etymologies have been suggested.

s: Of, relating to, or having clairvoyance.
Able to see things that cannot be perceived by the normal senses.
Relating to a form of parallel processing algorithm given advance information about the problem.
A person able to see things that cannot be perceived by the normal senses
A person able to foresee the future
e: From French clairvoyant, from clair (“clear”) + voyant (“seeing”), present participle of voir (“see”).

s: One who derives pleasure through cruelty or pain to others.
e: From the name of the Marquis de Sade; see sadism.

s: A fan, especially a young female fan of a male singer or rock group, who seeks intimacy (most often physical, sometimes emotional) with a celebrity; usually with a rock 'n' roll artist or band member.
A group photo including the photographer; a group self-portrait.
e: From group + -ie. In the fan sense, from 1967.
From group + -ie, by analogy with selfie, 2010s.

s: A bottle, flask or similar vessel having a vacuum between its inner and outer silvered walls; designed to maintain the temperature of its contents
A unit of measure whose identification remains very unclear.
e: Genericization of the trademark Thermos, from Ancient Greek θερμός (“warm”). Possibly related to English Doublet of warm.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek θέρμος.

s: A deep-bowled spoonlike utensil with a long, usually curved, handle.
A container used in a foundry or steel mill to transport and pour out molten metal.
The float or paddle on a mill wheel.
An instrument for drawing the charge of a cannon.
A ring, with a handle or handles fitted to it, for carrying shot.
To pour or serve something with a ladle.
e: From Middle English ladel, from Old English hlædel, derived from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną (“to load”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to put, lay out”), same source as Lithuanian kloti (“to spread”), equivalent to lade + -le (“agent suffix”).

s: The act of one who smirks.
Mixed in a circular pattern with both original components distinguishable.
The point in the launch of a rocket or an aircraft where it leaves contact with the ground.
The point at which a person or animal leaves the ground, as for example when jumping.
The point of launching into success or action.
e: From lift off.

s: The necrosis and rotting of flesh, usually caused by lack of blood supply.
To corrupt; To cause to become degenerate.
e: Borrowed from French gangrène, from Latin gangraena, from Ancient Greek γάγγραινα (“gangrene”).

s: A lewd and disreputable person, often female, especially an unattractive person with an air of tawdry promiscuity.
Anything that is particularly foul, unhygienic or unpleasant.
A dance performed to ska, dub, or reggae music.
A style of rhythmic guitar strumming in ska, reggae, and punk.
To play guitar with a skank rhythm.
To be dishonest or unreliable, to defraud or deceive, to steal.
The act of cheating a person.
To cheat or betray, especially a friend.
To steal, or otherwise acquire underhandedly.
e: Unknown. Perhaps from skag (“unattractive woman”), but the origins of skag are unknown. Compare scold (“troublesome woman”), skeevy (“disgusting”). Attested from the 1960s.

Originally Jamaican, attested from the twentieth century, but earliest source is uncertain. The verb sense be dishonest is evidently older. Perhaps originally Onomatopoeic. The dance senses may come from a resemblance to motorcyclists weaving between larger vehicles. Compare skanker.
Slang word used in Northern England. Unknown. Perhaps from etymology 2, above; attested in West Indian and UK black slang from the twentieth century.

s: The vice of eating to excess.
e: From Old French glutonie, from gloton + -ie, from Latin glutio, equivalent to glutton + -y.
From dope (“stupid person”) + -y.
head + mistress.

s: Of an object: not strong or sturdy, as because of poor construction or upkeep; not safe or secure.
Affected with or suffering from rickets; rachitic.
e: From dialectal ricket (“unstable, rickety”) + -y, and/or ricket (“to move noisily and in a reckless way”) + -y. Alternatively, and perhaps less likely, from rickets + -y.

s: Having an upbeat rhythm, suitable to skip to.
e: From skip + -y.

s: Carpet or a piece of carpet, especially when speaking of installation or removal.
Moving with a slow pace or motion; not swift.
Ineffectual; slow-witted, slow to act, or dull.
Unwary; unready (especially in the phrase take (someone) tardy).
A piece of paper given to students who are late to class.
An instance of a student's being marked as tardy by a teacher on the teacher's attendance sheet.
e: From an earlier tardive, from French tardif, from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus (“slow”, “sluggish”), of obscure origin.

s: A woman who has never been married, especially one past the typical marrying age according to social traditions.
One who spins (puts a spin on) a political media story so as to give something a favorable or advantageous appearance; a spin doctor, spin merchant or spinmeister.
Someone whose occupation was spinning thread.
A woman of evil life and character; so called from being forced to spin in a house of correction.
A spider; an insect (such as a silkworm) which spins thread.
e: From Middle English spynnestere (“woman who spins fibre”), from c. 1350; equivalent to spin + -ster. The semantic development is from a historical notion of unmarried women spinning thread for a living.

s: The act of fastening a buckle.
A folding into hills and valleys.
The action of giving in (slightly) to pressure or stress by developing a bulge, bending or kinking (with the eventual risk of collapsing).
A young male domestic goat of between one and two years.
e: From the verb to buckle, equivalent to buckle + -ing.
From buck + -ling.
From German Bückling or Swedish böckling. Cognate with Middle High German bockinc and Middle Dutch bocking (itself from bok (“buck”), referencing the foul smell).

s: The smooth transformation of one image into another using digital tweening.
To fall upon; fall all over; overtake.
Case; instance; circumstance; event; incident; accident.
e: From Middle English bifallen, from Old English befeallan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifallan, from Proto-Germanic *bifallaną; equivalent to be- + fall.

s: The act or process by which something is sanded; the application of sandpaper, etc.
A type of dancing where the floor is covered in sand. See Sanding (dance).
The process of testing the surface of gilding, after it has been fired, with fine sand and water.
The process of burying oysters in sand.
The process of applying sand to rails in railway track to aid adhesion.
A coating of sugar crystals on confectionery, especially on jellies.
e: From sand + -ing.
From Middle English sanding, sandyng, equivalent to sand + -ing.

s: The act of giving a frown.
The individual in a graduating class who delivers the farewell or valedictory address, often the person who graduates with the highest grades.
The individual in a graduating class who graduates with the highest grades.
e: Formed 1759, from valedictory (“of a speech made when leaving”) + -an.

s: The act or result of making a burrow.
To refuse to own, or to refuse to acknowledge one’s own.
To repudiate any connection to; to renounce.
To detach (a job or process) so that it can continue to run even when the user who launched it ends his/her login session.
e: From dis- + own.

s: The act by which something is flung.

e: From punctual + -ity.

s: Having one or more nicks; notched.
e: From nick + -ed.

s: Affected or covered with scurf or scabs; scurfy, scabby; also, of or relating to a skin disease causing scurf or to scurvy.
Of growths on plants: resembling scurf; scurfy.
Of a person or thing: disgustingly mean; contemptible, despicable, low.
Of the way someone is treated: poor, shabby.

A disease caused by insufficient intake of vitamin C, leading to the formation of livid spots on the skin, spongy gums, loosening of the teeth, and bleeding into the skin and from almost all mucous membranes; an occurrence of this disease.
A cattle disease, perhaps affecting the skin.
Mawkishly good; weakly benevolent or pious.
A well-behaved person with no obvious human failings, with the possible exception of smugness and self-satisfaction.
A long rope with a sliding loop on one end, generally used in ranching to catch cattle and horses.
An image-editing function allowing the user to capture an irregularly-shaped object by drawing an approximate outline.
e: From Spanish lazo, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of lace.

s: In a horrible or terrible manner; in a terrifying way.
e: From Middle English grisely, grysly, grissliȝ, griselich, grislich, from Old English grisliċ (“grisly, horrible; dreadful, horrid”), from grīsan (“to shudder with horror; to tremble, to be terrified; to make tremble, to terrify; to agrise, grise”) (unattested but implied in āgrīsan) + -lic.
From grisle (“horror, terror”) + -ly; compare Middle Dutch griselike, Middle Low German grislike.

s: A person who owns, plays or practices with the saxophone.
e: From saxophone + -ist.

s: An older person who accompanies other younger people to ensure the propriety of their behaviour, often an older woman accompanying a young woman.

A protein that assists the non-covalent folding/unfolding and the assembly/disassembly of other macromolecular structures, but does not occur in these structures when the latter are performing their normal biological functions.
An employee sent by a British company to the European Union to work with a client there, to circumvent restrictions imposed after Brexit.
e: See chaperon.

s: A great amount of amusement, usually accompanied by much laughter.
e: From Latin hilaritās (“cheerfulness”), from hilaris (“cheerful”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (“cheerful”). la:hilarō + -i- + -ty.

s: Having a punch; effective; forceful; spirited; vigorous.
Involving or resembling a punch with the fist.
Behaving or appearing punch-drunk, reacting poorly.
Of groomed snow: unable to support the weight of a skier, especially when the skier’s weight is all on one ski, resulting in a ski punching through the surface of the snow.
e: From punch + -y.
From punch (“short fat person”) + -y.

s: The motion of something that twirls.
To lay (someone, or part of their body) down to rest.
To rest (oneself), especially by going to sleep.
Followed by from or (obsolete) of: to cause (oneself) to take a rest from some activity; also, to allow (oneself) to recover from some activity.
To lean or recline, sit down, or lie down to rest; to rest.
Followed by on or upon: of a thing: to lie or be physically positioned on something, especially horizontally; to rest on or be supported by something.
Followed by on or upon: of light, a look, etc.: to fall or rest (and often remain for a while) on something; to alight, to dwell.
Followed by on or upon: to be based on; to depend or rely on.
To cease activity to rest or recover; also, to have a period free from activity or disturbance.
To have faith in; to confide, to trust.
Temporary cessation from activity to rest and recover, especially in the form of sleep; rest; an instance of this; a break, a rest; a sleep.
The state of being peacefully inactive or relaxed, or being free from disturbances or worries; calmness, ease, peace, quietness.
Calmness of the mind or temperament; composure.
Of the face, a muscle, etc.: the state of being relaxed and not in tension.
The state of lying still and unmoving; calmness, tranquillity; an instance of this.
Relief or respite from something exhausting or unpleasant; an instance of this.
e: From re- + pose.

s: Unimportant or insubstantial talk, events, or actions; drivel.
To spit, vent, or eject, as froth.
(literally) To spew saliva as froth; (figuratively) to rage, vent one's anger.
e: From Middle English froth, frooth, froþ, likely a borrowing from Old Norse froða, from Proto-Germanic *fruþǭ; Old English āfrēoþan (“to foam, froth”) is from same Germanic root. Verb attested from late 14th century. Compare Swedish fradga.
From zip + -ed.

s: A person who wanders from place to place; a nomad, a wanderer.
A person without settled employment or habitation who usually supports himself or herself by begging or some dishonest means; a tramp, a vagabond.
Any member of the species Vagrans egista of widely distributed Asian butterflies of the family Nymphalidae.
An animal, typically a bird, found outside its species' usual range.
Wandering from place to place, particularly when without any settled employment or habitation.
Of or pertaining to a vagabond or vagrant, or a person fond of wandering.
Moving without a certain direction; roving, wandering; also, erratic, unsettled.
e: From Middle English vagraunt, vagaraunt (“having no proper employment; having a tendency to go astray or wander; wayward”), from Anglo-Norman vagarant, wakerant, waucrant (“vagrant”) and Old French walcrant, waucrant (“roaming, wandering”); see further at etymology 1.

s: In the singular number; in terms of a single thing.
e: From Middle English singulerly; equivalent to singular + -ly.

s: Any computer that has a far greater processing power than others of its generation.
e: From super- + computer.

s: In an energetic manner; with great energy.
e: From energetic + -ally.

s: Past the middle of life; in the third stage.
Relating to colors associated with autumn.
e: Borrowed from Latin autumnālis. en + autumn + al.
From up- + standing.
From upstand.

s: Subject to frequent changes in direction.
Moving from one object to another; not looking directly and steadily at the person with whom one is speaking.
Having the appearance of being dishonest, criminal or unreliable.
full of, or ready with, shifts or expedients.
e: From shift + -y Cognate with Dutch schiftig (“loose-fitting, open-textured”).

s: To utter words indistinctly or unintelligibly; to utter inarticulate sounds
To talk incoherently; to utter meaningless words.
To talk too much; to chatter; to prattle.
To make a continuous murmuring noise, like shallow water running over stones.
To utter in an indistinct or incoherent way; to repeat words or sounds in a childish way without understanding.
To reveal; to give away (a secret).
Inarticulate speech; constant or confused murmur.
A sound like that of water gently flowing around obstructions.
A plant of the Brassicaceae family, Raphanus sativus or Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus, having an edible root.
