e: From Middle English forcible, forsable, from Old French forcible, from forcier (“to conquer by force”), equivalent to force + -ible.

s: A comprehensive summary of, or treatise on a subject, especially theology or philosophy.
e: From Latin summa.

s: The eldest son of the king of France. Under the Valois and Bourbon dynasties, the Dauphin of France, generally shortened to Dauphin, was heir apparent to the throne of France. The title derived from the main title of the Dauphin, Dauphin of Viennois.
e: Inherited from Middle English Dauphin, from Middle French dauphin, from Old French dalphin, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς; the modern pronunciation is sometimes remodelled on Modern French. Doublet of dolphin.

s: Lack of care; the state or quality of being careless.
e: From Middle English *carelesnes, *carlesnesse, from Old English carlēasnes (“freedom from care, security, carelessness”), equivalent to careless + -ness.

s: Not defensible; not capable of being defended.
Not capable of being justified or excused.
e: From in- + defensible.

s: Charming; likely to put one at ease.
Of or pertaining to volume or volumes.
Consisting of many folds, coils, or convolutions.
Of great volume, or bulk; large.
Having written much, or produced many volumes.
e: From Late Latin voluminosus, from volumen, from volvō (“roll, turn about”) + -men. Related to volume.

s: One of the hairs which grows along the edge of eyelids.
e: From eye + lash.
From green + -ery.

s: The rise and fall of the voice in speaking.
Emotive stress used to increase the power of delivery in speech.
A sound made by, or resembling that made by, a musical instrument.
Singing or playing in good tune or otherwise.
Reciting in a musical prolonged tone; intonating or singing of the opening phrase of a plain-chant, psalm, or canticle by a single voice, as of a priest.
e: From French intonation, from Medieval Latin intonatio, from intonō + -tiō.

s: A reel; a device around which thread, wire or cable is wound, especially a cylinder or spindle.
One of the rotating assemblies of a gas turbine engine, composed of one or more turbine stages, a shaft, and one or more compressor or fan stages.
A temporary storage area for electronic mail, etc.
A splinter caught in the skin.
To wind on a spool or spools.
To send files to a device or a program (a spooler or a daemon that puts them in a queue for processing at a later time).
A small swimming pool that can be used also as a spa.
e: From Middle English spole (possibly via spole, espole), from Middle Dutch spoele, from Old Dutch *spōla, *spuola, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ (“spool”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to cleave, split”).
From spa + pool.

s: A feast, or an occasion on which people or animals feast
Lying beyond the proton or neutron drip line; having a negative particle separation energy; capable of decaying by the spontaneous exothermic emission of one or more nucleons.
To split or sever something with, or as if with, a sharp instrument.
To break a single crystal (such as a gemstone or semiconductor wafer) along one of its more symmetrical crystallographic planes (often by impact), forming facets on the resulting pieces.
To make or accomplish by or as if by cutting.
(chemistry) To split (a complex molecule) into simpler molecules.
Of a crystal, to split along a natural plane of division.
Flat, smooth surface produced by cleavage, or any similar surface produced by similar techniques, as in glass.
A cut (slash) or a cut location, either naturally or artificially.
Followed by to or unto: to adhere, cling, or stick fast to something.
e: From Middle English cleven, from the Old English strong verb clēofan (“to split, to separate”), from Proto-West Germanic *kleuban, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną, from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ- (“to cut, to slice”). Doublet of clive.

From Middle English cleven, a conflation of two verbs: Old English clifian (from Proto-West Germanic *klibēn, from Proto-Germanic *klibāną) and Old English clīfan (from Proto-West Germanic *klīban, from Proto-Germanic *klībaną), both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gleybʰ- (“to stick”). Cognate with Dutch kleven, German kleben (“to stick”).

s: The pear-shaped fruit of a small tree of the rose family, Cydonia oblonga.
The deciduous tree bearing such fruit, native to Asia.
A soft yellow colour, like that of a quince.
e: From Middle English quynce, coince, a variant of coins, coin (“quince”), from Old French cooing (modern coing), from Late Latin cotōneum, from Latin mālum cotōneum, a variant of mālum Cydonium (“Cydonian apple”), translating Ancient Greek μηλοκυδώνιον.
Clipping of quinceañera.
From deft + handed.

s: Characterized by violence and agitation; wild; stormy.
e: From Middle English boistres, an alteration of Middle English boistous (“crude, unrefined”), of Uncertain origin. Likely from Anglo-Norman boystous, bustous (“rough, in a crude state, disabled, paralysed, unable to walk, lame”), Old French boitous (“limping; having a rough, uneven surface”).

s: Undisciplined, unruly; not able to be controlled.
Capricious, reckless of morality, justice etc.; acting without regard for the law or the well-being of others; gratuitous.
An overly playful person; a trifler.
A self-indulgent person, fond of excess.
A lewd or immoral person, especially a prostitute.
To rove and ramble without restraint, rule, or limit; to revel; to play loosely; to frolic.
To waste or squander, especially in pleasure (most often with away).
To act wantonly; to be lewd or lascivious.
e: From Middle English wantoun, wantowen, wantoȝen, wantowe (“uneducated; unrestrained; licentious; sportive; playful”), from wan- (“not, un-, mis-”) + towen, i-towen (“educated”), from togen, ġetogen, past participle of tēon (“to train, discipline”), equivalent to wan- + towed.
Borrowed from Cantonese 雲吞.
From numerical + -ly.

s: Characterized by exceptionally early development or maturity.
Exhibiting advanced skills and aptitudes at an abnormally early age.
e: From Latin praecox (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from praecoquō (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from prae (“before”) + coquō (“to cook, boil, ripen”). Doublet of apricot.

s: an instance of gallant behaviour or speech.
e: From French galanterie, equivalent to gallant + -ry.

s: A burning pain in the chest that is caused by stomach acid entering the gullet.
e: From Middle English hertbryne, herte-bren (“lust", also "heartburn”), equivalent to heart + burn. Compare also Middle English herte-brennyng (“anger, bitterness, heartburn”). Compare also Ancient Greek καρδιαλγία, from καρδία (“heart”) + ἄλγος (“pain”). From being a burning sensation near the location of the heart in the chest.

s: The act or operation of removing the fleece from a sheep, llama etc. with shears or a shearing machine
The removal of nap from cloth.
The material cut off in this way.
Deformation by forces acting in opposite directions.
The act or operation of reaping.
The act or operation of dividing with shears.
The process of preparing shear steel; tilting.
The process of making a vertical side cutting in working into a face of coal.
e: From Middle English scherynge; equivalent to shear + -ing.

s: of or relating to a spouse, spouses; to the relationship between spouses
e: From spouse + -al.
From Middle English spousaille, from Old French esposaille, espousaille, espousalle, Anglo-Norman (e)spusaille, esposalie, sposale, spousaille.

s: The action of perverting someone or something; humiliation; debasement.
The state of being perverted; depravity; vice.
or corruption of the original course, meaning or state of something.
A sexual practice considered abnormal; sexual deviance; immorality.
e: From Middle English perversion.

s: A junction or joining of ropes made by splicing them together.
The electrical and mechanical connection between two pieces of wire or cable.
That part of a bat where the handle joins the blade.
Bonding or joining of overlapping materials.
The process of removing intron sequences from the pre-messenger RNA, and then joining together exons.
To unite, as two ropes, or parts of a rope, by a particular manner of interweaving the strands, the union being between two ends, or between an end and the body of a rope.
To unite, as spars, timbers, rails, etc., by lapping the two ends together, or by applying a piece which laps upon the two ends, and then binding, or in any way making fast.
To remove intron sequences from the pre-messenger RNA, and then join together exons.
To add, remove and/or replace several array/data elements in one operation.
e: Circa 1525, borrowed from Middle Dutch splissen (Modern Dutch splitsen); akin to Middle Dutch splitten (“to split”), German spleißen (“to split, splice”), Spliss (“split ends, hair breakage”), French épisser (also from Dutch).

s: Emergency intervention to save a patient's life.
e: From hero + -ics.

s: To be overwhelmed by emotion, especially infatuation.
To overwhelm with emotion, especially infatuation.
To make a moan, sigh, or some other sound expressing infatuation or affection.
e: From Middle English swoune, swone, from the verb (see below).

s: having the surface cooked and crispened (particularly by cooking on a grill or pan)
The smoldering or glowing remains of a fire, smoldering ash.
Of a person or animal: large but not obese.
A narrow valley; a cleft in a hillside; a ravine, glen, or gorge.
A sluice used in returning water to a channel after depositing its sediment on the flooded land.
The cleft or fork of a tree; crotch.
e: From Middle English clough, clow, cloȝ, from Old English *clōh, from Proto-West Germanic *klą̄h (“cleft, sluice, abyss”), of Uncertain origin, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to form into a ball”).
From paradox + -ical.

s: A reflection after an act; a later or subsequent thought, action, or expedient.
Something additional to the original plan or concept.
e: From after- + thought, probably modelled on forethought. Compare also the verb afterthink.

s: Semi-formal trousers which are less formal than those that are part of a suit but nowadays are considered suitable casualwear in most offices.
To satisfy, especially a literal or figurative thirst.
To extinguish or put out (as a fire or light).
To cool rapidly by direct contact with liquid coolant, as a blacksmith quenching hot iron.
To terminate or greatly diminish (a chemical reaction) by destroying or deforming the remaining reagents.
To rapidly change the parameters of a physical system.
To rapidly terminate the operation of a superconducting electromagnet by causing part or all of the magnet's windings to enter the normal, resistive state.
The act of quenching something; the fact of being quenched.
The abnormal termination of operation of a superconducting magnet, occurring when part of the superconducting coil enters the normal (resistive) state.
A rapid change of the parameters of a physical system.
e: From Middle English quenchen, from Old English cwenċan, from Proto-Germanic *kwankijaną.

s: Bad weather involving blowing winds and snow, or blowing winds and heavy snowfall amount.
e: From earlier snow-storm, snow storm, equivalent to snow + storm.

s: Giving the appearance of carelessness; relaxedly.
Done without care or attention; inattentively.

e: From superficial + -ly.

s: Any of several local officials, with varying responsibilities.
The president of a township or municipal district council.
The holder of a proposed but unadopted commissioned rank of the Royal Air Force, equivalent to wing commander.
To pass (a rope) through a hole or opening, especially so as to fasten it.
A female of the species Philomachus pugnax, a highly gregarious, medium-sized wading bird of Eurasia; the male is a ruff.
e: From Middle English reve, from Old English rēfa, an aphetism of ġerēfa (also grœ̄fa), from Proto-West Germanic *garāfijō (“officer, official”). Compare Danish greve, Swedish greve, Dutch graaf, German Graf. The role, and eventually the word, was mostly replaced by bailiff, of Anglo-Norman origin.
Apparent alternative form of reef (“to pull or yank strongly”) or from Dutch reven (“to take in, insert”).
Variant of dialectal ree, but of obscure ultimate origin.

s: Strength of mind in regard to danger; the quality that enables a person to encounter danger with firmness; a feeling of upstanding bravery against adversity.
A brave man; a man of valour.
e: From Middle English valour, from Anglo-Norman valour, from Latin valor. Doublet of valure.

s: One who has a strong build.
One who firmly supports a cause.
e: Borrowed from Scots stalwart under the influence of Walter Scott, displacing earlier Doublet of stalworth, wherewith it forms a doublet.

s: A road open at both ends or connecting one area with another; a highway or main street.
The act of going through; passage; travel, transit.
An unobstructed waterway allowing passage for ships.
e: From Middle English thurghfare, corresponding to thorough- (“through”) + fare. Compare Old English þurhfaran (“to go through, go over, traverse, pierce, pass through, pass beyond, transcend, penetrate”). Compare also Old English þurhfær (“inner secret place”), German Durchfahrt (“passage through, thoroughfare”).

s: In a chronological manner; with reference to time.
e: From chronological + -ly.

s: An external or internal rib or rim, used either to add strength or to hold something in place.
The projecting edge of a rigid or semi-rigid component.
An ability in a role-playing game which is not commonly available, overpowered or arbitrarily imposed by the referees.
The electronic sound distortion produced by a flanger.
To be bent into a flange.
To make a flange on; to furnish with a flange; to bend (esp. sheet metal) in the form of a flange.
To mix two copies of together, one delayed by a very short, slowly varying time.
e: Thumb|upright|Flanges (ribs or rims) thumb|Flanges on railway wheels keep the wheels on the track. From dialectal English flange (“to project”), flanch (“a projection”), from Middle French flanche, from Old French flanche (“flank, side”), from Frankish *hlanku (“bend, curve; side, flank”). See Doublet of flank.

s: intercalated with slate; said of a seam of coal.
A sandbank or sandbar creating a shallow.
A shallow in a body of water.
To arrive at a shallow (or less deep) area.
To cause a shallowing; to come to a more shallow part of.
Any large number of persons or things.
A large number of fish (or other sea creatures) of the same species swimming together.
To collect in a shoal; to throng.
e: From Middle English schold, scholde, from Old English sċeald (“shallow”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *skalidaz, past participle of *skaljaną (“to go dry, dry up, become shallow”), from *skalaz (“parched, shallow”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to dry out”). Cognate with Low German Scholl (“shallow water”), German schal (“stale, flat, vapid”).

1570, presumably from Middle English *schole (“school of fish”), from Old English sċeolu, sċolu (“troop or band of people, host, multitude, division of army, school of fish”), from Proto-West Germanic *skolu, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to divide, split, separate”).

s: A strong thread composed of two or three smaller threads or strands twisted together, and used for various purposes, as for binding small parcels, making nets, and the like; a small cord or string.
The act of twining or winding round.
To wind, as one thread around another, or as any flexible substance around another body.
To wind about; to embrace; to entwine.
To mutually twist together; to become mutually involved; to intertwine.
To wind; to bend; to make turns; to meander.
To ascend in spiral lines about a support; to climb spirally.
e: From Middle English twyn, twyne, twin, from Old English twīn (“double thread, twist, twine, linen-thread, linen”), from Proto-West Germanic *twiʀn (“thread, twine”), from Proto-Germanic *twiznaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dwisnós (“double”), from *dwóh₁ (“two”).

From Middle English twinen, twynen, from Old English *twīnian (“to twine, thread”), from Proto-Germanic *twiznōną (“to thread”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwisnós (“double”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ (“two”).

s: The feathers covering the body of a bird collectively.
Feathers used ornamentally; feathering; a bunch or tuft of such feathers; a plume.
Feathers which are fed to a hawk to cause it to regurgitate, for the purpose of cleaning its crop; a type of casting.
A person's dress, especially when elaborate or fine.
A person's external appearance, especially when showy.
Looking exhausted, worried, or poor in condition
A hunting bird captured as an adult.
A young or untrained hawk or falcon.
A stackyard, an enclosure on a farm for stacking grain, hay, etc.
e: From Middle French haggard, from Old French faulcon hagard (“wild falcon”) (> French hagard (“dazed”)), from Middle High German hag (“coppice”) (> archaic German Hag (“hedge, grove”)). Akin to Frankish *hagia (> French haie (“hedge”))
From Old Norse heygarðr (“hay-yard”).

s: To reproduce in a new form.
To assign (roles in a play or performance) to different actors.
The act or process of recasting.
An utterance translated into another grammatical form.
e: From re- + cast.

s: Tending or able to repel; driving back.
A substance or solution used to repel insects, dangerous animals, or other pests.
A substance or treatment for a fabric etc to make it impervious to something.
e: From Latin repellēns. Equivalent to repel + -ent.

s: The act of one who fumes or shows suppressed anger.
A fixed verse form of Italian origin consisting of fourteen lines that are typically five-foot iambics and rhyme according to one of a few prescribed schemes.
To celebrate in sonnets; to write a sonnet about.
e: Borrowed from Middle French sonnet, from Italian sonetto, from Old Occitan sonet (“a song”), diminutive of son (“song, sound”), from Latin sonus (“sound”). [[File:Rossetti on sonnet, 1880.jpg|400px|thumb|A sonnet about sonnets by Dante Gabriel Rossetti. (1880)]].

s: The state, or kinship of being sisters.
The quality of being sisterly; sisterly companionship; especially, the sense that women have of being in solidarity with one another.
The idea of universal experience amongst women, regardless of other traits or factors. (Considered obsolete in third-wave feminism.)
e: From Middle English susterhede; equivalent to sister + -hood (with a modification in the suffix).

s: In tarot cards, the card between the valet and the dame.
e: From Middle English chivaler or chevaler (also shyvalere while code-switching), from Anglo-Norman chevaler or chivaler, later refashioned after French chevalier, from Late Latin caballārius (“horseman”), from Latin caballus (“horse”). Doublet of caballero, cavalier.

s: The action of increasing or becoming greater.

An amplification without strict climax, as in the following passage: "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report, think on these things."
The amount of time added to a player's clock after each move.
A syllable in excess of the number of the nominative singular or the second-person singular present indicative.
To increase by steps or by a step, especially by one.
e: From Middle English encrement, increment, from Latin incrēmentum, from incrēscō (whence increase), from in- + crēscō (“grow”). Equivalent to increase + -ment.

s: A man who labours for wages.
e: From Middle English werkman, from Old English weorcmann (“workman”), from Proto-West Germanic *werkamann, from Proto-Germanic *werkamann- (“workman”), equivalent to work + -man. Compare Dutch werkman (“workman”), German Werkmann (“labourer, workman”), Icelandic verkamaður (“workman”).

s: To throw into disorder; to break the array of.
To take off the dress of; to unrobe.
A lack of array or regular order; disorder; confusion.
e: From Middle English disareyen (“to disarray”), from Middle French desarroyer, from Old French desareer, from des- (“dis-”) + areer (“to array”).
From Middle English dogged, doggid, doggyd (“characteristics similar to that of a dog”), equivalent to dog + -ed.

s: Bored or lacking enthusiasm, typically after having been overexposed to, or having consumed too much of something.
Worn out, wearied, exhausted or lacking enthusiasm, due to age or experience.
Made callous or cynically insensitive, by experience.
Embittered, disillusioned, emotionally worn down by disappointment
e: From jade (“worn-out horse”), possibly from Old Norse jalda (“mare”). Jade as a term of abuse for a woman dates from 1560.
From fancy + -ful.

s: To clean, polish, or wash (something) by rubbing and scrubbing it vigorously, frequently with an abrasive or cleaning agent.
To remove debris and dirt (from something) by purging; to sweep along or off by a current of water.
To clear the digestive tract (of an animal) by administering medication that induces defecation or vomiting; to purge.
To (cause livestock to) suffer from diarrhoea or dysentery.
The removal of sediment caused by swiftly moving water.
A place scoured out by running water, as in the bed of a stream below a waterfall.
A place where wool is washed to remove grease and impurities prior to processing.
To run with speed; to scurry.
To move swiftly over; to brush along.
e: From Middle English scǒuren, scure, skoure (“to move quickly; to travel around in search of enemies”), from scǒur (“attack, conflict; pang of emotional suffering”), from Old Norse skýra (“to rush in”) and skúr (“a shower; a shower of missiles”), perhaps influenced by the verb scǒuren: see etymology 1.

s: A viscous preparation of oils and/or fats, usually containing medication, used as a treatment or as an emollient.
A substance used to anoint, as in religious rituals.
e: A later form (as if oint + -ment) of Middle English oinement, borrowed from Old French oignement (“an anointing”), from oigner, oindre, ongier (“to anoint”), from Latin ung(u)ō (“I anoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to smear, anoint”). Partly displaced native Old English sealf, whence modern salve.

s: That self-adjusts its trajectory to home in on a target; shooting such projectiles.
Fitted with a guiding electronic device that allows it to find and hit a target.
The act of wandering; deviation from truth, moral rectitude; abnormal; divergence from the straight, correct, proper, normal, or from the natural state.

The convergence to different foci, by a lens or mirror, of rays of light emanating from one and the same point, or the deviation of such rays from a single focus; a defect in a focusing mechanism that prevents the intended focal point.
A small periodical change of the apparent positions of the stars and other heavenly bodies, due to the combined effect of the motion of light and the motion of the observer.
The tendency of light rays to preferentially strike the leading face of a moving object (the effect underlying the above phenomenon).
Any creature with supernatural powers not found in the organized classes of beings in a given setting.
A mental disorder, especially one of a minor or temporary character.
Atypical development or structure; deviation from the normal type; an aberrant organ.
A deviation of a tissue, organ or mental functions from what is considered to be within the normal range.
A defect in an image produced by an optical or electrostatic lens system.
e: A Learned borrowing from Latin aberrātiō (“relief, diversion”), first attested in 1594, from aberrō (“wander away, go astray”), from ab (“away”) + errō (“wander”). Compare French aberration. en + aberrate + ion.

s: Chaotic; without clear order; in a state of disorder.
in an incorrect or unexpected order.
Having a bad or foul taste.
e: From distaste + -ful or dis- + tasteful.

s: A bedroom or private apartments, especially for a woman in a medieval castle.
A dwelling; a picturesque country cottage, especially one that is used as a retreat.
A shady, leafy shelter or recess in a garden or woods.
A large structure made of grass, twigs, etc., and decorated with bright objects, used by male bower birds during courtship displays.
Either of the two highest trumps in the card games euchre and five hundred (where the joker is omitted).
A type of ship's anchor, carried at the bow.
A muscle that bends a limb, especially the arm.
One who plays any of several bow instruments, such as the musical bow or diddley bow.
A young hawk, when it begins to leave the nest.
e: From Middle English bour, from Old English būr, from Proto-West Germanic *būr, from Proto-Germanic *būrą (“room, abode”). Cognate with Búur (“storage room, utility room; cage”), German Bauer (“birdcage”), Old Norse búr (“cage”) (Danish bur, Norwegian bur, Swedish bur).

From Middle English boueer, from Old English būr, ġebūr (“freeholder of the lowest class, peasant, farmer”) and Middle Dutch bouwer (“farmer, builder, peasant”); both from Proto-West Germanic *būr, from Proto-Germanic *būraz (“dweller”), from or related to *būaną (“to dwell”).
From German Bauer. A doublet of etymology 2 and of the German-origin surname Bauer.
From the bow of a ship -er.
From bow + -er.
From bow + -er.
From bough + -er, compare brancher.
From regiment + -al.

s: To subdue, put down, or silence (someone or something); to force (someone) to submit.
To suppress, to put an end to (something); to extinguish.
To be subdued or abated; to diminish.
An emotion or sensation which rises suddenly.
e: From Middle English quellen, from Old English cwellan (“to kill”), from Proto-West Germanic *kwalljan, from Proto-Germanic *kwaljaną (“to make die; kill”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-. Cognate with German quälen (“to torment; agonise; smite”), Swedish kvälja (“to torment”), Icelandic kvelja (“to torture; torment”).

From Middle English *quelle (suggested by the verb quellen (“to well up; gush forth”)), from Old English cwylla, cwiella (“spring; source”), from Proto-West Germanic *kwalljā (“spring, well”). Compare German Quelle.

s: To make less heavy; to lighten; to alleviate, to relieve.
Often followed by from or off: to get off an animal which one has been riding; to dismount; to descend or exit from a vehicle; hence, to complete one's journey; to stop.
Often followed by at, on, or upon: of something aloft: to descend and settle; to land, to lodge, to rest.
Often followed by on or upon: to find by accident; to chance upon, to come upon.
To cast light on (something); to illuminate, to light up.
To set light to (something); to set (something) on fire; to ignite, to light.
Often followed by with: shining with light; luminous, radiant; also, brightly coloured; vivid.
Of an electrical light source: switched on and emitting light.
Chiefly in set alight: in flames, on fire; aflame.
e: The verb is probably derived partly: The English word is analysable as a- + light (“to start (a fire); to burn, set fire to; to become ignited, take fire; to provide light, illuminate; to show the way by means of a light”).

s: A device with a mesh, grate, or otherwise perforated bottom to separate, in a granular material, larger particles from smaller ones, or to separate solid objects from a liquid.
A process, physical or abstract, that arrives at a final result by filtering out unwanted pieces of input from a larger starting set of input.
One of several techniques for counting integers.
A collection of morphisms in a category whose codomain is a certain fixed object of that category, which collection is closed under precomposition by any morphism in the category.
A person, or their mind, that cannot remember things or is unable to keep secrets.
An intern who lets too many non-serious cases into the emergency room.
To strain, sift or sort using a sieve.
e: From Middle English sive, syfe, from Old English sife, from Proto-West Germanic *sibi (“sieve”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyp-, *seyb- (“to pour, sieve, strain, run, drip”). Akin to German Sieb, Dutch zeef, *sito (Russian си́то, сев, се́ять).
From smeg + head, from television series Red Dwarf.
Coined in the television series Red Dwarf, possibly from gimp + -oid.
From smeg + -y.
From smeg + -ing.

s: Term of address for a young man.
e: Diminutive of my lad with -o.
From dismantle + -er.
From groin + -al.
Coined in the television series Red Dwarf, from smeg + -er.

s: A more extreme form of the mullet hairstyle, in which the hair at the back is kept long, whilst the hair on the top and the sides is shaven in a buzzcut or skinhead style.
e: skull + mullet.
From un- + quarantined.

s: The gravitational stretching of objects into long, thin shapes, usually near a black hole.
The act of turning something into long, thin strands like spaghetti.
Failure in which extruded filament forms tangled, stringy, or chaotic strands instead of the intended structure, often due to adhesion issues, improper settings, or printer malfunction.
e: [[File:Spaghettification (from NASA's Imagine the Universe!).png|thumb|An illustration of an astronaut undergoing spaghettification (sense 1) as they fall towards a black hole, being stretched vertically and compressed horizontally. (The process would, of course, be fatal before it became this apparent.)]] From spaghetti + -ification, alluding to the appearance of a strand of spaghetti.
From clothes + brush.
From cosmological + -ly.

s: A metal-headed golf club with a large highly lofted head. Replaced by a sand iron or wedge in a modern set of clubs.
To strike, or take a shot, with a niblick.
e: Possibly from nib + -le + -ock.

s: Done or made with a polygraph.
Overcome to the point of being mindless or inarticulate.

e: From bleary + -ly.

s: Resembling a chameleon: readily changing color or other attributes.
e: From chameleon + -ic.

s: The shins or knees, chiefly in references to kneeling.
e: From marrow + bone.

s: The abrupt sound of two hard objects coming into contact.
A stick-like tool used to strike the surface of the water and produce a sound that causes nearby fish to attack the bait.
e: Onomatopoeic. Compare clink, clank, clunk.
From weasel + -y.

s: To walk; to relocate oneself under the power of one's own legs.
e: From Latin ambulātus, past participle of ambulō (“to walk, go about”). Doublet of amble.

s: A robot that is designed to look and act like a human.
e: From mechano + oid.
From centre + fold.

s: A baked good such as a cake or biscuit intended to be eaten with tea or at an afternoon tea.
A flat, round bread bun, usually containing currants, sultanas or peel and often served toasted and buttered with tea.
A bread roll without fruit; a barm.
A snack consisting of shortbread or wafer topped with meringue or marshmallow, coated in chocolate.
A traditional type of dense, large cookie, typically hard-baked, not particularly sweet, and with few extra fillings.
A small delicate cake or pastry; a petit four.
A sweet cake similar to pound cake, sometimes sprinkled with cinnamon and caster sugar, often served warm.
A fruit cake similar to a barmbrack (but often without yeast) flavoured with tea and whiskey, especially associated with Halloween.
e: From tea + cake.

s: Chiefly in scarper the letty: to depart quickly or run away from (a place); to flee.
To depart quickly; to escape, to flee, to run away.
Chiefly in do a scarper: an act of departing quickly or running away; an escape, a flight.

e: From psychotic + -ally.

s: To bump fists in greeting or celebration.
e: From fist + bump.

From sarn- (“perhaps from a dialectal pronunciation of the first syllable of sandwich”) + -ie. Alternatively, perhaps a misreading or an intentional dissimilation of samie (i.e. sammie), where the 'm' is mistaken for or replaced with 'rn'.

s: Resembling or characteristic of a list, or tending to use lists.
e: From list + -y.

s: A long time (especially a longer time than expected); ages
e: Unknown. First seen in print around 1960. One theory is that it comes from donkey's ears; another is that it is an abbreviation of years, months and weeks.

s: Denoting a distinguishing mark applied to a letter or character.
A special mark added to a letter to indicate a different pronunciation, stress, tone, or meaning.
A letter added to another letter serving a similar indicative function.
e: Ancient Greek διακριτικός (“distinguishing, separative”), from διακρῑ́νω (“to distinguish, separate”), from δια- (“between”) + κρῑ́νω (“I separate, distinguish”).

s: To move or run away quickly.
The act of running away; a scurrying off.
e: First use appears c. 1861, in the New York Tribune. The word appeared and gained prominence in Civil War military contexts around 1861, and rapidly passing into more general use.

s: One who or that which wobbles.
A person who remains undecided, and may ultimately align with either position.
A stone that rocks from side to side as it travels because it is not resting on its running surface.
A case with an indeterminate outcome, contingent upon factors beyond the parties' control.
A class of crime that can be charged as a lower penalty or a higher penalty, e.g. a crime punishable as either a misdemeanor or a felony at the discretion of the prosecutor.
A fishing lure made to resemble a prey fish and that wobbles in the water; plug, minnow.
A sudden unexpected outburst of anger or rage; a tantrum.
A small publicity notice which appears to float at eye level, being attached to a fixture by a flexible arm.
The end of the roll in a roller mill for shaping steel.
e: From wobble + -er.

s: A burble, the sounds of a burble.
The quantity contained on a plate.
e: From plate + -ful.

s: The act of producing a snivel.
Of someone who whines, cries, or acts weak and unpleasant in an annoying way.
Something (such as a canyon or road) with a sharp bend or turn in it.
A configuration of stairs where a flight ascends to a half-landing before turning 180 degrees and continuing upwards.
A sharp bend in the fairway before reaching a hole.
A single intersection consisting of two opposing T-junctions in close proximity; an intersection with a staggered cross street.
To bend in the shape of the hind leg of a dog, especially to turn and then turn back sharply to the original direction.
e: The noun is derived from dog + leg, referring to the shape of the hind leg of a dog. The verb is derived from the noun.

s: A pan used for urination and defecation while in bed, now usually for reasons of medical necessity or convenience.
e: From bed + pan ("chamber pot").
From idol + -ise.
From see + -est.
From Middle English foulnesse, foulnes, from Old English fūlnes (“foulness”), equivalent to foul + -ness. Compare Dutch vuilnis (“rubbish; garbage; trash”).

s: Lacking intelligence, sense or understanding; foolish.
e: From dialectal English gaum (“heed, attention”) + -less (“without”), from Old Norse gaum, from Proto-Germanic *gaumaz, *gaumō (“heed, attention”). The ‘r’ found in this spelling is a vowel-lengthening device common in non-rhotic dialects of English.

s: Originally, garbage, rubbish, or waste; later the portions of a crop which are discarded, such as husks, stalks, etc.; also, agricultural waste such as weeds.
Coarse or rough plant material such as hay and silage used as animal fodder.

Substances, generally of plant origin, consisting mostly of complex carbohydrates which are undigested when eaten by humans, and which therefore help the passage of food and waste through the alimentary tract; dietary fibre.
e: From rough (“not smooth; crude, unrefined”) + -age.

s: An instance of somebody being outsmarted.
A period of refreshment or rest.
Food or drink that may be consumed as a meal.
Something that is intellectually or spiritually nourishing.
The consumption of food; also, refreshment obtained from eating; refreshment; rest.
To supply (an animal or person) with food; to feed.
To provide (a person) with intellectual or spiritual nourishment; to enlighten, to feed.
To refresh (oneself or someone) through eating and drinking.
Usually followed by on or upon: to take food and drink; to feast, to feed.
e: Partly.
From un- + selfish + -ly.

s: Comparative of dead; or at least more evidently dead.
One who is deceased, or will shortly become so.
e: From dead + -er or er.

s: A blend of chilis, tamarind, ginger, cumin, and mustard seeds, originally from Goa.
A hot curry made with this spice.
e: From विंदालू, from Portuguese vin-d’alho (“wine and garlic sauce”), from vinho (“wine”) + alho (“garlic”). Not related to English aloo, from Hindi आलू, but by confusion with this term the dish is often based on potatoes.
Originally Scots, probably Onomatopoeic.

s: The internal organs of poultry birds, used as food.
e: From Middle English giblets, from Old French gibelet (“game bird stew”), probably from gibier (“birds hunted for sport”).

s: Abounding in or infested with mice.
e: From mouse + -y.
From mouse + -y.

s: A base or outpost located on a moon.
e: moon + base.

s: Prone to meaningless vocalization, especially excited and confused utterances, like a beast or monster.

e: From French limpide, from Latin limpidus.

s: Strikingly appropriate or relevant; well suited to the circumstance or in relation to something.
Positioned at rest in respect to another, be it side-to-side, front-to-front, back-to-back, or even three-dimensionally: in apposition.
That which is apposite; something suitable.
e: From Latin appositus, past participle of adponere, from ad- + ponere (“to put, place”). See apposition.
From Middle English tuix, twyx (“among; between”) + English -t. Tuix, twyx is an form of atwix, atwixen, atwixt (“between”), or bitwix, bitwixe, bitwixen, bitwixt (“among; between”)

s: A malocclusion in which the upper teeth extend over the lower ones.
To use excessive acid in an etching process, so that the result is too deep.
e: From over- + bite.

s: The action of the verb cluck; a cluck sound.

e: From direction + -less.

s: To join in the festivities of Shrovetide.
The action of the verb to fizz.
The sound made by something that fizzes.
To kneel and bow low enough to touch one’s forehead to the ground.
To grovel, act in a very submissive manner; to show obeisance to (someone or something) in such a manner; to bow.
e: From either Cantonese 叩頭 or Mandarin 叩頭..

s: Capable of plying or bending; readily yielding to force or pressure without breaking.
e: From Middle English pliaunt, from Old French ploiant, present participle of ploiier (“to fold”).

s: A cold soup of Spanish origin, made with olive oil, vinegar, bread and raw vegetables such as tomatoes, garlic, onion, cucumber and sweet peppers.
e: From Spanish gazpacho, perhaps via *gazpelağo from Latin gazophylacium (“treasure-chest in a church”), alluding to the diversity of its contents. Alternatively, related to Spanish caspicias (“remnants”).

s: Rebellious or defiant to authority; contumacious.
e: From in- + subordinate, on model of French insubordonné.

s: A person who dresses in a manner that is not socially acceptable and is supposed to reject conventional norms of thought and behavior; nonconformist in dress and behavior.
A person associated with the Beat Generation of the 1950s and 1960s or its style.
e: Coined by Herb Caen. From beat generation + -nik (“person who exemplifies or endorses something”). Compare jazznik. The suffix, a cutesy or ironic use of the Russian suffix -ник, experienced a surge of use in English coinages for nicknames and diminutives after the 1957 Soviet launch of the Sputnik satellite.

s: An often truck-mounted lift for reaching heights; a cherry picker.
e: From teleport + -er.
From tele- + porter.

s: A hypothetical particle that travels faster than the speed of light.
A flaw in a physical theory that predicts the existence of tachyons or similar paradoxical results. Compare with ghost.
e: Formed as: tachy + on, from τᾰχῠ́ς (“swift”, “rapid”). Coined by Gerald Feinberg.

s: A wig of false hair worn to cover a bald spot, especially as worn by a man.
A small tuft; a curl or artificial lock of hair.
A small wig, or a toppiece of a wig, worn by both sexes.
e: 1727, from French toupet (“small tuft of hair, forelock”), from Middle French toupet (“small tuft of hair, forelock”), from Old French toupet (“small tuft of hair, forelock”), diminutive of toupe, top (“tuft of hair”), from Frankish *topp (“summit, crest, tuft of hair”), from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz (“summit, crest, tuft of hair”).

s: Wealthy or of high social position; of or pertaining to a nob (person of great wealth or social standing).
e: From nob + -y.

s: In a good mood; happy and energetic.
An electronic device which uses a piezoelectric transducer to make chirping noise, often designed to be hidden and function as an annoyance
Specifically, a version of the above designed to be thrown for placement. Similar to a throwie.
e: From chirp + -y.

s: A swift, witty reply, especially one that is amusing.
A conversation marked by a series of witty retorts.
A skill in replying swiftly and wittily.
To have a repartee (a conversation marked by witty retorts or replies).
e: From French repartie, a deverbal of repartir (“to retort”).

s: Synonym of pancake, a portion of batter fried on a pan.
A dish made by coating various other foods in batter and frying or deep-frying them together, typically in small portions.
A fragment; a shred; a small piece.

To squander or waste time, money, or other resources; e.g. occupy oneself idly or without clear purpose, to tinker with an unimportant part of a project, to dally, sometimes as a form of procrastination.
To cut (meat etc.) into small pieces for frying.
To break into small pieces or fragments.
e: Inherited from Middle English fryture, from Middle French friture, from Old French friture, from Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīgō (“to fry”); compare fry. For the development of Middle English /iu̯r(ə)/ into /ə(ɹ)/, compare armour, batter, border, solder.

s: Provincial: from a province (of the same land).
Foreign: from abroad, from a foreign land.
Living abroad, living in a foreign land, expatriate.
Any outlying area of a country; the provinces.
To land more (punches, kicks etc.) than.
e: From Middle English outland, outlond, from Old English ūtland (“foreign land, land abroad”), from Proto-Germanic *ūtlandą (“outland”), equivalent to out- + land. Cognate to Dutch uitland, Afrikaans uitland, German Ausland, Danish udland.
From out- + land.

s: a choice article of food or drink.
To please or entertain (someone), especially with stories, tales or jokes.
To provide hospitality for (someone); to supply with abundant food and drink.
To entertain with something that delights; to gratify; to refresh.
e: From French régaler (“to entertain, feast”), from Old French regale, rigale, from gale (“merriment”), probably of origin (see Old French galer). Influenced by Old French se rigoler (“amuse oneself, rejoice”), of unknown origin. Compare Middle High German begalen (“to charm; enchant”), English gale (“to sing; charm”). Compare also English gala.

s: To lower the rank or status of.
e: From de- (“down”) + promote (“advance in rank/status (ending abstracted)”).

s: The sound made by a hen, especially when brooding, or calling her chicks.
A kind of tongue click used to urge on a horse.
To make low clicking sounds (refers to hens).
To cause (the tongue) to make a clicking sound.
To call together, or call to follow, as a hen does her chickens.
e: From Middle English clokken, clocken, from Old English cloccian (“to cluck, make a noise”), from Proto-West Germanic *klukkwōn, from Proto-Germanic *klukkwōną (“to make a sound, cluck”), of imitative origin.

s: In an astounding manner; so as to astound, surprise, or amaze.
e: From astounding + -ly.

s: A small arctic and subarctic rodent of the tribes Lemmini, Dicrostonychini and Lagurini.
Any member of a group given to conformity or groupthink, especially a group poised to follow a leader off a cliff.
e: From Danish and Norwegian lemming, from Old Norse lómundr, læmingi, læmingr (“lemming”), perhaps from luomek. Sense 2 derives from a longstanding myth that they exhibit so much herd mentality that populations jump off cliffs to their deaths together.
From dry + -ly.

s: A piece of art that depicts the sea or shoreline.
e: From sea + -scape.

s: A cotton fabric made from dyed and white yarn woven in checks.
A dress made from that material.
e: From Malay genggang (“ajar; apart”), or a corruption of French Guingamp, the name of a town in Brittany, France, where this cloth may have been made.

s: Any musical instrument (percussion idiophone) made of wooden slats graduated so as to make the sounds of the scale when struck with a small drumstick-like mallet; the standard Western concert xylophone or one of its derivatives.
To play a xylophone or to play something else as though it was a xylophone.
To move above a ridged surface or series of surfaces so as to hit every ridge, in a manner similar to playing quickly and sequentially on a xylophone.
e: From xylo (“of wood”) + phone (“sound”).

s: Any of several four-player card games, similar to bridge.
A session of playing this card game.
Alternative spelling of whisht. Silence!, quiet!, hush!, shhh!, shush!
To hush or shush; to still.
e: Alteration of whisk, perhaps so called from the notion of “whisking” up cards after each trick. Altered perhaps on assumption that the word was an interjection invoking silence, by influence of whist#Etymology 2 (“silent”).
From Middle English whist (“silent”), possibly Onomatopoeic.
From jeopardy + -ise.

s: A motion or gesture that jabs; a jab.
Fragments or splintered pieces; numerous tiny disconnected items.
e: Uncertain. The following words, all first attested later than the headword, have been compared.

s: A member of one of several species of small, jumping, mouselike rodents of the subfamily Gerbillinae, native to Africa, India, and Southern Europe.
To rotate inside a monowheel or similar apparatus due to sudden acceleration or braking.
To insert a small animal (typically a gerbil, supposedly) into one's rectum (a sexual practice in urban myth).
e: From French gerbille, from Latin gerbo, from Arabic جَرْبُوع or يَرْبُوع (“jerboa”). Doublet of jerboa.

s: That cannot be fashioned; unshapely, distorted.
e: From un- + fashionable.

s: A brief audio or audiovisual sequence serving to identify the broadcaster.
A protocol serving to identify the user of a particular TCP connection, used especially on IRC networks.
To activate the aircraft transponder identification feature.
e: From a later form of ithand, itself an alteration (due to assimilation to suffix -and) of Middle English ithen, from Old Norse iðinn (“assiduous, diligent”), from iðja, iðna (“to do, perform”), from ið (“a restless motion”), equivalent to ithe + -and and/or ithe + -en.
A shortened form of identification.
A shortened form of identify.

s: To force (open) with a lever; to pry.
To extract something that is difficult to obtain.
e: From the Middle English noun prise (“taking of something”), from Old French prise (“seizure; taking; capture”), past participle of prendre (“to take”). Doublet of prize.

s: A surgical operation involving cutting into a lobe of a body organ, specifically, a procedure, now largely disused, involving severing connections between the prefrontal cortex and the thalamic region of the frontal lobe of the brain to treat certain mental illnesses.
An operation involving the severing of the sympathetic nerve trunk.
An act of removing or separating, and often disregarding or forgetting, something.
e: From lobe + -otomy (a variant of -tomy).

s: Relating to spatial representations: linked to a reference frame based on one's own location within the environment (as when giving the direction as "right" rather than "north"); opposed to allocentric.
The act of standing on one's hands, most often in an inverted way.
The position of standing on one's hands.
e: From hand + stand.

s: A fellow sailor; often used affectedly, especially when portraying a pirate.
e: From mate + -y.

s: A simple-minded person lacking common sense.
e: From simple + -ton (as in a surname). Compare French simplet, Italian semplicione.

s: A daring or adventurous act; an undertaking which goes against convention.
e: Borrowed from French escapade (“the act of escaping; a trick”), itself borrowed from Old Spanish escapada, from escapar (“to escape”), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre.

s: An implement for cutting, trimming, or ornamenting the rim of anything, as the edges of pies, etc.
A mixture of confections, spices, and/or salt applied to the rim of a beverage glass or mug.
A bowl (part of a pipe or bong) which is completely filled with marijuana.
e: From rim + -er.

s: A program-length television commercial, typically between thirty minutes and one hour long, that advertises a product or service by presenting supposedly impartial information about it.
e: information + commercial.
From in- + offensive.

s: A strong, coarse fabric made from hemp or jute, often used for making sacks.
e: See Hessian. Attributed to the historic use of the fabric as part of the uniform of soldiers from the former Landgraviate of Hesse and its successors, who were called Hessians.

s: Used to report the speaker's assessment of the credibility of a reported statement
e: From credible + -ly.
From gut + -less.

s: To induct (someone) into a dignity or office with a formal ceremony.
To dedicate (a building, monument, etc.) for public use by a formal ceremony.

To initiate or usher in (something, as a (significant) course of action, development, organization, or period of time) with a formal ceremony or in a ceremonious manner; also, to begin or commence (something); to start.
To cause (something) to be auspicious or good-omened; also, to declare or make (something) holy; to consecrate, to sanctify.
Inducted into a dignity or office with a formal ceremony or in a ceremonious manner; inaugurated.
e: [[File:President Obama takes the oath of office DVIDS146283.jpg|thumb|Barack Obama being inaugurated as the 44th president of the United States on January 20, 2009.

Borrowed from Latin inaugurātus (“having been taken as an omen, divined; having been approved, consecrated, or inaugurated on the basis of omens; installed, having been installed”) (the perfect passive participle of inaugurō: see etymology 1). See -ate.

s: The state of having gas, often malodorous, trapped (and when released, frequently with noise) in the digestive system of a human and some other animals; wind; and when released, a flatus, a fart.
The release of such gas; breaking wind.
e: From French flatulence, ultimately from Latin flō (“breathe, blow”).

s: A fastener or a fastening method that secures parts by bending metal around a joint and squeezing it together, often with a tool that adds indentations to capture the parts.
The natural curliness of wool fibres.
Hair that is shaped so it bends back and forth in many short kinks.
A small hold with little surface area.
A grip on such a hold.
To press into small ridges or folds, to pleat, to corrugate.
To fasten by bending metal so that it squeezes around the parts to be fastened.
To pinch and hold; to seize.
To style hair into a crimp, to form hair into tight curls, to make it kinky.
To bend or mold leather into shape.
To gash the flesh, e.g. of a raw fish, to make it crisper when cooked.
An agent who procures seamen, soldiers, etc., especially by decoying, entrapping, impressing or seducing them.
e: From Middle English crimpen (“to be contracted, be drawn together”), from Middle Dutch crimpen, crempen (“to crimp”), from Proto-Germanic *krimpaną (“to shrink, draw back”) (compare related Old English ġecrympan (“to curl”)). Cognate with Dutch krimpen, Low German krimpen, Faroese kreppa (“crisis”), and Icelandic kreppa (“to bend tightly, clench”).
Uncertain. Likely from etymology 1, above, but the historical development is not clear. Attested since the seventeenth century.

s: A narrow crack or fissure, as in a rock or wall.
e: From Middle English crevice, from Old French crevace, from crever (“to break, burst”), from Latin crepō (“to break, burst, crack”). Doublet of crevasse.

s: A hairstyle worn by Rastafarians and others in which the hair is left to grow long, and twisted into matted strings.
e: Borrowed from dreadlocks, from dread (“of or relating to a dread”) (from dread (“(usually black) male member of the Rastafarian movement who wears his hair in dreadlocks”), from English dread (“reverential or respectful fear; awe”), referring to the awe inspired by God) + English locks (plural of lock (“length or tuft of hair”)).

s: A member of a crew, especially the crew of a ship.
e: From crew + -man.
See -illion. An arbitrary coinage, appearing by 1916, on analogy of million, billion, trillion.

s: A hard outer structure that provides both structure and protection to creatures such as insects and Crustacea.
A wearable robotic machine used for aided or augmented mobility.
e: From exo- + skeleton.

s: Characterized by fallacy; false or mistaken.
e: From Old French fallacieux (whence -acious), from Latin fallācia, from fallāx, from fallere.

s: In a state of astonishment, wonder, expectation, or eager attention; as with mouth hanging open.
In a state of astonishment, wonder, expectation, or eager attention.
The love of God for mankind, or the benevolent love of Christians for others.
Spiritual, altruistic, beneficial love which wills good for others.
A love feast, especially one held in the early Christian Church in connection with the Eucharist.
e: From a- + gape. First known use by John Milton in Paradise Lost (1667).
[[File:Image from page 132 of The Century dictionary and cyclopedia (1897) (14598639177).jpg|thumb|Agape, or Love-feast (from Roller's Catacombes de Rome).]] From Ancient Greek ἀγάπη.

s: One billion (109, or 1,000,000,000) bytes or 1,000 megabytes.
e: From giga- + byte.

s: Any one of several species of small herring which are commonly preserved in olive oil or in tins for food, especially the European sardine (Sardina pilchardus, syn. Clupea pilchardus). The American sardines of the Atlantic coast are mostly the young of the Atlantic herring and of the menhaden, and m
Someone packed or crammed into a small space.
to pack or cram together tightly.
e: Borrowed from French sardine (cognate with Spanish sardina, Italian sardina), Latin sardīna; from Ancient Greek σαρδίνη.
Pliny states that its name was ultimately derived from Sardis, in Lydia, where the sard was first discovered; but probably ultimately derived from Persian sered ("yellowish-red").

s: An elongated, boneless, flexible organ or limb of some animals, such as the octopus and squid.
One of the glandular hairs on the leaves of certain insectivorous plants.
An officer employed to drive out to troops and transmit back requests for support via a special radio link.
e: From New Latin tentāculum, from tentō. Doublet of tentaculum.

s: To beat in a competition of wits.
e: From out- + smart.

s: Wet sand that appears firm but in which things readily sink, often found near rivers or coasts.
Anything that metaphorically pulls one down or buries one; a treacherous, risky danger
e: From Middle English quyksande, from Old English cwecesand (“quicksand”), equivalent to quick (“living”) + sand. Cognate with Swedish kvicksand (“quicksand”), Icelandic kviksandur, kviksyndi (“quicksand”). More at quick, sand.

s: A game played on a lawn, in which players use mallets to drive balls through hoops (wickets).
A shot in this game in which the striker's ball and another ball are moved by hitting the striker's ball when they have been placed in contact following a roquet.
To play a shot in the game of croquet in which the striker's ball and another ball are moved by hitting the striker's ball when they have been placed in contact following a roquet.
e: Borrowed from Norman croquet (“hook”), from croquet. Doublet of crochet, crocket, crotchet.
See croquette.

s: Any plant whose foliage is covered with stinging, mildly poisonous hairs, causing an instant rash.
Especially, most species of herb genus Urtica, stinging nettles
bull nettle and spurge nettle (Cnidoscolus spp.)
Certain plants that have spines or prickles
bull nettle, silver-leaf nettle, white horse-nettle (Solanum elaeagnifolium)
Certain non-stinging plants, mostly in the family Lamiaceae, that resemble the species of Urtica
dead nettles, dumb nettle (Lamium spp.), particularly Lamium album, white nettle
flame nettles or painted nettle (Coleus spp.)
e: From Middle English netle, netel, from Old English netle, netele, netel, from Proto-West Germanic *natilā (cognate with Old Saxon netila, Middle Dutch netele (modern Dutch netel), German Nessel, Middle Danish nædlæ (“nettle”)), a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *natǭ (of unknown origin, perhaps from the same source as net).

s: A belvedere, either a type of summer-house or a roofed, detached porch-like structure, usually in a yard, park or lawn.
A dismountable shelter comprising a roof or awning supported by poles, and often having removable sides; a canopy tent
a gaudy, incongruous, or flimsy structure or object
e: Possibly from gaze + Latin future indicative conjugation-ending -bō, as in vidēbō (“I will see”), comparable perhaps to lavabo from Latin lavābō (“I will wash”); alternatively from Arabic قَصَبَة (“fort, casbah”), itself possibly refashioned after the former.

s: In an inward manner; to or toward the inside or to oneself.
e: From inward + -ly.

s: Any of many tens of thousands of species of herbivorous beetles, ranging in size from tiny to large, in the superfamily Curculionoidea, the most characteristic species having the head projecting in a distinctive snout with the mouthparts at the tip.
Any of many tens of thousands of species of herbivorous beetles of various sizes, in the family Curculionidae within the superfamily Curculionoidea.
Any of many similar, but more distantly related, beetles such as the biscuit weevil (Stegobium paniceum).
e: From Middle English wevel, from Old English wifel (“beetle”), from Proto-West Germanic *wibil, from Proto-Germanic *wibilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *webʰel-, from *(h₁)webʰ- (“to wave, to weave”), said to be from the woven appearance of a weevil’s larval case, + *-el-, *-l̥-; see also wave and weave.

s: A sweet or savory but usually spicy condiment, originally from eastern India, made from a variety of fruits and/or vegetables, often containing significant amounts of fresh green or dried red chili peppers.
A style of Indo-Caribbean music from the West Indies, associated especially with Trinidad and Tobago.
e: Borrowed from चटनी / چَٹْنِی.

s: Picked by hand rather than by machinery.
Selected with great care or by insiders or an individual.
e: From hand + picked.

s: An erotic massage that involves lots of soap and body contact.
e: From soap + -y. Compare Low German sepig (“soapy”), German seifig (“soapy”), Swedish såpig (“soapy”).

s: To separate or break down (something) into its components.
e: Borrowed from Middle French décomposer. Equivalent to de- + compose.

s: To regard as arising from a specified cause or source.
To attribute (a book, painting or any other work of art or literature) to a writer or creator.
To believe in or agree with; to subscribe.
e: From Middle English ascriben, from Old French ascrivre (“inscribe, attribute, impute”), from Latin āscrībere (“to state in writing”), equivalent to a-#Etymology_6- + scribe.

s: A bluff; a false expression of the strength of one's position in order to intimidate.
A small straight knife with a very sharp blade used for surgery, dissection and craftwork.
To hit, thrust, or pierce with a scalpel.
e: Borrowed from Latin scalpellum, from scalprum (“knife”), from scalpere (“to cut”). Doublet of scalpellum.

s: A type of polymorphism, where different functions, operators or variables with the same name are invoked based on the data types of the parameters passed.
The loading of a vehicle etc. with too heavy a weight.
e: From over + loading.

s: The breaking of the ground into furrows (with a plough) for planting.
Any of many symbiotic organisms, being associations of algae and fungi, often found as white or yellow-to-blue–green patches on rocks, old walls, etc.
Something which gradually spreads across something else, causing damage.
e: Borrowed from Latin līchēn, from Ancient Greek λειχήν, from λείχω (“to lick”). Originally used of liverwort; the modern sense first recorded 1715.

s: A soft, legless larva of a fly or other dipteran insect, that often eats decomposing organic matter.
A worthless, obnoxious or contemptible person.
A fan of the American metal band Slipknot.
The act by which something is sawn.
A shaving or fragment of sawn material.
An instance of unexpected benefit or good fortune; a windfall.
The wreck of a ship which has washed up on shore, from which cargo, timber, etc., may be obtained.
A person who provides greatly needed assistance.
e: A variant of God’s send, from God + -'s + send (“(obsolete) act of sending”), in the sense of someone or something sent by God.

s: To evade or escape from (someone or something), especially by using cunning or skill.
To shake off (a pursuer); to give someone the slip.
To escape being understandable to; to be incomprehensible to.
To escape someone's memory, to slip someone's mind.
e: From Latin ēlūdō (“to evade, elude”), from ē- (“out of”) + lūdō (“to play; to trick”).

s: A mixture consisting of beaten egg whites and either sugar or other flavorings; it is often baked to brown the surface and may be used as a topping or in other ways, most often as a dessert.
A shell made of this mixture which serves as the receptacle for fruit, ice cream or sherbet.
To prepare as a meringue dish.
e: Borrowed from French meringue.

s: Having the power to carry something or someone above, over or beyond others.
Exceptionally good; of the highest quality.
Of or relating to the superlative degree (a degree of comparison of adjectives and adverbs).
The extreme (e.g. highest, lowest, deepest, farthest, etc) extent or degree of something.

The degree of comparison of an adjective or adverb used when comparing three or more entities in terms of a certain property or a certain way of doing something. In English, the superlative of superiority is formed by adding the suffix -est or the word most (e.g. tiniest, most fully);
An adjective or adverb in the superlative degree.
e: From Middle English superlatyf, from Old French superlatif, from Late Latin superlātīvus, from Latin superlātus (“carried above, over; extravagant, of hyperbole”), past participle of superfero (“carry over”), from super (“above”) + fero (“bear, carry”).

s: The act of doing what is magnificent; the state or quality of being magnificent.
e: From Middle English magnificence, from Old French magnificence, from Latin magnificentia.

s: A disease characterised by inflammation of the intestines, especially the colon (large intestine), accompanied by pus (white blood cells) in the feces, fever, pain in the abdomen, high-volume diarrhea, and possible blood in the feces.
e: From Middle English dissenterie, from Old French dissenterie, from Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία, from δυσ- (“bad”) + ἔντερα (“bowels”).

s: An eccentric, insane, crazy or reckless person.
e: From Middle English nutter, notere, equivalent to nut + -er.
nut + butter.

s: A covering, usually a bandage, for the eyes, blocking light to the eyes.
Having the eyes covered so as to obscure vision
With the eyes covered so as to obscure vision.
To cover the eyes, in order to make someone unable to see.
e: From Middle English blyndefolde, blyndfuld, blynfold, blindfeld, blindfelt, yblynfeld, variants of y-blyndfalled, blyndfelled, etc. ("stricken blind, blindfolded"), past participle of Middle English blindfellen (“to strike blind”), from blind (“to blind”) and fellen (“to fell”), equivalent to blind + felled.

s: A collision where something is rammed.

e: From the past participle form of the phrasal verb trump up.

s: A small, usually wooden, stick, often pointed at both ends, for removing food residue from between the teeth.
To spear food on a toothpick.
To transfer a sample of bacteria, etc. by means of a toothpick.
e: From tooth + pick.

s: Without an aim, purpose or direction; in an aimless manner.
e: From aimless + -ly.

s: To wish for with eagerness; to desire possession of, often enviously.
To long for inordinately or unlawfully; to hanker after (something forbidden).
To yearn; to have or indulge an inordinate desire, especially for another's possession.
e: From Middle English coveten, coveiten, coveyten, from Old French covoitier (modern French convoiter), from covoitié (“desire”), presumably modified from Latin cupiditas.

s: In a cheerful or merry way.
e: From Middle English myriely, from Old English myriġlīċe; equivalent to merry + -ly.

s: In a malicious manner, or for malicious reasons.
e: From Middle English maliciousli; equivalent to malicious + -ly.

s: A person who inquires, especially searchingly or ruthlessly.
An official of the ecclesiastical court of the Inquisition.
e: From Old French inquisiteur, from Latin inquīsītor.

s: The motion of something that bobs.

e: Borrowed from Spanish pronto, from Latin prōmptus. Doublet of prompt.

s: A cry before jumping out of or into something.
e: Various theories; see Wikipedia. In any case, likely ultimately from the name of Geronimo the Apache. Originally used by American paratroopers.

s: A marine mollusc, of the family Nautilidae native to the Pacific Ocean and Indian Ocean, which has tentacles and a spiral shell with a series of air-filled chambers, of which Nautilus is the type genus.
A kind of diving bell that sinks or rises by means of compressed air.
e: From Latin nautilus, from Ancient Greek ναυτίλος (“paper nautilus, sailor”).

s: To undo the integrity of; to break into parts.
To cause to break up into infinitesimal parts through the use of a disintegrator.
To fall apart; to break up into parts.
e: Recorded since 1785, from dis- + integrate.

s: Those who are for military engagement.
Having a quantity or amount that is generous or plentiful; ample.
e: From bounty + -ful.
From Middle English rudely, rudeliche, equivalent to rude + -ly.

s: Any structure built above the top full deck (FM 55-501).
Any material structure or edifice built on something else; that which is raised on a foundation or basis.
All that part of a building above the basement.
The sleepers and fastenings, in distinction from the roadbed.
The social sphere of ideology which includes religion, art, politics, law and all traditional values.
e: From super- + structure.

s: Having a key, mated to a keyseat and/or keyway, to either control or prevent movement.
Praiseworthy and admirable, often through exhibiting independence and security; based.
Intoxicated by recreational or illegal drugs; drunk or high.
e: Most likely simply from the verb key; in slang perhaps connected to the "securing" action of a lock and key (compare e.g. scored).

s: A subset of a space which is a space in its own right.
Any (often unspecified) method of communicating or travelling faster than light speed.
An alternative dimension or universe, access to or use of which permits faster-than-light travel or communications; hyperspace.
The psychological state of the submissive or bottom during sadomasochistic activity.
e: From sub- + space.
+ (BDSM) From sub + space.

s: A sensory perception of something that does not exist, often arising from disorder of the nervous system, as in delirium tremens.
The act of hallucinating; a wandering of the mind; an error, mistake or blunder.
A confident but incorrect response given by an artificial intelligence; a confabulation.
e: From hallucinate + -ion, from Latin hallucinatus. Compare French hallucination. The first known usage in the English language is from Sir Thomas Browne.

s: Situated on or outside the dura mater.
Of or pertaining to the space immediately outside the dura mater.
An injection of anaesthetic into the epidural space of the spine, especially associated with pain relief during childbirth.
e: From epi- + dural.

s: Of, via or related to the rectum.
e: From rectum + -al.

s: Any of the several species of plant in the genus Taraxacum, characterised by yellow flower heads and notched, broad-ended leaves, especially the common dandelion (Taraxacum officinale).
The flower head or fruiting head of the dandelion plant.
A yellow colour, like that of the flower.
Of a yellow colour, like that of the flower.
e: From Middle English dentdelyon, from Old French dent de lion (“lion's tooth”), also in Latin dēns leōnis, referring to the jagged shape of the plant's leaves.

s: Exhibiting the behaviors and personality traits of a psychopath.
e: From psycho- + -pathic.

s: An international distress signal used by shipping and aircraft.
e: From the distress signal mayday, from French m'aider, short for Venez m'aider! (“Come to help me!”). The term was conceived in the early 1920s by Frederick Stanley Mockford, officer-in-charge of radio at Croydon Airport in England. He had been asked to think of a word that would indicate distress and would easily be understood by all pilots and ground staff in an emergency.

s: In a physically flat or level manner.
In a definite manner; in a manner showing complete certainty.
In a manner that shows no emotion.
e: From flat + -ly.

s: A sheet of plastic embedded with microscopic crystals of herapathite or similarly acting material, so that light passing through it is polarized.
Spectacles made with lenses of this material, once used to view certain 3-D movies, now used as sunglasses.
A camera that develops its own film.
A print from such a camera.
To photograph with a polaroid camera.
e: A genericization of the trademark Polaroid, owned by Polaroid Corporation.
From Latin noxius (“hurtful, injurious”), from noxa (“hurt, injury”), from nocere (“to hurt, injure”); see nocent.

s: The act of one who patches.

One of the simple machines; a sheave, a wheel with a grooved rim, in which a pulled rope or chain lifts an object (more useful when two or more pulleys are used together, as in a block and tackle arrangement, such that a small force moving through a greater distance can exert a larger force through
To raise or lift by means of a pulley.
e: Inherited from Middle English puly, poley, from Old French poulie, polie (“a pulley, windlass”), from Vulgar Latin *polidia, plural mistaken for the feminine of neuter *polidium, from Ancient Greek *πολίδιον (“little pivot”), diminutive of πόλος (“pivot, hinge, axis”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to turn”).

s: A type of round, brimless cap with a soft top and a headband to secure it to the head; usually culturally associated with France.
e: Borrowed from French béret, from Occitan (Gascon) berret (“cap”), from Old Occitan berret, from Medieval Latin birretum, from Late Latin birrus (“large hooded cloak”), from birrus (“short cloak”), from Proto-Celtic *birros (“short”) (compare Welsh byr, Middle Irish berr). Compare biretta.

s: A children's game in which the players hide together, lying side by side.
e: The game name refers to sardines tightly packed in a can.

s: Tending to upset the mind or senses.
Exhilarating or exciting; producing a feeling of high energy or confidence
typically of economic or industrial trends
rapid, substantial, or breakneck in growth.
e: From Middle English hedi, hevedi, equivalent to head + -y.

s: A man who works with birds.
A mythological creature that is part man and part bird.

One of a class of caustic bases, such as soda, soda ash, caustic soda, potash, ammonia, and lithia, whose distinguishing characteristics are dissolving in alcohol and water, uniting with oils and fats to form soap, neutralizing and forming salts with acids, turning to brown several vegetable yellows
Soluble mineral matter, other than common salt, contained in soils of natural waters.
e: From French alcali, from Medieval Latin alcali, ultimately from Arabic اَلْقِلْي (“alkali, ashes (in reference to ashes of the saltwort)”), related to قَلَى (“to roast in a pan, fry”).

s: A sensitive elongated erectile sex organ at the anterior part of the vulva in female humans and other mammals.
A similar erectile sexual organ present in the cloacas of female amniotes.
e: From post-classical New Latin clītoris (16th century), from Koine Greek κλειτορίς, probably from Ancient Greek κλείω (“to sheathe, shut”), in reference to it being covered by the labia minora.

s: A man's headdress made by winding a length of cloth round the head.
A woman's close-fitting hat with little or no brim.
The complete set of whorls of a spiral shell.
A towel wrapped around long wet hair in a manner resembling a turban.
To cover (a person's head) with a turban.
e: Borrowed from Middle French turbant, from Italian turbante, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند, from دلبند, also the root of Doublet of tulip.

s: The nearness of objects with little or no delimiter.
An absence of linking elements in a group of words that are listed together.
An absence of operators in an expression.
The extra emphasis given to a comparison when the contrasted objects are close together.
Two or more contrasting sounds, colours, styles etc. placed together for stylistic effect.
The close placement of two ideas to imply a link that may not exist.
e: Borrowed from French juxtaposition, from Latin iuxtā (“near”) (from Latin iungō (“to join”)) + French position (“position”) (from Latin pōnō (“to place”)).

s: Tending to give orders to others, especially when unwarranted; domineering.
e: From boss + -y.
Diminutive of dialectal English boss + -y, as used in the term boss-calf (which, like buss-calf, is a variant form of boose-calf, a calf kept in a boose (“stall”)).
From boss + -y.

s: Inclined to resent, who tends to harbor resentment, when wronged.
Harboring resentment, full of resentment, at a given moment.
e: From resent + -ful.

s: A fish of the family Mullidae (order Syngnathiformes).
Those of the genus Mullus within that family.
A fish of the family Mugilidae (order Mugiliformes).
Any of several species of freshwater fish in the sucker family.
A men's hairstyle where the hair is kept short on the top and sides and long at the back.
A person who mindlessly follows a fad, a trend, or a leader.
A star with straight edges and usually with five or six points.
e: Thumb|Mullet catch From Middle English molet, mulett, from Old French mulet (now ‘grey mullet’), from Latin mullus (“red mullet”), from Ancient Greek μύλλος.
Also termed a mullethead, possibly derived from the fish (see Etymology 1) or from mull (meaning to stupefy) though neither is certain.
+ (haircut) 1994 US. Popularized and possibly coined by hip hop group the Beastie Boys in their song "Mullet Head".
From Middle English molet, from Old French molette (“rowel”).

s: To sleep, especially briefly; to nap, doze.
To pause; to postpone for a short while.
A brief period of sleep; a nap.
The snooze button on an alarm clock.
e: Unknown, attested since 18th century. Compare Dutch snoezelen (“to snooze”) or Swedish snusa (“to snore lightly”). Compare also Ancient Greek νυστάζω (“to doze, drowse”) and Russian сон (“sleep, dream”).

s: Word called out by the victor when making a move that wins the game.
Said when one has placed a person in a losing situation with no escape.
The conclusive victory in a game of chess that occurs when an opponent's king is threatened with unavoidable capture.
Any losing situation with no escape; utter defeat.
To put the king of an opponent into checkmate.
To place in a losing situation that has no escape.
e: From Middle English chekmat, from Old French eschec mat, from Arabic شَاه مَاتَ, from شاه مات (“the king [is] amazed”).

s: A part of a helmet, arranged so as to lift or open, and so show the face. The openings for seeing and breathing are generally in it.
The fore piece of a cap, projecting over, and protecting the eyes.
A rigid adjustable flap on an automobile windshield that can shield the eyes of a driver from direct sunlight or glare.
To cover with, or as if with, a visor.
e: From Middle English viser, from Anglo-Norman viser and Old French visiere.

s: A slackening or arrest of the blood current, due not to a lessening of the heart’s beat, but to some abnormal resistance of the capillary walls.
Inactivity; a freezing, or state of motionlessness.
A technology allowing something to be artificially frozen in time, so that it does not age or change.
One of the sections of a cathisma or portion of the psalter.
e: From New Latin stasis, from Ancient Greek στάσις. See the doublet Doublet of stead.

s: shining unsteadily or varying rapidly in brightness (referring to a light or a source of light)
Having been visually enlarged by the process of magnification.
The place of business of a barber; a store where a person (usually a male) can go to get a haircut.
A style of a cappella vocal music, usually sung in four-part harmony.
To perform in the barbershop musical style.
e: barber + shop.

s: To cause to take physical form, or to cause an object to appear.
To take physical form, to appear seemingly from nowhere.
To become real (of a plan, idea, etc.); to come to fruition.
To regard as matter; to consider or explain by the laws or principles which are appropriate to matter.
To perform materialization; to save the results of a database query as a temporary table or materialized view.
e: From material + -ize.

s: A large, powerful computer able to manage very many simultaneous tasks and communicate with very many connected terminals; used by large, complex organizations (such as banks and supermarkets) where continuously sustained operation is vital.
A computer chassis that hosts and interconnects modules that perform various tasks.
The main frame of a vehicle etc., more commonly main frame.
e: From main + frame.

s: A collection of goods to be sent, in transit or having been sent.

The sale of one's own goods (clothing, furniture, etc.) through a third-party vendor, in exchange for a portion of the sale price, and with the consigner retaining ownership of the goods until they are sold or abandoned.
e: From consign + -ment.

s: To make invalid (especially in to contract law)
To make or declare (an argument, statement, or theory) unsound or erroneous; disprove.
e: Borrowed from Middle French invalider, from invalide + -er. in- + validate or invalid + -ate.

s: That has not been discovered; unknown, unexplored.
e: From un- + discovered.
From undiscover + -ed.

s: To roam about for pleasure without any definite plan.
e: 1809, from gallant (“wooing women”), originally in sense “to flirt”, broadened to mean “roaming without plan”.

s: Used to show encouragement or approval to a boy, man, or male animal.
A cry of encouragement; an accolade.
e: A variant pronunciation of That's the boy!, a cry of encouragement, especially to children and pet dogs.

s: A receptacle for spit (saliva); especially, one used by people using chewing tobacco or snuff.
e: From spit + -oon.

From Middle English vyntener, variant of viniter, from Old French vineter, vinetier (“wine-merchant, grape-harvester”), from Medieval Latin vīnētārius (“wine dealer”), from vīnētum (“vineyard”), from vīnum (“wine”).

s: Marked by irritation or annoyance; disagreeable; troublesome by reason of long continuance or repetition
e: From Middle English irkesome, irksum, equivalent to irk + -some, or perhaps continuing (in altered form) from Old English weorcsum (“painful, hurtful”).
Of Pampers, itself from pamper.
From un- + pretentious.

s: Able to be refunded in case of customer dissatisfaction, loss, breakage etc.
Something that is eligible to be refunded.
e: From refund + -able.

s: Incapable of being successfully operated on.
Incapable of operation or function; inoperative.
