Modicus is derived from modus (“a measure; a bound, limit”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”)) + -icus. The plural form modica is derived from Latin modica.

s: To defer; to put off temporarily or indefinitely.
To end or suspend an event.
To move as a group from one place to another.
e: From Middle English ajournen, from Old French ajorner (French ajourner), from the phrase a jor (nomé) ("to an (appointed) day").

s: Lacking skill in physical movement with the hands; clumsy.
e: {| class="floatright" | | |}Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- From ham (“thigh and buttock of an animal slaughtered for meat”) + fisted, probably referring to someone being clumsy as if they have hams at the end of their arms instead of hands.

s: To cause two or more events or actions to happen at exactly the same time or same rate, or in a time-coordinated way.
To occur at the same time or with coordinated timing.
To cause (video and audio) to play in a coordinated way.
To set (a clock or watch) to display the same time as another.
To cause (a set of files, data, or settings) on one computer or device to be (and try to remain) the same as on another.
To agree, be coordinated with, or complement well.
e: From Ancient Greek συγχρονίζω, equivalent to syn- + chrono- + -ize.

s: A particle from 64 to 256 mm in diameter, following the Wentworth scale.
A piece of steel that becomes malformed during its manufacture or rolling.
To make shoes (what a cobbler does).
To assemble in an improvised way.
To use cobblestones to pave a road, walkway, etc.
e: From Middle English cobill, kobill (used in various combinations with ston, stan (“stone”), note, nutt (“nut”), etc.), probably a diminutive of Middle English *cob, *cobb, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kubb- (“lump; round object”). Equivalent to cob + -le.
See coble.
From re- + focus.
From un- + verified.

s: Having some specific type of fist.
Brown discoloration on the leaves of plants caused by heat, lack of water or by fungi.
To burn the surface of something so as to discolour it
To wither, parch or destroy something by heat or fire, especially to make land or buildings unusable to an enemy
(To cause) to become scorched or singed
To move at high speed (so as to leave scorch marks on the ground, physically or figuratively).
To burn; to destroy by, or as by, fire.
To attack with bitter sarcasm or virulence.
To ride a bicycle furiously on a public highway.
e: From Middle English scorchen, scorcnen (“to make dry; parch”), perhaps an alteration of earlier *scorpnen, from Old Norse skorpna (“to shrivel up”).

s: A pupil who lives at school during term time.
Someone who pays for meals and lodging in a house rather than a hotel.
A sailor attacking an enemy ship by boarding her, or one repelling such attempts by an enemy.
Someone who takes part in a boardsport, such as surfing or snowboarding.
e: From board + -er.

s: An estimate, judgment or opinion made by guessing, from limited information.
e: From guess + work. Compare Dutch giswerk (“guesswork”).

s: Having a tendency of streaming, flapping, or spreading broadly as if within a current of air or in outer space.
The act of something that flares.
The deliberate open-air burning of natural gas that is generated as a by-product of various petrochemical processes, especially oil extraction; gas flaring.
To be quiet; to keep quiet.
To ask someone to be quiet, especially by saying shh.
e: Imitative. Compare shh and hush.

s: A large kerchief, usually colourful and used either as headgear or as a handkerchief, neckerchief, bikini, or sweatband.

A style of calico printing, in which white or bright spots are produced upon cloth previously dyed a uniform red or dark colour, by discharging portions of the color by chemical means, while the rest of the cloth is under pressure.
e: Borrowed from Hindi बंधन (“the act of binding, a bond”), from Sanskrit बध्नाति (“he binds”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to bind, bond”). Related to Hindi बाँधना (“to tie”). Doublet of bind.

s: confidently or arrogantly overstepping reasonable bounds.
A similar mass action of people leaving a place as a form of protest.
A part of the squat exercise wherein one has to step out from the rack (“walk out” the weight) in order not to hit it during execution.
e: A.

s: The text character ’, which serves as a punctuation mark in various languages and as a diacritical mark in certain rare contexts.
A sudden exclamatory piece of dialogue addressed to someone or something, especially absent.
An arrangement of chlorophyll grains perpendicular to the outer surface of plant cells, as opposed to epistrophe (an arrangement on the outer surface).
e: From French apostrophe, or Latin apostrophus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (“accent of elision”), a noun use of an adjective from ἀποστρέφω (“to turn away”), from ἀπό (“away from”) + στρέφω (“to turn”).
From Latin apostrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή, from ἀποστρέφω (“to turn away”), from ἀπό + στρέφω (“to turn”).

s: The act of something being squirted.

e: From controversial + -ly.

s: Someone who takes advantage of any opportunity to advance their own situation, placing expediency above principle.
e: From French opportuniste, equivalent to opportune + -ist.

s: Each of the two triangular pieces of cloth on the front of a jacket or coat that are folded back below the throat, leaving a triangular opening between.
e: From lap + -el (“diminutive suffix”)

s: An uneven shape or mess created by something dispersing on impact.
Spurious emissions resulting from an abrupt change in a transmitted radio signal.
To splash; to scatter; to land or strike in an uneven, distributed mess.
e: Uncertain. Emerged 1780s.[https://www.etymonline.com/word/splatter] Possibly a splash + spatter.

s: To the point of embarrassment; to an extreme or bewildering degree.
e: From embarrassing + -ly.

s: To be inherited by someone else; to pass down upon the next person in a succession, especially through failure or loss of an earlier holder.
To delegate (a responsibility, duty, etc.) on or upon someone.
of a central government to a local one, a federal one to a federated one, etc.
To transfer authority and responsibility for (something) to (another entity).
To fall as a duty or responsibility on or upon someone.
To shift or to be transferred from a central government to a local one, a federal one to a federated one, etc.
A device or fixture used for urination, particularly
A glass vial used for examining or storing urine.
A chamber pot specially designed or considered as a device for urination.
A device for urination worn or used by patients suffering urinary incontinence.
A plumbing fixture intended for standing urination, typically by men and boys.
Any oblong glass vessel shaped like the old alchemist's urinal.
A room or structure used for urination: a latrine; an outhouse; a lavatory.
e: From Middle English urinal, urynal, orynal, from Old French urinal, orinal (“vessel for urination”), from Latin ūrīnālis (“urinary”). Use for plumbing fixtures attested from 1851.
From Middle French urinal, from Late Latin ūrīnālis, equivalent to urine + -al.

s: A style of humor focusing on physical comedy, such as slipping on a banana peel, and with foolish characters who get into humiliating situations.
A pair of sticks attached at one end and used to create a slapping sound effect, used especially in slapstick comedy; a type of clapper.
e: From slap + stick, Calque of Italian batacchio. The pair of sticks was used by the comic character Harlequin in the commedia dell'arte.

s: A Japanese female entertainer skilled in various arts such as tea ceremony, dancing, singing and calligraphy.
e: Borrowed from Japanese, from +.
From gleeful + -ly.

s: Straightforward; not evasive; candid and direct.
Straight forward, in a straight direction.
e: From Middle English forþright, forþriʒt, forþriht, from Old English forþriht (“direct, plain”). en + forth#Adverb + right#Etymology_1.
From Middle English forthright, forþriʒt, forthricte, from Old English forþrihte (“straightway, at once, plainly”), from forþriht + -e (“adverbial suffix”). en + forth#Adverb + right#Etymology_1.

s: Having a hard, strong, and determined look about oneself.
Having a hard, strong, and determined mentality or mindset.
e: From steely + eyed.

s: The act of forming a shape with the mouth.
Ranting; passionate speech devoid of meaning.
A person who maintains the administration and upkeep of his or her residence, especially one who is not employed outside the home; one who runs the household.
e: From home + maker.

s: Something to be derided; a laughing stock.
e: From Old French derision, from Latin dērīsiōnem, accusative of dērīsiō, from dērīdēre ("to mock, to laugh at, to deride").

s: To shuffle something again, especially playing cards.
To reorganize or rearrange something, especially government posts.
An instance of reshuffling, a reorganization.
e: From re- + shuffle.
From gall + bladder.

s: Having a rough, surly, and harsh demeanor and nature.
e: Middle Dutch odt 16th century, from Dutch grof and/or Middle Low German grof (both “rough, coarse, rude”), from Old Dutch *grof or Old Saxon *grof, both from Proto-West Germanic *grob, from Proto-Germanic *grubaz (“coarse, rough”), possibly from an earlier *gahrubaz and then related with *hreubaz (“scabby, rough, scrubby”).
Perhaps related to Dutch grof (“rough, coarse”).

s: The electronic panel that is used to direct telephone calls to the desired recipient.
A large piece of power-distribution equipment that directs electricity to multiple loads.
To transmit or relay through, as if through, a switchboard.
e: From switch + board.

s: Any of many New World fish of the genus Poecilia, formerly called Mollienesia; more commonly molly.
e: Diminutive abbreviation; compare Mollie (“Molotov”).

s: To react too much or too intensely.
e: From over- + react.
From retrospective + -ly.
Mid-15th century, "pertaining to infants," from Latin infantilis (“pertaining to an infant”), equivalent to infant + -ile, from īnfāns. Sense of "infant-like" is from 1772.

s: Something that is used to pick a winner from a tied situation.
e: From tie + breaker.

s: The mental power or ability of choosing; the will.
A concept that distinguishes whether or not the subject or agent intended something.
e: From French volition, from Medieval Latin volitiō (“will, volition”), from Latin volō (“to wish; to want; to mean or intend”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose; to want”)) + -tiō (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-tis).

s: A thin mortar used to fill the gaps between tiles and cavities in masonry.
A kind of beer or ale.
e: From Middle English growte, grut, from Old English grūt (“dregs; coarse meal”), from Proto-West Germanic *grūt, from Proto-Germanic *grūtą (compare Dutch gruit (“dregs”), German Grauß, Norwegian grut (“ground”)), lengthening of Proto-Germanic *grutą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to grind, rub”). Related to grit.

s: A long, spearlike implement with a barbed head, attached to a line and used to catch and haul in large marine animals such as whales and other cetaceans, seals, walruses, sharks, etc.
Such an implement armed with explosives in the head, used to strike and fatally wound cetaceans when whaling.
A sharp tip within a disposable syringe, used to penetrate the stopper.
To shoot something with a harpoon.
e: From Old French harpon, from Latin harpaga, a variant of Latin harpagō, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (“hook”), from ἁρπάζω (“to snatch away, to carry off, to seize, to captivate”). Sense and spelling perhaps influenced by Dutch harpoen (“harpoon”). Doublet of harpagon.

s: A woman or man of stunning beauty or handsomeness, a knockout.

A professional wrestling maneuver in which an attacking wrestler applies a facelock to an opponent and falls to a seated position, forcing the opponent's jaw or neck to drop on the attacker's shoulder.
A pistol firing a beam capable of stunning an enemy.
A person or machine that stuns an animal before slaughter.
e: From stun + -er.

s: To take (a substance, e.g., food) into the body of an organism, especially through the mouth and into the gastrointestinal tract.
To cause (an undesired object or fluid) to enter the engine, generally via the intake.
To bring or import into a system.
The process of importing data or other material into a system.
e: From Latin ingerō (“to carry in”).

s: The quality or state of being technical.
That which is technical, or peculiar to any trade, profession, sect, or the like.
A minor detail, rule, law, etc., seemingly insignificant to a non-specialist but which has significant consequences in larger matters.
e: From technical + -ity.

s: To verify something by supplying evidence; to authenticate or corroborate.
To give material form or substance to something; to embody; to record in documents
e: From Medieval Latin substantiatus (“given substance”), from the verb substantiare, first used 1657.

s: The effect of being shadowed (in the sense of blocked), as from a light source or radio transmission.
The situation where a person repeats speech immediately as they hear it (usually through earphones).
Secretly or discreetly tracking or following someone, keeping under surveillance.
The technique of copying ROM contents to RAM to allow for shorter access times. The ROM chip is then disabled while the initialized memory locations are switched in on the same block of addresses.
A work experience option where students learn about a job by walking through the work day as a shadow to a competent worker.
e: From shadow + -ing.

s: A worker who shapes something to prepare it for a finishing operation.
A piece of woollen cloth prepared for fulling.
Lightly edited versions of the previous day's filming; rushes.
Suffering from claustrophobia; being scared of being enclosed in a confined space.
Cramped and confined, so as to induce claustrophobia.
e: From claustrophobia + -ic.

s: Having no consequence; not consequential; of little importance.
Not logically following from the premises.
Something unimportant; something that does not matter.
e: From in- + consequential.

s: A writing board finished with a hard white material, which can be written upon using special non-permanent markers and subsequently wiped clean.
A collaborative tool allowing several users to write and draw on the same shared display.
To use a whiteboard, to write on a writeboard
e: From white + board, modelled on blackboard.

s: An Italian savoury dish made with rice and other ingredients.
A similar dish made without rice.
e: From Italian risotto, from riso (“rice”).

s: The act of one who champions something; fervent support.
An Italian coffee-based beverage made from espresso to which milk that has been steamed or frothed is added.
A medium- to dark-brown colour like that of the coffee drink (sense 1) or the habit of a Capuchin monk.
e: Thumb|A cappuccino (sense 1).

s: The association of a new brand, trademark, image, or appearance with a product or service.
Pale, lacking colour, having a pallor.
A type of seasoned meat and vegetable hand pie, usually of a semicircular shape.
e: From paste + -y.
Thumb|A Cornish pasty in a bowl From Middle English paste (“pie”), from Anglo-Norman paste and Old French pasté. Doublet of patty.
Pasties (nipple coverings) thumb|Woman wearing pasties From paste + -y.

s: The region of the mammalian body between the neck and abdomen as well as the cavity containing the heart and lungs.
The middle of three distinct divisions in an insect, crustacean or arachnid body to which the legs are attached.
e: From Latin thorax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (“a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).

s: A kicking, as with a booted foot.
The act by which a computer is booted.
Advantage; gain; gain by plunder; booty.
The materials used to harness an animal.
Something which gives the appearance of something.
coverings or harnesses for a horse; caparisons.
e: From trapping.

s: To change the brand name, logo, or image of a product or organization.
A change to the brand name, logo, or image of a product or company.
e: From re- + brand.

s: Any set of machine-readable parallel bars or concentric circles, varying in width, spacing or height, encoding information according to a symbology.
A portion of a gene that identifies a particular species.
An instance of self-harm, typically with multiple parallel cuts along a line, similar in form to a machine barcode.
To apply a barcode (machine-readable code) to.
e: bar + code. for.

s: That is propelled in a narrow stream or jet.
The process or result of something being spouted; that which is spouted.
A gutter under the eaves of a building; guttering.
To leave the country in which one lives, especially one's native country, in order to reside elsewhere.
e: From Latin emigratus, perfect passive participle of emigro (“to move away, remove, depart from a place”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + migro (“to move, remove, depart”).

s: Meriting condemnation, censure or blame, especially as something wrong, harmful or injurious; blameworthy, guilty.
e: From Middle English culpable, from Old French culpable, from Latin culpābilis (“blameworthy”), from culpō (“to blame, condemn”), from culpa (“a fault, crime, mistake”). Compare also culprit#Etymology.

s: Heavily laden, as if to creak under the strain.
A low sound associated with extended suffering, sorrow, and toil.
e: From Middle English gronynge (“groaning”), from Old English grānung; equivalent to groan + -ing. Conflated with Middle English gronende, present participle of gronen, from Old English grāniende, present participle of grānian (“to groan”). Analyzable as groan + -ing.

s: A synthetic compound used as a dissociative anesthetic and analgesic drug and also recreationally as a hallucinogen.
e: ketone + amine. First use appears c. 1966.

s: An act of stabbing with a stake.
e: From Middle English stakyng, staking, from Old English stacung (“staking”), from Old English *stacian (“to drive stakes”), equivalent to stake + -ing.

s: A plant (Cyperus papyrus) in the sedge family, native to the Nile river valley, paper reed.
A material similar to paper made from the papyrus plant.
A scroll or document written on papyrus.
e: From Middle English papirus, borrowed from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος, of unknown origin. Doublet of papyros.

s: An animal of a hairless breed.
e: From hair + -less.. Cognate with German haarlos.

s: A vessel for brewing and serving tea, typically with a handle and spout.
e: tea + pot.

s: The act or fact of launching again.
e: From re- + launch.

s: Infl of liquefy; Alternative spelling of liquified.
Making a person seem or become slimmer.
The process of making or becoming slimmer.
In pain, especially in an emotional sense.
An area in which land mines or naval mines have been laid.
A matter or situation presenting multiple risks, dangers, complications or difficulties.
A pitch that has dried out and crumbled and on which the ball is bouncing and spinning unpredictably.
A quiz that terminates when the test-taker answers a question incorrectly.
e: From mine + field. Compare Mienenfäield (“minefield”), West Frisian mynfjild (“minefield”), Dutch mijnenveld (“minefield”), Low German Minenfeld (“minefield”), German Minenfeld (“minefield”), Danish minefelt (“minefield”), Swedish minfält (“minefield”).

s: The great artery which carries the blood from the heart to all parts of the body except the lungs; the main trunk of the arterial system.
e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (“the arteries springing from the heart”), from ἀορτέω, lengthened form of ἀείρω (“to lift, raise”).

s: The profession of being a firefighter.
e: From fire + fighting.

s: A little mass of lead, or the like, attached to a line, and used by builders, etc., to indicate a vertical direction.
A weight on the end of a long line, used by sailors to determine the depth of water.
Truly vertical, as indicated by a plumb line.
Describing an LBW where the batsman is hit on the pads directly in front of their wicket and should be given out.
To determine the depth, generally of a liquid; to sound.
To attach to a water supply and drain.
To think about or explore in depth, to get to the bottom of.
To use a plumb bob as a measuring or aligning tool.
To accurately align vertically or horizontally.
To fall or sink like a plummet.
To trace a road or track; to follow it to its end.
e: From Middle English plumbe, plumme, from Old French *plombe, from Latin plumba, plural of plumbum.

s: The favoring of relatives (most strictly) or also personal friends (more broadly) because of their relationship rather than because of their abilities.
e: Borrowed from French népotisme, from Italian nepotismo, from Latin nepōs (“nephew”), a reference to the practice of popes appointing relatives (most often nephews) as cardinals (cardinal-nephew) during the Middle Ages and Renaissance.

s: Having been overstated; exaggerated; stated, displayed, or presented too grandly or prominently.
Covered or furnished with a floor.
Struck down or leveled with the floor.
Hung near the base of a wall.
Of a pedal, pushed all the way down, especially to accelerate.
Silenced by a conclusive answer or retort.
The playing of music on a fiddle.
Of petty or trivial importance; footling
Showing empathy for others, recognizing their feelings.
e: Derived from empathic, modified to sound more similar to sympathetic.

s: A person or thing that raises.
A kind of armchair with a standing-up system.
The upright board on the front of a step in a flight of steps.
e: From raise + -er.

s: An act by which individuals are herded.
Manipulation of poll results by a polling organization so that they match those produced from other organizations.
Alternative form of of people smuggler.

e: From obstruct + -ive.

s: The terminal part of the large intestine through which feces pass after exiting the colon, but before leaving the body through the anus or cloaca.
e: Borrowed from New Latin rectum, clipping of Latin rectum intestinum, rectum, neuter of rectus (“straight”). See right.

s: In ski jumping, the flat or uphill area past the landing point, where the skier can slow down.
The sheepdog's initial run towards the sheep, done in a curving motion so as not to startle them.
A piece of outlying grazing land on an arable farm.
e: From out- + run.

s: To read wrongly; misconstrue; misinterpret; mistake the sense or significance of.
e: From Middle English misreden, from Old English misrǣdan (“to advise wrongly; read wrongly”), equivalent to mis- + read. Cognate with misräide (“to go wrong, fail”), Dutch misraden (“to guess wrongly”), German missraten (“to fail; go wrong; become wayward”). For the noun, compare Old English misrǣd (“misguidance; misconduct”).

s: praise or approval, which is often insincere and sometimes contrived to win favour.
e: From Middle English flaterye, flaterie, from Old French flaterie, from the verb flater (“to flatter”). flatter + -y.

s: One who shreds or tears something.
A machine that tears up objects into smaller pieces, especially a paper shredder, garbage shredder or gardening or farming shredder.
A program that overwrites deleted data to prevent recovery.
One who shreds, or plays (especially the guitar) very fast.
e: From shred + -er.

s: A blow that produces a muffled sound.
The sound of such a blow; a thud.
Used to replace the vulgar or blasphemous element in "what the hell" and similar phrases.
To hit (someone or something) as if to make a thump.
To cause to make a thumping sound.
To throb with a muffled rhythmic sound.
(of a rabbit) to hit the ground with the back legs to signal agitation.
e: Mid 16th century, probably Onomatopoeic.

s: The act of one who farts; a sound like a fart.
e: From Middle English fartynge, fartyng, ferting, from Old English feorting (“farting”), equivalent to fart + -ing.
Variant of titty. Attested from the late eighteenth century.
Likely from Romani didikai; compare didicoy.

s: To expel (one or more people) from their property; to force (one or more people) to move out.
To eject from a memory cache to reduce the cache's size.
e: From Middle English evicten, evycten, borrowed from Latin ēvictus, past participle of ēvincō (“to vanquish completely”). Doublet of evince.

s: Involving or engaged in much successful trade or activity. (of an economy, business etc.)
e: From buoy + -ant.

s: The sound made by the whistle of a steam locomotive or ship.
A locomotive, especially a train or ship.
e: Onomatopoeic.

s: A breakfast and snack food consisting of loose, crispy pellets made of nuts, rolled oats, honey and other natural ingredients.
Eating healthy food, supporting the protection of the environment, and having liberal views.
e: From Granola, a brand of breakfast cereal registered in 1886 by Will Keith Kellogg and in use into the early 20th century. It was initially known as Granula and renamed Granola to avoid legal problems with James Caleb Jackson, who invented a similar cereal in 1863, named Granula after the granules of Graham flour, the main ingredient. The food and name were revived in the 1960s.

s: To combust or decompose supersonically via shock compression.
e: Either Borrowed from French détoner or directly from Latin dētonātus, perfect passive participle of dētonō (“to thunder down (strongly); (figuratively, of a person) to thunder, speak threateningly, to rage; to stop thundering”) (see -ate), from dē- (“off, from”) + tonō (“to thunder”)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂-.

s: or remote in time or space.
Not mentally present, as when daydreaming.
One who lives a great distance away.
A hip-hop dance generally performed by moving one's body in a shimmy style and passing a hand through or near the hair on one's own head.
e: From Dougie. Named after 1980s rapper Doug E. Fresh who performed similar moves.

s: Deposited from a solution, vapour or state of suspension into gas.
The process of ingesting, or consuming something orally, whether it be food, drink, medicine, or other substance. It is usually referred to as the first step of digestion.
The process of ingesting something into a jet engine or an instance.
Any intake of a substance into an organism.
Intake of data into a computer system.
e: Borrowed from Latin ingestionem, accusative of ingestio (“a pouring in”), action noun of the perfect passive participle of ingerere (“pour in”), from in-- + gero.

s: A hired strongman, especially working for the underworld.
The member of a group, especially of a gang, charged with keeping dissident members obedient.
A battering ram used by the emergency services for gaining access to locked premises.
A player who physically intimidates or confronts the opposition.
e: From enforce + -er.

s: The act by which someone is escorted; provision of an escort.
Of a person, having a sharp, pointed face reminiscent of a ferret.
A young man or boy in service; a servant.
A country labourer; a countryman, a rustic.
A rural lover; a male sweetheart in a pastoral setting.
e: From Middle English swayn, swain, sweyn, swein, from Old English sweġen (attested also as personal name Swein, Sweġen), from Old Norse sveinn, from Proto-Germanic *swainaz (“relative, young man, servant”), from Proto-Indo-European *swé (“oneself; separate; apart”), thus properly one's own.
From uncomfortable + -ly or un- + comfortably.
From jazz + -y.

s: Furnished with beams, as the head of a stag.
The state or condition of being blocked.
The thing that is the cause of such a state, blocking a passage.
Occlusion of a lumen (especially that of a blood vessel or intestine), or the thing that is causing it; as
e: From block + -age.

s: To have an unfortunate accident of some kind; to be killed, or come to harm.
To go astray; to do something wrong.
To have a miscarriage; to involuntarily abort a foetus.
To fail to achieve some purpose; to be unsuccessful, to go wrong (of a business, project etc.).
Of a letter etc.: to fail to reach its intended recipient.
e: From Middle English miscarien. en + mis + carry.
From nose + -y.

s: A form of programming (cinematic, television, live action, etc.) that provides both information and entertainment, consisting of mostly celebrity news and human drama.
e: information + entertainment.

s: The repetition of an earlier (usually historic) event, as a performance or social event.
e: From re + enact + ment.

s: To make high; to raise higher; to elevate.
To advance, increase, augment, make larger, more intense, stronger etc.
e: From Middle English heightenen, hyghtenen, equivalent to height + -en.
Shortening.

s: simulated; in effect or essence, rather than in fact or reality.
A Turkish and Greek dish of fish roe (carp or cod), lemon juice, breadcrumbs, onion, garlic, and olive oil; often served as a meze or with pitta bread.
e: From Greek ταραμοσαλάτα, from ταραμάς (“cod roe”) (from Turkish tarama) + σαλάτα (“salad”) (from Italian insalata, cognate to English salad).

s: The concluding section of a discourse, either written or oral, in which the orator or writer sums up and commends his topic to his audience, particularly as used in the technical sense of a component of ancient Roman oratorical delivery.
A discourse or rhetorical argument in general.
e: From Latin perōrō (“to speak at length, to conclude a speech”) (from per- (“very”) + ōrō (“to speak, to orate”) (English orate)) + -ation (“action (nominalizer)”) (from Latin -ātiō).

s: Of, relating to, or characteristic of a ponce.
Intended to impress others, particularly in an excessively refined or ostentatious manner; affected, pretentious.
Chiefly of a male person: effeminate; gay, homosexual.
e: From ponce (“kept man; pimp; effeminate man; homosexual man”) + -y.

s: The process by which something is cheapened (made more affordable or made vulgar).
An engorged, dilated and easily broken varicosity in the perianal area, often accompanied by intense itching and throbbing pain: piles.
e: From Middle English emerowdes, emeroides, emeroydez, from Old French emorroides, from Latin haemorrhoidae, from Ancient Greek αἱμορροΐς, a feminine adjective from αἱμόρροος (“flowing with blood”), from αἷμα (“blood”) and the root of ῥέω (“flow”). Doublet of emerod.

s: An organ formed of the mammary glands of female quadruped mammals, particularly ruminants such as cattle, goats, sheep and deer.
e: From Middle English udder, uddyr (also as uther, iddyr), from Old English ūder (“udder; breast”), from Proto-Germanic *ūdarą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥ (“udder”).

s: An act in which someone mumbles something
The condition of lacking basic mathematical skills caused by a brain injury, or more specifically an injury to the parietal lobe.
e: From a- + calculo (“to calculate”) + -ia (“pathological condition”)
Borrowed from Latin nūntius (“messenger”)

s: Stupid or inept, like a knucklehead.
e: From knuckle + headed.
From onomatopoetic + -ally.
From un- + nuanced.

s: Capable of being poached, or stolen.
Suitable for being cooked by poaching.
e: From poach + -able.
From Middle English unfavored; equivalent to un- + favored.
From counter- + proliferation.
From nut + bar.

s: To confuse; to fluster; to flabbergast.
To give in, to give up, to collapse.
e: Uncertain, probably risen out of a British dialect (OED finds candidate words in Herefordshire, Gloucestershire, southern Cheshire, and Sheffield). The formation seems to be onomatopœic, expressive of the notion of throwing down roughly and untidily. [OED]. First use appears c. 1837 in the writings of Charles Dickens.

s: A long, often calf-length, loose-fitting dress chiefly with short sleeves which is made of lightweight fabric printed with colourful, stylized Hawaiian themes (such as flowers and palm branches).
e: From muʻumuʻu (“to be cut off; to be shortened”), probably because the garment is a short-sleeved and often calf-length version of the floor-length holoku or Mother Hubbard dress which has long sleeves and originally a train.

s: A non-Jewish girl, especially one who is attractive and young.
e: From Yiddish שיקסע, which is partly derived from the Hebrew שֶׁקֶץ (“abomination, impure, object of loathing”).

s: An instrument for measuring the air capacity of the lungs.
e: From spīro (“to breathe”) + -meter.
Borrowed from Spanish feminista. Doublet of feminist.

s: A bag or bladder to hold a reservoir of gas, as in a hot-air balloon.
A lighter-than-air aircraft; a balloon or dirigible.
A person who is overly garrulous or prone to making empty, unsupportable statements; a windbag.
To speak foolishly, pompously, or at length; to blather.
e: From gas + bag.

s: A person of the lowest social or economic class.
A broker who sold securities in the street.
e: From gutter + snipe.

s: A cowhand (one who tends free-range cattle)

A 19th-century device used around the necks of cows and other livestock to prevent them from challenging fencing. The action of the device was to poke the cow when the device came into contact with the fence.
e: From cow + poke.
From laudable + -ly.

s: A long speech or prose work that bitterly laments the state of society and its morals, and often contains a prophecy of its coming downfall.
e: From French jérémiade, from Jérémie, from Latin Ieremias, from Hebrew ירמיה (“Jeremiah”). Named after Jeremiah, who lamented the moral state of Judah and predicted her downfall.

s: The condition or quality of being phony or fake.
e: From phony + -ness.

s: To make or treat as babish.
e: From babe + -ish.
From pant + -less.
From saw + bones.

s: A thick quantity of sputum, usually containing phlegm.
e: Unknown; possibly from Luger, Lou, Lue or Louie; possibly from the name of the baseball player Lou Gehrig (from the habit of baseball players of spitting); possible variant of booger.

s: A card game, similar to bezique.
A meld of the jack of diamonds and queen of spades in that card game.
e: Perhaps from Austro-Bavarian pronunciation of German Binokel (where b>p change is common), French binocle, a related card game.

s: To beat (someone) in a competition of wits with superior cleverness or cunning; to outsmart.
e: From out- + fox.
From un- + threatening.

s: lively, spirited, or frenzied due to being ardent, passionate, and zealous.
e: Borrowed from Latin fervidus, from ferveō. la:fervere + id.

s: The room in a public building where press conferences are given
e: From press + room.

s: Having more than one syllable; having multiple or many syllables.
Characterized by or consisting of words having numerous syllables.
A word having more than one syllable
e: From poly- + syllabic.

s: The attitude or belief that a particular doctrine, culture, or social system, particularly a religious or political one, is superior and that it will or should triumph over all others.
e: From triumphal + -ism.

s: A box holding papers to be transmitted to others, usually by mail.
An electronic folder serving the same purpose, for electronic mail.
e: From out + box.
From out- + box.

s: The act by which something slackens; loss of speed, tautness, etc.

e: From dis- + proportional.

s: An informal beach party in which food, usually seafood, is cooked in a firepit dug in the sand, filled with hot coals.
An instance of smoking (usually marijuana) in an enclosed space.
To smoke marijuana in an enclosed space such as a car with the windows up.
To enclose something and fill it with smoke by smoking (usually marijuana) inside it.
e: From clam + bake.

s: Someone who acts in a disreputable, unethical, or unscrupulous way, especially in the practice of law and politics.
To act in a disreputable, unethical, or unscrupulous way, especially in the practice of law and politics.
To exploit (someone or something) in this way.
e: US origin, 19th century. The etymology of the word is not generally agreed upon. The Oxford English Dictionary describes it as "of obscure origin," possibly deriving from a historical sense of shy meaning "disreputable", equivalent to shy + -ster.
From Middle English wyndbagge, equivalent to wind + bag.
From Middle English ungracious; equivalent to un- + gracious.

s: Left too long in a chemical bath.

e: From geopolitical + -ly or geo- + politically.

s: In an enduring manner or fashion; so as to endure or last.
e: From enduring + -ly.

s: The living quarters of a ship designated for the commissioned officers other than the captain.
The commissioned officers of a ship, excluding the captain.
e: From ward + room.

The first known uses of lily-livered are in William Shakespeare’s works written; see quotations below. From the medieval belief that the liver was the seat of courage, and the pale color of the lily flower. A person who had no blood in their liver would have no courage and would thus be a coward. Equivalent to lily + livered.

s: The state of being solicitous; uneasiness of mind occasioned by fear of evil or desire for good; anxiety.
Special or pronounced concern or attention.
A cause of anxiety or concern.
e: From Middle English solicitude, from Old French sollicitude, from Latin sollicitūdō (“anxiety”), from sollicitus, solicitus (“anxious, solicitous”). See solicitous.

s: To bully in an intimidating, bossy, or supercilious way.
e: From brow + beat.

s: Born on or in the sea.
e: From sea + born.
From blues + man.
From say + -eth.

s: A particular pronunciation or custom that is regarded as distinguishing members of a group from non-members, especially when used as a test.
A common or longstanding belief, custom, or catchphrase associated with a particular group, especially one with little current meaning or truth.
e: Hebrew שִׁבֹּלֶת//שיבולת (“ear [of wheat] or stream, torrent”). Doublet of sebboleth and Middle English sebolech, both from Late Latin sebboleth in the Vulgate.
From admonish + -ment.

s: Any of several long-bodied mammals of the subfamilies Mustelinae and Ictonychinae, both in the weasel family Mustelidae.
Notably, the European polecat, Mustela putorius.
A base or despicable person; a wretch.
A tubular device used to support lights on a set.
e: From Middle English polcat, pulkat, of Uncertain origin. Perhaps from Middle English *pole, *poule (“hen”), from Old French poule (“hen”) + Middle English cat. Compare English foumart.

s: To be of a higher rank than.
e: From out- + rank.

s: Having an aspect of great depth, drawing the eye to look downwards.
Pertaining to vertigo (in all its meanings).
Inducing a feeling of giddiness, vertigo, dizziness or of whirling.
e: From Middle French vertigineux, from Latin vertīginōsus.

s: A strong, downward air current; an air pocket or air hole.
e: From down- + draft.

s: Recently started but not fully formed yet; just begun; only elementary or immature.
Chaotic, disordered, confused; also, incoherent, rambling.
Of a crime, imposing criminal liability for an incompleted act.
To cause or bring about. In the field of criminology, to encourage, assist, conspire, aid and abet, incite, etc.
e: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb circa 1631; Borrowed from Latin incohātus (“begun, unfinished”), perfect passive participle of incohō (“to begin”), see -ate. Cognate with Spanish incoar (“to initiate, commence, begin”).

s: Clouded, especially due to accidental exposure to light.
Too unimportant to be worthy of attention.
Impossible to consider as a possibility; inconceivable.
e: From Middle French inconsidérable. in- + considerable.

s: A counselor or advisor, especially to Mafia bosses.
e: Borrowed from Italian consigliere, from Italian consiglio (“advice", counsel”), from Latin cōnsilium (“council”). Entered the popular English lexicon through Mario Puzo's “Godfather” novels and the subsequent films made from them.

s: An excess of logs being conveyed on a river, so that their motion halts.
A clog or such jam or mess that halts or greatly delays progress.
To deliberately impede or delay the progress of.
e: From log + jam.

s: A sleep-inducing agent, especially a drug.
e: Borrowed from French soporifique, from sopor, -ific.
From Middle English laughynglie, leiȝingly, equivalent to laughing + -ly.

s: of, or relating to oratory or an orator.
e: From orator or oratory + -ical, or else from Latin ōrātōrius.

s: The act of placing a saddle on an animal.
e: From saddle#Verb + -ing. Compare Middle English saddyllynge,sadyllynge (“a saddlecloth or horsecloth”).

s: To introduce or insert surreptitiously or without warrant.
To force another to accept especially by stealth or deceit; to stick.
To pass off as genuine or worthy.
A type of light and fast-sailing ship.
e: Probably from archaic Dutch vuisten (“to take into one’s hand”), from Middle Dutch vuysten, from vuyst (“fist”); akin to Old English fyst (“fist”).
From Old French fuste (“stick, boat”), from Latin fustis (“cudgel”).
From Old French fust (whence also French fût), from Latin fustis.

s: An inaccurate statement or statistic believed to be true because of broad repetition, especially if cited in the media.
An interesting item of trivia; a minor fact.
e: From fact + -oid (“similar, but not the same”); Coined by Norman Mailer in Marilyn: A Biography, defined as "facts which have no existence before appearing in a magazine or newspaper, creations which are not so much lies as a product to manipulate emotion in the Silent Majority".

s: A sweet liqueur made from marasca cherries.
e: From Italian maraschino, from marasca (“morello cherry”) + -ino (“diminutive suffix”), from amarasca, from amaro (“bitter”).

s: The property of a word that sounds like what it represents.
A word that sounds like what it represents, such as gurgle, stutter or hiss.
A word that appropriates a sound for another sensation or a perceived nature, such as thud, beep or meow; an ideophone, phenomime.
The use of language whose sound imitates that which it names.
e: Borrowed from Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιΐα (“the coining of a word in imitation of a sound”), from ὀνοματοποιέω (“to coin names”), from ὄνομα (“name”) + ποιέω (“to make, to do, to produce”)..

s: A room used for receiving and sending mail.
e: From mail + room.

s: The person who does the prompting.
One who inputs prompts to an artificial intelligence system.
e: From prompt + -er.

s: That can or must be certified.
Mentally ill to such an extent that involuntary institutionalization is appropriate; crazy.
e: From certify + -able.
From pod + iatry.
From huff + -y.

s: A bald person, especially a man.
An intellectual, especially one who is insensitive, pedantic, or out of touch.
e: From egg + head.

s: A boy who delivers newspapers to houses on a paper round.
e: From paper + boy.

s: Clipping of ultrasonogram: A medical image produced by an ultrasound echo.
e: From sonus + -gram, equivalent to sono- + -gram.

s: The state of being a pundit.
The opinion or advice of a pundit.
e: From pundit + -ry.

s: The skill of being a good statesman, the ability to perform well in political office.
e: From statesman + -ship.
From Hindi शरीफ़/Urdu شریف, from Arabic شَرِيف. Arabic ش ر ف.

s: A person who makes articles out of silver usually larger than jewellery.
e: Inherited from Middle English silver smyth, from Old English seolforsmiþ (“silversmith”), from Proto-Germanic *silubrasmiþaz (“silversmith”), equivalent to silver + smith.

s: Of, relating to, or derived from voyeurism or a voyeur.
e: From voyeur + -istic.

s: Someone who sells products or services by making unsolicited telephone calls.
e: From tele- + marketer.

s: To engage in or discuss politics.
To give something political characteristics; to turn into a political issue.
To make someone politically active or aware.
e: From politic + -ize.

s: A person who greets people on their arrival.
A volunteer who shows tourists around their home city or region for free.
e: From Middle English greter, gretter, equivalent to greet + -er.
From Middle English bluntnes, bluntnesse, equivalent to blunt + -ness.

s: One of a pair of red lights mounted on the rear of a vehicle, so it can be seen from the rear at night.
e: From tail + light.

s: One of the two vertical side poles of a goal.

The tall Y-shaped upright, now usually of fiberglass, at either end of the playing field, through which a football must go in order for a field goal to be scored. (They were originally H-shaped, with one wooden post on either side.)
A rule or target that is "moved" (changed) unfairly; see move the goalposts.
e: From goal + post.

s: Showing enthusiastic and unconditional commitment; having no reservations.
e: From whole + hearted. First appears before 1628 in the publications of John Preston, a clergyman in the Church of England.

s: The act by which something is ratcheted.
A conjurers' trick of bending an object back and forth to induce metal fatigue, so that it can be broken later by rubbing it.
To deliberately make more confusing in order to conceal the truth.
To alter code while preserving its behavior but concealing its structure and intent.
e: The adjective is, in Middle English, the verb in 1536; either Borrowed from Middle French obfusquer, offusquer, from Old French offusquer, or directly from Late Latin obfuscātus, offuscātus, the perfect passive participle of obfuscō, offuscō (see -ate and -ate), from Latin ob- + fuscō (“to darken”). Doublet of dusken.

s: Someone who tends to dabble in a variety of activities or interests.
Pertaining to or like a dilettante.
e: From Italian dilettante, present participle of dilettare (“to delight”), from Latin dēlectāre (“to delight”).

s: An exhaust pipe exhausting to the aft of the vehicle.
An exhaust pipe (on a vehicle) (in any configuration).
To fasten an object to the tail of (an animal) as a prank.
e: From tail + pipe.

s: To make into, or to become, a nation.
To bring a private company, or an industry comprising such companies, under the control of a specific government.
To bring a concept such as a political issue or commercial campaign to the attention of the entire country.
To change from having local and regional variation to being national in character and scope.
To make national; to make a nation of; to endow with the character and habits of a nation, or the peculiar sentiments and attachment of citizens of a nation.
e: From French nationaliser. national + -ize.

s: A sensation that smarts or stings.
e: From Middle English smertyng, smertinge, from Old English smeortung, smertung (“smarting, itching”), equivalent to smart + -ing.

s: The state or quality of being attentive.
e: From attentive + -ness.

s: The skin which a deer frays from its horns.
To make something fixed and stable; to fix.
To attend to something to the exclusion of all others.
To attach oneself to a person or thing in a pathological, neurotic, or obsessive manner.
e: From fix + -ate or fixus (“fixed, solid”) + -ate.

s: The act of one who dithers.
To hit or strike heavily and repeatedly.
To scornfully criticize someone or something.
e: Alteration of pommel.

s: A clergyman; especially a settled minister or parson.
A West Indian fish (Epinnula magistralis), of the family Trichiuridae.
e: From Latin dominus. Doublet of dom, dominie, dominus, don.

s: An act or instance of deferring or putting off.
Officially sanctioned postponement of compulsory military service.
e: From defer + -ment.
From studious + -ly.

s: According to a procedure; following a procedure.
In a manner that is concerned with procedure.
Following a computer algorithm, often in a randomized way.
e: From procedural + -ly.

s: Effeminacy; indulgence in soft living or luxuriousness.
Pleasantness, especially of behaviour or personality; agreeableness.
A value determining how much processor time to concede to a running process. (See also nice, renice.)
e: From nice + -ness.

s: With a hermetic seal; so as to be airtight.
e: From hermetic + -ally.

s: A small open boat propelled by oars (by rowing).
To row a boat of this kind.
e: From row + boat.

s: Having a full, voluptuous figure, especially possessing large breasts.
Full of health, vigour, and good temper.
Morally pliant; obedient and easily yielding to pressure.
e: From Middle English buxom, also ibucsum, ibuhsum (“bendsome, flexible, pliant, obedient”), from Old English bōcsum, *būhsum, *ġebūhsum (“bendsome, pliant, obedient”), from Proto-West Germanic *beuhsam, *beugsam, equivalent to bow (“to bend, bow at the waist”) + -some or buck (“to bend, buckle, kick”) + -some.

s: An amusingly eccentric or irrational person.
e: From wacky + -o.
From divisive + -ness.

s: A tactic or artifice designed to gain the upper hand, especially one involving underhanded dealings or deception.
Specifically, such a tactic or artifice in military operation.
e: From Middle English stratageme, from Old French stratageme, from Latin strategema, from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (“the act of a general, a piece of generalship”), from στρατηγέω (“to be a general, command an army”), from στρατηγός (“a general, the leader or commander of an army”). See strategy.

s: To sew with long or loose stitches, as for temporary use, or in preparation for gathering the fabric.
To sprinkle flour and salt and drip butter or fat on, as on meat in roasting.
A basting; a sprinkling of drippings etc. in cooking.
To beat with a stick; to cudgel.
e: Late Middle English, from Old French bastir (“build, construct, sew up (a garment)”).
From Middle English basten, of uncertain etymon, possibly from Old French basser (“moisten, soak”), from bacin (“basin”).

From the surface, either an indigenous cognate or borrowed from; compare: Old Norse bausta, Icelandic beysta, Norwegian bøysta, Swedish bösta, bysta, Danish bøste (“to smack, thresh”), to a Proto-Germanic *baustjaną. Compare derivatives Old Norse bǫstl (“arrow”), Swedish böstel (“racket, pestle”), böste (“crowbar”).
From Middle English nobeliche,nobely,nobilliche,nobilly,nobliche,noblike,nobly,noblye, equivalent to noble + -ly.

s: The act or process of overreach (e.g. reaching beyond or extending past acceptable limits).
e: From overreach + -ing.
From overreach + -ing.
From incumbent + -cy.

s: Naturally and genuinely easy to get along with.
Making a show of friendliness; attempting to be on intimate terms but insincerely or inappropriately; cozying up.
In a close friendship or relationship.
On intimate terms but in an inappropriate way, for dishonest or selfish motives, etc.
A chimney sweep; or a sweep's assistant, especially a young boy.
Nickname for a person, especially a suspect or criminal.
A felt hat with a low crown.
A person or thing with a name that one cannot immediately recall.
e: From chum + -y.
From un- + feeling.

s: The spending of too much money.
A room intended for holding guests' cloaks and other heavy outerwear, as at a theater or night club.
A room intended for holding luggage, as at an airport.
A private lounge next to a legislative chamber.
A lavatory, now particularly a small secondary lavatory or a men's room.
e: From cloak + room.

s: An element of a lineage, especially of a lineage given in the Bible
An expression which inveighs or rails against a person.
A severe or violent censure or reproach.
Something spoken or written, intended to cast shame, disgrace, censure, or reproach on another.
e: From Middle French invective, from Medieval Latin invectiva (“abusive speech”), from Latin invectīvus, from invectus, perfect passive participle of invehō (“bring in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). See vehicle, and compare with inveigh.

s: A cup of coffee larger than grande, usually 20 ounces.
e: From the Italian venti (“twenty [ounces]”).

s: of tone in speech or writing
e: From folks + -y or folk + -sy.

s: enjoyment derived from observing someone else's misfortune; counterempathy.
e: An German Schadenfreude (“joy in the misfortune of others”), from Schaden (“damage, misfortune”) + Freude (“joy”). The word gained popularity in English in the late and likely entered mainstream usage through an episode of The Simpsons (more in citations).

s: A certain sport, similar to squash, but played with a bigger ball.
A ball used for this sport.
e: From racquet + ball.

s: Someone who writes speeches for others, especially as a profession.
e: From speech + writer.
From Middle English blythely, blyþely, bliþeliche, from Old English blīþelīċe (“gladly, blithely”), from Proto-West Germanic; compare Dutch blijdelijk. blithe + -ly.

s: The extent to which something is deniable.
e: From deny + -ability.

s: A person who assaults and robs others, especially in a public place.
A person who makes exaggerated faces, as a performance; a gurner.
A large crocodile, Crocodylus palustris, of southwest Asia, having a very broad wrinkled snout.
e: From mug + -er.

s: Exposing the bare or pantyhose-clad legs, especially the thighs.
e: From leg + -y.
From leg + -y.

s: Opposition to the spread of something, especially nuclear weapons.
e: From non- + proliferation.

s: To intrude unrightfully on someone else’s rights or territory.
To advance gradually beyond due limits.
e: From Middle English encrochen, from Old French encrochier (“to seize”), from Old French en- + croc (“hook”), of origin. More at crook.

s: To keep repeating a particular sound involuntarily during speech.
To utter with a stammer, or with timid hesitancy.
The involuntary repetition of a sound in speech.
A speech defect whereby someone speaks with a stammer
e: From Middle English stameren, from Old English stamerian, from Proto-West Germanic *stamrōn, from Proto-Germanic *stamrōną (“to stammer”). Compare German stammeln, Dutch stameren, Old Norse stammr. Doublet of stumble.

s: An act of multiplying by three.
A small landing area for helicopters.
e: From heli- + pad.

s: Inclined to consume a significant amount of alcohol.
Involving a large consumption of alcohol.
e: From booze + -y.

s: To make (a person, an animal, etc.) a captive; to take prisoner; to capture, to subdue.
To capture or control (the mind, etc.); to subdue, to subjugate.
To attract and hold (someone's) attention and interest; to charm, to entrance, to fascinate, to enchain.
Made captive; taken prisoner; captured, subdued.
e: Late Latin captīvātus, the perfect passive participle of captīvō (“to capture”), from Latin captīvus (“captive, prisoner”) (ultimately from capiō (“to capture, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to hold; to seize”)) + -ō. Equivalent to captive + -ate.
See Etymology 1. Equivalent to captive + -ate.

s: A person who believes in being prepared to survive and is actively preparing for possible future emergencies and disruptions in local, regional, national, or international social or political order.
e: From survival + -ist.

s: In a brazen (shamelessly shocking and offensive) manner.
e: From brazen + -ly.

s: Of, relating to, or practicing polygamy.
e: From poly + gamous.

s: Full of pep; energetic, cheerful, and vigorous; bouncy
A tree of species Agonis flexuosa, commonly known as Western Australian peppermint or peppermint tree.
e: From pep + -y.

s: Italian pasta-like dumpling(s) made of potato or semolina.
e: From Italian gnocchi, plural of gnocco (“dumpling”), related to nocchio (“knot (in wood)”), a borrowing from knohha (“knuckle, bone, knot”), from Proto-Germanic *knukô (“bone”), *kneukaz (“tuber, knuckle”), from Proto-Indo-European *gnew- (“knot, bundle”).

s: The act of making a previously legal activity illegal, the act of making something a criminal offence.
The act of turning someone into a criminal by making their activities illegal.
e: From criminal + -ization or criminalize + -ation.

s: Manmade objects that are short-lived (under usual conditions), usually because their design intent is to be inexpensively made and thus affordably bought, a goal that often is an engineering trade-off versus durability.
e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερᾰ, neuter plural form of ἐφήμερος.

s: Confined to the Earth; unable to leave Earth, either physically or spiritually.
e: From earth + -bound.

s: The repetition of consonant sounds or letters at the beginning of two or more words immediately succeeding each other, or at short intervals; such repetition specifically involving stressed syllables.
The recurrence of the same letters or sounds in accented parts of words, as in Anglo-Saxon alliterative meter.
e: From New Latin allīterātiō, from allīterātus, from allīterō, from Latin ad (“to, towards, near”) and lītera (“a letter”).

s: To reject or repudiate (an authority, a person, a court judgment, etc.).
Of a judge, juror, or prosecutor: to declare (oneself) unable to participate in a court case due to an actual or potential conflict of interest or lack of impartiality.
To object to (a judge, juror, or prosecutor) participating in a court case due to an actual or potential conflict of interest or lack of impartiality.
e: From Late Middle English recusen, from Old French recuser (modern French récuser (“to challenge; to impugn; (formal) to make an objection; (law) to recuse”), and from its etymon Latin recūsāre, the present active infinitive of recūsō (“to decline, refuse, reject; (law) to object to, protest”), from re- + causa (“cause, reason; (law) case, claim; etc.”) + -ō.

s: Haughty, pompous, snobbish; inclined to turn up one's nose.
Of an event, a thing, etc.: elite, exclusive.
Easily angered or irritated; irritable, short-tempered.
e: The is derived from snoot (“(UK, dialectal, and slang) snout; nose”) + -y, probably referring to a snobbish person often having their nose in the air (that is, acting disdainfully towards others). Snoot is a dialectal variant of snout. The is derived from the adjective.

s: A mottled appearance given to ribbons and silks in the process of dyeing.
A diversity of colours in yarn, recurring at regular intervals.
To release government control (of a business or industry) to private industry.
To render (a variable, etc.) private in scope.
To render a thought or an idea, private in scope.
e: From private + -ize.

s: The ability to shoot accurately at a target.
e: From marksman + -ship or marks + -manship.

s: Any small house or structure or enclosure used to house a dog.
A structure of small size, similar to a doghouse, but offering useful shelter for a human.
Mechanically, an equipment cover with an opening, with a shape resembling a doghouse.
A traffic signal with five sections: two on the bottom, two in the middle, and one on top.
The condition of being in the doghouse (subject to someone's anger or disapproval).
e: dog + house.

s: A type of light sweet pastry or bun of French origin.
A knitted cushion for the feet.
e: Borrowed from French brioche.

s: Seriousness in bearing or manner; dignity.
e: Borrowed from Latin gravitās (“weight, heaviness”). Doublet of gravity.

s: A game, often played by children, in which a player leaps like a frog over the back of another person who has stooped over. One variation of the game involves a number of people lining up in a row and bending over. The last person in the line then vaults forward over each of the others until they re
The process by which a case is appealed or allowed to be appealed directly to a supreme court, bypassing an intermediate appellate court.
To jump over some obstacle, as in the game of leapfrog.
To appeal or allow to be appealed (a case) directly to a supreme court, bypassing an intermediate appellate court.
To advance by engaging the enemy with one unit while another moves further forward.
e: From leap + frog.

s: To carry forward the stake and winnings from a bet on to a subsequent wager or series of wagers.
To increase (an asset, money, etc.) by gambling or investing in a daring manner.
To convert (a situation, thing, etc.) into something better.
A bet or series of bets where the stake and winnings are cumulatively carried forward; an accumulator.
Agent noun of possess; one who possesses
e: From possess + -or.
From diplomatic + -ally or diplomatical + -ly.

s: The path where a river runs, or where a river once ran; the bottom earthen part of a river, not including the riverbanks.
e: From river + bed. Compare Dutch rivierbedding (“riverbed”), German Flussbett (“riverbed”), Swedish flodbädd (“riverbed”).

s: A dry, or sweet apéritif wine flavored with aromatic herbs, and often used in mixed drinks.
e: From French vermout, vermouth, from German Wermut (“wormwood”). Doublet of wormwood.

s: Supplying electrical energy to (a component or device).
Leading to an increase in vitality and enthusiasm.
A variety of cultivated cherry (Prunus cerasus var. austera), having a dark skin
e: Probably either.

s: The act or process of reverting something.
The act or process of reverting a database to a prior state.
The action of returning to a former condition or practice.
The fact of being turned the reverse way.
The action of turning something the reverse way.
The return of an estate to the donor or grantor after expiry of the grant.
An estate which has been returned in this manner.
The right of succeeding to an estate, or to another possession.
The right of succeeding to an office after the death or retirement of the holder.
The return of a genetic characteristic after a period of suppression.
A sum payable on a person's death.
The act of conversion to Islam, due to the belief that all people are born Muslim.
e: Borrowed into late Middle English from Old French reversion (modern réversion), from Latin reversio, from revertō. revert + -sion.

s: To surround, form a circle around.
To move or go around completely.
e: From en- + circle.

s: Of one who, or something that, administers.
The act of one who ministers; ministration.
To exhibit a conspicuous (sometimes malevolent) pleasure or sense of self-satisfaction, often at an adversary's misfortune.
To triumph, crow, relish, glory, revel.
An act or instance of gloating.

e: From prohibitive + -ly.

s: A political philosophy maintaining that all persons are the absolute owners of their own lives, and should be free to do whatever they wish with their persons or property, provided they allow others that same liberty.
The doctrine of free will, as opposed to necessitarianism.
e: From libertarian + -ism.

s: The state of being contrite; sincere penitence or remorse.
The act of grinding or rubbing to powder.
e: From Old French contriciun (French contrition), from Latin contrītiō.

s: One who advocates or supports isolationism.
e: From isolation + -ist.

s: The quality of a sound independent of its pitch and volume.
The pitch of a sound as heard by the ear, described relative to its absolute pitch.
The crest on a (helmet atop a) coat of arms.
e: From French timbre, ultimately from Ancient Greek τύμπανον (“drum”). Doublet of tympanum, timpani, timbal, tymbal.

s: Having been blamed or criticized for wrongdoing.

e: From Middle English humanly; equivalent to humane + -ly..

s: A person who furthers the illicit love-affairs of others; a pimp or procurer.
An offer of illicit sex with a third party.
An illicit or illegal offer, usually to tempt.
One who ministers to the evil designs and passions of another.
To tempt with, to appeal or cater to (improper motivations, etc.); to assist in gratification.
To offer (something or someone) in order to tempt or appeal, especially to base or improper motivations.
To offer illicit sex with a third party; to pimp.
To act as a pander for (somebody).
e: From Middle English pandare, from Chaucer’s character Pandare (in Troilus and Criseyde; see also Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida), from Italian Pandaro (found in Boccaccio), from Latin Pandarus (found in Greek mythology), from Ancient Greek Πάνδαρος.

s: Mutually dependent; reliant on one another.
e: From inter- + dependent.

s: To argue for a better deal, especially over prices between a buyer and seller.
To stick at small matters; to chaffer; to higgle.
e: 1570s, "to cut unevenly" (implied in haggler), frequentative of Middle English haggen (“to chop”), variant of hacken (“to hack”), equivalent to hack + -le. Sense of "argue about price" first recorded c.1600, probably from notion of chopping away.

s: Done without consideration for morality or immorality.
Not believing in or caring for morality and immorality.
e: From a- (“not”) + moral.

s: An umbelliferous plant (Pimpinella anisum) growing naturally in Egypt, and cultivated in Spain, Malta, etc., for its carminative and aromatic seeds, which are used as a spice. It has a licorice scent.
often qualified as "sweet anise" or "wild anise"
e: From Middle English anys, borrowed from Old French anis, from Latin anīsum, from Ancient Greek ἄνισον, from Egyptian jnst.

s: To fail to see the difference; to mix up; to confuse right and wrong.
To combine in a confused fashion; to mingle so as to make the parts indistinguishable.
To cause to be ashamed; to abash.
To defeat, to frustrate, to thwart.
To destroy, ruin, or devastate; to bring to ruination.
e: From Middle English confounden (“destroy, ruin, perplex”), from Anglo-Norman cunfundre and Old French confondre, from Latin cōnfundō (“to mingle, mix together”). Related to found (“to melt (metals in a foundry)”) (but not to found (“to start”), nor to find) and to fusion.
From Middle English harsknes; equivalent to harsh + -ness.

s: A weight class in many combat sports; e.g. in professional boxing of a maximum of 126 pounds or 57.2 kilograms.
A sportsman who fights in this division.
The lightest weight that may be carried by a racehorse.
e: From feather + weight.

s: A table or tray scattered with sand which was used for calculating or drawing.

A device used for performing arithmetical calculations; a table on which loose counters are placed, or an instrument with beads sliding on rods, or counters in grooves, with one row of beads or counters representing units, the next tens, etc.
The uppermost portion of the capital of a column immediately under the architrave, in some cases a flat oblong or square slab, in others more decorated.
A board, tray, or table, divided into perforated compartments for holding bottles, cups, or the like; a kind of buffet, cupboard, or sideboard.

e: From let down.
From resiliō (“to spring back”) + -ency.

s: Expressing words or behaviors that one does not genuinely feel or endorse; not genuine; artificial; factitious.
e: From Latin insincerus.
From un- + affordable.

s: A lengthy and extravagant speech or argument usually intended to persuade.
An early form of rap music.
To give a sales pitch; to promote by speaking.
e: Borrowed from German Spiel (“game, performance”) or Yiddish שפּיל, both from Middle High German spil, from Old High German spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil. Cognate with Old English spilian (“to revel, play”). See speel.
From the Scots spiel (“game, play; curling match”) from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German spel.

s: An advantage or improvement that necessitates the corresponding loss or degradation of something else.
e: From trade off.

s: A blow or blows with the fist; a beating.
The act of hitting a ball hard; slogging.
The practice of smothering one's face with vaseline in order to moisturize it.
The state of being obsolete—no longer in use; gone into disuse; disused or neglected.
The process of becoming obsolete, outmoded or out of date.
e: From Latin obsolēscēns (present participle of obsolēscere).

s: The contents of a full truck or lorry.
e: From truck + load.

s: Having, characterized by, or done with good judgment or sound thinking.
e: From French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico. Related to judge, judicial.
A toponym from 1735–45 German Selterser (“of Selters”), after Selters, a village known for its carbonated mineral springs.
Of expressive origin, likely inspired by huge, with the termination of monstrous.

s: A clay earth pigment containing silica, aluminum and ferric oxide.
A somewhat dark yellowish orange colour.
Any of various brown-coloured hesperiid butterflies of the genus Trapezites.
Referring to cultures that covered their dead with ochre.
To cover or tint with ochre.
e: Thumb|right|An Australian ochre pit. From Old French ocre and its source Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (“pale yellow”), from ὠχρός (“pale, ocher”) (modern Greek ωχρός).
From an Unknown West African language, probably ọ́kụ̀rụ̀, but compare ŋkrũmã and ŋkrakra (“broth”).
From rabble + rousing.

s: In a steadfast manner; firmly; with conviction.
e: Inherited from Middle English stedefastly, stedefastliche; equivalent to steadfast + -ly.

s: An expert of law or someone who researches jurisprudence.
e: From Middle French juriste.

s: Causing a visceral sensation of panic or terror.
To deliberately remove the head of; to cut off (someone's) head.
e: From Middle English beheden, bihefden, biheveden, from Old English behēafdian (“to behead”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihaubudōn, *bihaubidōn (“to behead”), equivalent to be- (“off, away”) + head. Cognate with Middle High German behoubeten (“to behead”).

s: A Hindu monarch ranking above a raja, an emperor.
e: Borrowed from Hindi महाराजा.

s: An official providing honorable service in a royal or high noble household, ranking between a squire and a page. Especially, a yeoman of the guard, a member of a ceremonial bodyguard to the UK monarch (not to be confused with a Yeoman Warder).
A dependable, diligent, or loyal worker or someone who does a great service.
A former class of small freeholders who farm their own land; a commoner of good standing.
A subordinate, deputy, aide, or assistant.
A clerk in the US Navy, and US Coast Guard.
In a vessel of war, the person in charge of the storeroom.
A member of the Yeomanry Cavalry, officially chartered in 1794 originating around the 1760s.
A member of the Imperial Yeomanry, officially created in 1890s and renamed in 1907.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the genus Cirrochroa, of Asia and Australasia.
e: From Middle English yeman, yoman, of disputed etymology.
From Middle English unwasched, unwasschyd, unwessched, a weak verb conjugation of earlier Middle English unwaschen (“unwashen”), equivalent to un- + washed.

s: The act of one who plunders; pillaging or looting; plunder.
The state of being subjugated; forced control by others.
e: Borrowed from Latin subiugātiō, from Latin subiugō (“to subjugate”). subjugate + -ion.

s: Not funded; having received no funding.
Of a pension: paid out like a salary by the employer, without advance contributions from the employee.
e: From un- + funded.

s: The characteristic or practice of being a fanatic.
e: From fanatic + -ism.

s: Carrying a gun, especially a pistol.
The process by which an organism produces others of its biological kind
The sexual activity of conceiving and bearing biological offspring
e: From Old French procreacion, from Latin prōcreātiō (“generation”), the noun of action from prōcreāre (“to bring forth”), itself from prō- + creō..

s: Someone who oppresses another or others.
e: From Middle English oppressour, from Old French opressor and Latin oppressor; equivalent to oppress + -or.

s: A procession of cars carrying VIPs, especially political figures.
e: motor + cavalcade.

s: The act of trampling someone or something, an instance of trampling.
The phenomenon of making an unplanned, fortunate discovery through a combination of unexpected circumstances and insightful recognition.
An unsought, unintended or unexpected, but fortunate, discovery or learning experience that occurs by accident.
The occurrence and development of events by chance in a happy or beneficial way.
e: From Serendip (“variant of Serendib: Ceylon, Sri Lanka”) + -ity. Coined by Horace Walpole based on the Persian story of the Three Princes of Serendip, who (Walpole wrote to a friend) were “always making discoveries, by accidents and sagacity, of things which they were not in quest of”.

s: A delay, hindrance, or impediment; the act of holding back.
The act by which someone is detained; detention.
A sore or an ulcer of the skin.
The condition of something that festers; a festering; a festerment.
To become septic; to become rotten.
To worsen, especially due to lack of attention.
To cause to fester or rankle.
e: Inherited from Middle English festre, festur, borrowed from Old French festre (cognate with Italian fistola, Occitan fistola, Spanish fístula), from Latin fistula. The verb is derived from the noun, while the “condition of something that festers” noun sense is derived from the verb. Doublet of fistula.

s: To supply with energy, especially electricity; to turn on power to (something).
To use strength in action; to act or operate with force or vigor; to act in producing an effect.
e: From energy + -ize.

s: The act of one who confers.
To examine something with great care or detail, as to look for hidden or obscure flaws.
To audit accounts etc in order to verify them.
e: From scrutiny + -ize.

s: Someone or thing who lives in a place.
A possible value for a type.
e: From Middle English inhabitantes and inhabitaunt, from Old French inhabitant, from Latin inhabitāns, present participle of inhabitō (“to inhabit”), from in- (“in”) + habitō (“to dwell”) (frequentative of habeō (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *ghabh- (“to seize, take, hold, have”). inhabit + -ant.

s: Of, pertaining to, or suffering from anemia.
Weak; listless; lacking power, vigor, vitality, or colorfulness.
e: From anemia + -ic.

s: A hole formed in soluble rock by the action of water, serving to conduct surface water to an underground passage.
A depressed area in which waste or drainage collects.
A hole in the playfield that rewards the player when the ball is guided into it.
A domain name server that has been configured to hand out non-routeable addresses for all domains, so that every computer that uses it will fail to get access to the real website.
An attack which redirects requests, whether network or memory accesses, to a new location defined by the attacker.
To configure as a sinkhole (domain name server that gives non-routeable addresses).
e: From Middle English sinkehole, sinkeholl, equivalent to sink + hole.

s: To make sweet to the taste.
To make (more) pleasant or to the mind or feelings.
To make mild or kind; to soften.
To make less painful or laborious; to relieve.
To soften to the eye; to make delicate.
To make pure and healthful by destroying noxious matter.
To raise the pH of (a soil) by adding alkali.
To restore to purity; to free from taint.
To make more attractive; said of offers in negotiations.
To supplement (a composition) with additional instruments, especially strings.
e: From sweet + -en. Eclipsed non-native Middle English doucen and endoucen, borrowed from Old French adoucir and endoucir (“to sweeten”).

s: To make something happen suddenly and quickly.
To throw an object or person from a great height.
To send violently into a certain state or condition.
(chemistry) To come out of a liquid solution into solid form.
(chemistry) To separate a substance out of a liquid solution into solid form.
To have water in the air fall to the ground, for example as rain, snow, sleet, or hail; be deposited as condensed droplets.
To cause (water in the air) to condense or fall to the ground.
To act too hastily; to be precipitous.
With a hasty impulse; hurried; headstrong.
Moving with excessive speed or haste; overly hasty.
A product resulting from a process, event, or course of action.
A solid that exits the liquid phase of a solution.
e: From Latin praecipitātus, perfect passive participle of praecipitō (“throw down, hurl down, throw headlong”) (see -ate for more), from praeceps (“head foremost, headlong”) (praecipit- in its oblique stem), from prae (“before”) + -ceps (“headed”).
From Latin praecipitātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate for more).
From New Latin praecipitātum. Equivalent to praecipitō + -ate.

s: Not returned; not reciprocated; not repaid.
e: From un- + requited.

s: A dry measure, containing four pecks, eight gallons, or thirty-two quarts; equivalent in volume to approximately 0.0364 cubic meters (imperial bushel) or 0.0352 cubic meters (U.S. bushel).
A vessel of the capacity of a bushel, used in measuring; a bushel measure.
A quantity that fills a bushel measure.
The iron lining in the nave of a wheel.
To pack grain, hops, etc. into bushel measures.
e: From Middle English busshel, from Old French boissel, from boisse, a grain measure based on *bostyā (“handful”), from Proto-Celtic *bostā (“palm, fist”) (compare Breton boz (“hollow of the hand”), Old Irish bas), from Proto-Indo-European *gwost-, *gwosdʰ- (“branch”).

s: The state of being in poor condition, in need of repair.
To get into a state of disrepair.
e: From dis- + repair.

s: Not intentional; not on purpose; not conscious.
e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin inadvertēns, back-formation from inadvertence, from in-, advertent.

s: A condition of total, interlocking traffic congestion on the streets or highways of a crowded city, in which no one can move because everyone is in someone else's way.

On a smaller scale, the situation in which cars enter a signal-controlled intersection too late during the green light cycle, and are unable to clear the intersection (due to congestion in the next block) when the light turns red, thus blocking the cross traffic when it's their turn to go. Repeated
Any paralysis of a complex system due to severe congestion, conflict or deadlock.
e: From grid + lock.

s: Specified (especially when fully specified) by an enumeration or list of steps, parts, values, amounts, etc.
Defined to consist of a specified list of possible values.
Having been included or listed in an enumeration of possibilities.
Having one of the possible values specified in advance for a type defined by an enumeration.
Having been specified by a precise numeric value.
Youth; the condition of being immature or not fully grown
e: Borrowed from Latin immaturitas.

s: In a fiscal manner; concerning finance.
e: From fiscal + -ly.

s: A person who habitually scolds, in particular a troublesome and angry woman.
Of birds, to make harsh vocalisations in aggression.
Of birds, to make vocalisations that resemble human scolding.
e: The noun is from Middle English scold(e), skald(e), first attested in the 12th or 13th century (as scold, scolde, skolde, skald). The verb is from Middle English scolden, first attested in the late 1300s.

s: Something, such as a towel, that is used for wiping.
Something, such as a windscreen wiper, that is designed for wiping.
A movable electric contact in some devices.
A program or process that erases data.
A junior role in the engine room of a ship, someone who wipes down machinery and generally keeps it clean.
A hybrid fish variety artificially bred from eggs of striped bass (Morone saxatilis) fertilized with white bass (Morone chrysops) sperm, or the opposite combination.
e: From wipe + -er.
From white (bass) and striper.

s: A bet in which the bettor must select the first three placegetters of a race in the order in which they finish.
The attainment of three important achievements, qualities, etc.
A set of three related things, often things that cause problems.
The complete legislative and executive control of state or federal government by one party: governorship, the upper house and the lower house of state or federal legislatures.
e: From tri- (per)fecta.

s: A dummy or other crude representation of a person, group or object that is hated.
e: From French effigie, from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).

s: Those qualities or features that are imperfect; the characteristic, state, or quality of being imperfect.
Something that makes something else less than perfect; a blemish, impurity, error, etc.
e: From Old French imperfeccion, from Latin imperfectiōnem, accusative of imperfectiō, from in- + perfectiō. im- + perfection.

s: A machine that is complicated and precarious.
e: Possibly a Western US English dialectal word of Unknown origin.. Perhaps from contrive + trap + -tion, while also possibly approximating construction. Chambers suggests contrivance + adaption.
